# QUILL User Guide

## Introduction

Welcome, and thank you for giving QUILL a try.

QUILL is a writing studio for Windows and macOS, made for people who use a
screen reader. I am blind, I use one every day, and I wanted an editor that
was built around the keyboard and the ear from the very first line. QUILL is
what came of that. You can write in it, of course. You can also open almost
any document, have it read to you, dictate into it, check its spelling,
compare two drafts, tidy up a scanned PDF, turn a manuscript into an
audiobook, and a good deal more, all without reaching for the mouse.

The name stands for **Quality, Usable, Inclusive, Lightweight, Literate**.
QUILL is free, and it is made by Community Access.

This guide is written for QUILL 1.0.0. QUILL 1.0 is not out yet, so now and
then the guide may describe something your copy does not have. QUILL is still
in beta, which means you will find rough edges and the odd surprise. If
something confuses you or does not work, please tell us. Chapter 15 shows you
how, and every report makes QUILL better for the next person.

### What you will be able to do

By the time you have read this guide you will be able to open, write and save
documents in all the common formats, and move around a long document by
heading, paragraph or bookmark. You will know how to search and replace,
check your spelling, format text, and have QUILL read your work back to you.
You will be able to dictate, transcribe a recording, and, if you want it, ask
the AI for help with a piece of writing. You will have QUILL set up to say as
much or as little as you like, with your own keys and your own choice of
features. And when something puzzles you, you will know where to find help.

None of this needs to happen on day one. Chapter 1 gets you writing in a few
minutes. Everything after that is there for when you are curious.

### How this guide is laid out

The chapters follow the order you are likely to want things. Read from the
beginning if you are new to QUILL, or jump to the chapter for the job in front
of you.

1. [Chapter 1: Your first session](#chapter-1-your-first-session). A short,
   hand-held start: write something, save it, and learn the handful of keys
   that do most of the work.
2. [Chapter 2: Finding your way around](#chapter-2-finding-your-way-around).
   The window, the status bar, F1 help, the Command Palette, the QUILL key,
   and a tour of the menus.
3. [Chapter 3: Opening, saving and converting files](#chapter-3-opening-saving-and-converting-files).
   Every format QUILL reads and writes, converting between them, and files on
   other computers and on GitHub.
4. [Chapter 4: Writing and editing](#chapter-4-writing-and-editing). Selecting,
   copying, the Copy Tray, inserting dates, symbols and emoji, abbreviations,
   and links.
5. [Chapter 5: Formatting, structure and markup](#chapter-5-formatting-structure-and-markup).
   Headings, lists, tables, Markdown and HTML, maths and citations.
6. [Chapter 6: Moving around and finding things](#chapter-6-moving-around-and-finding-things).
   Find and replace, jumping by heading, bookmarks and marks, Quick Nav mode,
   and Quill Eraser.
7. [Chapter 7: Spelling and words](#chapter-7-spelling-and-words). Spell
   checking, the thesaurus, the dictionary and document statistics.
8. [Chapter 8: Reading, reviewing and listening](#chapter-8-reading-reviewing-and-listening).
   Read Aloud, Reveal Codes, comparing documents, OCR, audiobooks and keeping
   your place.
9. [Chapter 9: Dictation and transcription](#chapter-9-dictation-and-transcription).
   Speaking into a document and turning recordings into text, on your own
   computer.
10. [Chapter 10: AI, when you want it](#chapter-10-ai-when-you-want-it). The
    free AI, your own keys, the assistant, and exactly what is sent where.
11. [Chapter 11: Accessibility, speech and braille](#chapter-11-accessibility-speech-and-braille).
    How much QUILL says, low-vision settings, sounds, braille files and GLOW.
12. [Chapter 12: Making QUILL yours](#chapter-12-making-quill-yours). Feature
    profiles, keyboard packs, your own keys, Quillins and languages.
13. [Chapter 13: Keeping your work safe](#chapter-13-keeping-your-work-safe).
    Autosave, recovery, restore points, sessions and safe mode.
14. [Chapter 14: Projects, notes and the QuillVille family](#chapter-14-projects-notes-and-the-quillville-family).
    Story Studio, the Vault, sticky notes, Git, Mastodon, and the apps that

    F1, tutorials, updates, release channels and getting help from a person.

After the chapters come the appendices: the Developer Console, writing your
own AI skills, the full list of emoji QUILL can insert, notes from earlier
versions, and the Developer Console's design document. Last of all are the
[Glossary of QUILL Terms](#glossary-of-quill-terms) and
[Getting help](#getting-help).

QUILL also has guided tutorials, short lessons you do with QUILL open in front
of you, on **Help > Tutorials...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F1`). Whenever a lesson covers
the same ground as part of this guide, the chapter gives you its name, so you
can choose between reading about something and being walked through it. If
you would rather learn by listening, [QUILL, Step by Step](quill-step-by-step.md)
is a slower companion book written to be read aloud, one skill per chapter.

Now and then a short note from QUILLBee, QUILLVille's guide, is set apart as
a quote: a faster key, a word explained, or something worth knowing before it
catches you out. QUILLBert, the curious porcupine, wanders in once or twice
when he has found something. The guide reads perfectly well if you skip every
one of them, and you can meet the pair properly on the [Meet QUILLBert and
QUILLBee](https://www.quillforall.org/meet-quillbert-and-quillbee.html) page.

### Reading this guide with a screen reader

The guide is built from headings so you can move through it quickly. Each
chapter is a level 2 heading, and the main topics in a chapter are level 3
headings. When a topic has parts of its own, those parts sit one level deeper,
at level 4, and sometimes at level 5. In JAWS or NVDA, press 2 to move from
chapter to chapter, 3 to move between the main topics, and 4 to step through
the parts of a topic. Shift with any of those numbers goes back. To see every
heading at once, press Insert+F6 in JAWS or Insert+F7 in NVDA and choose
headings.

The notes from QUILLBee and QUILLBert are block quotes. In a web browser, Q
moves to the next one in JAWS and NVDA, and Shift+Q goes back, so they are as
easy to skip as they are to find.

Every chapter ends with a short section called What you learned, and where to
go next. If you are skimming, those are a quick way to hear what a chapter
covers before you read it.

Keys are written the way QUILL writes them in its menus. `Ctrl+Shift+P` means
hold down Ctrl and Shift together and press P. A menu path such as
**File > Save As...** means open the File menu and choose Save As. If you
have changed a key in QUILL, your key is the one that works; **Help > Open
Keyboard Reference** always lists the keys you have right now.

When a section walks you through something, the steps are numbered. Follow
them with QUILL open beside the guide and you will learn faster than by
reading alone. Alt+Tab moves you between the two.

You do not always need this guide to answer a question. Press `F1` on almost
anything in QUILL, a field, a button, a menu item or the editor itself, and
QUILL tells you what it does and which keys go with it.

## Chapter 1: Your first session

This chapter is your first sit-down with QUILL, and I will stay with you the
whole way. You will open QUILL, write a few lines, save them, and meet the
handful of keys that do most of the work. If you have never used QUILL before,
start here. If you have, skim the key list near the end and move on to Chapter
2.

### Getting started

If you only have five minutes, do this.

1. The first time QUILL starts, the **Personalise QUILL** wizard offers to set
   up your keyboard layout, your profile and any optional features you want. It
   takes about two minutes. Finish it, or close it and come back later from
   **Help > Personalise QUILL...** whenever you like.
2. Press `Ctrl+N` to make a new document, or `Ctrl+O` to open one you already
   have.
3. Type a few lines.
4. Press `Ctrl+Shift+P` to open the Command Palette. Type `guide`, `spell`,
   `compare` or `glow`, and listen to how quickly QUILL finds what you meant.
5. Press `F6` to move out of the editor and on towards the status bar along the
   bottom of the window. QUILL treats that strip as a place you can work, not
   just something to read. `Shift+F6` brings you back.
6. Try `F7` for spell check, `Ctrl+F` to search, or `Ctrl+K` to insert a link.
7. Press `F1` on any control to hear what it does and which keys work there.

If you ever feel lost, `F1` is the first thing to try. For ideas about the
document you have open, choose **Help > What Can I Do Here?**
(`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F1`). Between them, they are like having a friend at your
elbow.

> **QUILLBee's tip:** Forgotten where something lives? Press `Ctrl+Shift+P` and
> type a word, like "sort" or "print". The palette says each command's key as
> you arrow past it, so you pick up the keys while you work.

### What QUILL is like to use

A few promises shape everything in QUILL.

- The keyboard always comes first.
- Screen readers are part of the plan from the start, never an add-on.
- Every major action can be reached from the menus, from the Command Palette and
  through the command system.
- Your documents open on your computer and stay there, unless you choose an
  action that uses the network.
- QUILL tells you what changed, where you are and what you can do next.

In day-to-day use, that means QUILL pays a lot of attention to where your focus
goes, gives you status updates that mean something, makes commands easy to
discover, and uses the standard Windows controls your screen reader already
knows. It also tries hard to take the worry out of things. Opening a recovered
draft, comparing two files or checking how well text came out of a scanned
document are all made to be safe and easy to undo.

### A first proper session

Here is what your first real visit to QUILL is likely to look like.

You start QUILL. There is no splash screen to wait through. The window appears
quickly, with a menu bar across the top, the editor in the middle and a status
bar along the bottom. If QUILL finds a screen reader running, it adjusts its
hints and the way it announces things to suit. If QUILL finds signs of an
earlier crash, or work it saved automatically, it offers to recover it for you
straight away.

From there, a good first session goes like this.

1. Open a file with `Ctrl+O`, or make a new one with `Ctrl+N`. If you would like
   a smaller file picker that is easier to use with a screen reader, open
   Preferences (`Ctrl+,`), go to **General** and turn on
   **Use simple file open dialog**.
2. Read or write in the editor.
3. Press `Ctrl+Shift+P` and explore commands, without memorising anything.
4. Open the **Navigate** menu to jump by line, heading, block, region or page.
5. Open the **Tools** menu for spelling, word count, checking extracted text,
   comparing files, macros and help with regular expressions.
6. Choose **Help > Open Keyboard Reference** to see every shortcut that works in
   your setup right now. QUILL builds this reference on the spot, so it always
   matches your current feature profile and any keys you have changed.

The habit this teaches is the most useful one in QUILL: you do not need to go
hunting. If QUILL can do something, you can reach it from wherever you are.

> **QUILLBert found something.** He pressed `Ctrl+Shift+Grave` twice in a row to
> see what would happen, and suddenly every letter he typed moved him around the
> document instead of writing. H took him to a heading, P to a paragraph. That
> is Quick Nav, and it stays on until you press `Esc`, which is how he got his
> typing back. Chapter 2 explains the QUILL key properly.

### The keys that do most of the work

If you want a small set of keys to learn first, start with these.

- `Ctrl+N` new document, `Ctrl+O` open, `Ctrl+S` save, `Ctrl+Shift+S` save as.
- `Ctrl+Shift+P` the Command Palette.
- `Ctrl+F` find, `F3` find next, `Shift+F3` find previous. `Alt+F3` turns Reveal
  Codes on and off, so you can hear the formatting that is normally hidden.
- `Ctrl+G` go to a line. `Ctrl+Shift+G` Document Statistics, the word count and
  more.
- `Ctrl+K` insert a link, `Ctrl+Enter` follow the link at the cursor.
- `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, L` (press the QUILL key, then L) for the List Manager,
  `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+L` for the Structured List Studio, and `Ctrl+Shift+F2` for
  Insert Special Character.
- `Ctrl+F9` starts and stops Locked Dictation, and `Alt+F9` says what dictation
  is doing.
- `F9` says the last result again, if you missed it.
- `F7` spell check, `Ctrl+F7` next misspelling, `Ctrl+Shift+F7` previous
  misspelling, `Shift+F7` the thesaurus.
- `Ctrl+Tab` and `Ctrl+Shift+Tab` move between open documents.
- `F6` and `Shift+F6` move between the parts of the window.
- `Alt+Z` turns soft wrap on and off.

When those feel familiar, open **Help > Open Keyboard Reference** and let QUILL
show you the rest, taken from the keys you actually have.

### What you learned, and where to go next

You have opened QUILL, written something, found commands by name with the
Command Palette, and met the keys you will use every day. You also know the two
ways out of any muddle: `F1` on whatever you are on, and
**Help > What Can I Do Here?**.

If you would like to go over this with QUILL keeping you company, open
**Help > Tutorials...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F1`) and take the track called Your first
hour. Its lessons "Write and save your first document", "Do anything by name"
and "Getting unstuck" follow this chapter closely. On the website, [Your first
hour with QUILL](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/01-your-first-hour.html)
walks the same ground at a gentler pace.

When you are ready, Chapter 2, Finding your way around, takes you on a tour of
the window, the menus and the QUILL key.

## Chapter 2: Finding your way around

This chapter is a walk around QUILL. You will learn how to get help on whatever
you are on, how to run any command by name, how the QUILL key opens up the rest
of QUILL, and what lives where in the window and the menus. Read it once from
top to bottom, then come back to it whenever you wonder where something is.

### Getting around QUILL

QUILL is built so you never have to memorise an action to reach it. Three things
carry most of the load: `F1` for help on what you are on, the Command Palette
for running anything by name, and the QUILL key for the bigger features.

#### Help on the focused control (F1)

Press `F1` on anything that can take focus, whether that is a field in a dialog,
a button, a menu item or the editor itself, and a small help window opens. It
tells you what the control does and which keys work there. All of the text sits
in one read-only field, so your screen reader reads the whole thing as soon as
the window opens.

The help keys are:

- `F1` help on the focused control.
- `Ctrl+Shift+F1` open the full User Guide.
- `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F1` open **What Can I Do Here?**, ideas for the document you
  have open.
- `Ctrl+F1` the Key Cheatsheet, a list of shortcuts.
- `Shift+F1` About QUILL.

Chapter 15, Help, updates and support, covers context-sensitive help in full.

F1 works the same way in every QuillVille app: Radio, Cast, the Media Player,
Audio Studio, Inkwell, Weather, the Converter and Beacon. It answers two
questions at once. First it says what the *window* you are in is for, in a
sentence or two written for that window. Then it describes the *control* under
your cursor: what it wants, what format it expects, what its default is and what
changing it affects. A field that asks for a number of seconds says so, and says
which number it starts at.

Some controls already explain themselves by name, such as "Reload the
highlighted source from the internet". For those, F1 gives you the name plus a
line on how to work that kind of control ("A list: Up and Down move between
rows, Enter acts on the row, and Shift+F10 lists everything else you can do to
it"). Nothing answers F1 with silence.

If you would rather read it all in one place, every help sentence in the family
is collected in [the F1 help reference](../f1-help-reference.md). The default
keyboard shortcuts have a companion document, [the keyboard
reference](../keyboard-reference.md). Both are made from the app itself, so they
always match what QUILL really does.

#### The Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P)

`Ctrl+Shift+P` opens the Command Palette, a list of every command in QUILL that
you can search. Type any part of a command's name to narrow the list, then press
Enter to run it. It is the quickest way to any action when you do not know its
key or where it lives in the menus. Searching for `guide`, `spell`, `compare` or
`glow` is good practice. You can also open it from
**Tools > Command Palette...**.

Your search can be looser than the exact name:

- Words can come in any order. `url open` and `open url` both find
  **Open From URL...**.
- A shortcut works as a search. `ctrl+o` finds Open.
- Everyday words are understood. `settings` finds **Preferences...**, and `quit`
  finds **Exit**.

As you arrow through the results, QUILL says each command's shortcut along with
its name. Before long you will find you reach for the key and not the palette.

Every on/off command in the palette says which way it is set right now, for
example **Toggle Soft Wrap (currently On)** and
**Toggle Dark Mode (currently Off)**. The same goes for find wrap, the tab
control, persistent undo, spell check as you type, word prediction, overwrite
mode, extend-selection mode, tab insert mode, abbreviation expansion and more. A
menu can show a check mark, but a list in the palette cannot, so the state goes
in the name. You never have to flip a switch just to find out which way it was.

When a command cannot run right now, the palette tells you why. A command
switched off by a safety update reads as "(unavailable: Turned off by a safety
update: ...)", and trying to run it says the reason again.

The palette learns from you, too. The commands you use most rise towards the top
of the list.

##### Palette search modes

Start your search with one of these characters to change how the palette looks:

- Normal search, or `>`, searches all commands.
- `:` searches command IDs.
- `?` favours commands that have a key.
- `~` puts recently used commands first.

#### The QUILL key

The **QUILL key** is `Ctrl+Shift+Grave`. The grave key is the back-tick key,
just above Tab. Press it, then one more key, and you reach most of QUILL's
bigger features without leaving the keyboard.

Everywhere QUILL shows one of these keys, in menus, in
**About > Keyboard Reference**, in the QUILL Key Help dialog, on the cheat sheet
and in the status bar, it writes it as `QUILL Key + <key>`: `QUILL Key + S`,
`QUILL Key + Shift+O` and so on. When you type one into the Keymap Editor you
write it as `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, <key>`. Both mean the same thing.

The QUILL key works in two ways.

1. **Prefix Mode (One-shot).** Press it once and QUILL waits a moment for your
   next key. That key runs a command, such as `G` to open a file from a
   favorite folder or `M` to
   paste rich text as Markdown, and then QUILL goes back to normal.
2. **Browse Mode (Locked).** Press the QUILL key twice in a row and QUILL locks
   **Quick Nav (Browse) mode** on. Now single letters move you through the
   document: `H` for headings, `P` for paragraphs, `S` for sentences and more.
   It stays on until you press `Esc`.

Every one of these chords can be changed in the Keymap Editor, which the next
topic covers. The full cheat sheet is one key away: `QUILL Key + ?`.

##### The QUILL key chords

These are the chords QUILL starts with.

- `QUILL Key + N` Quick Nav (browse) mode for your next move. If
  **Sticky browse mode** (the `browse_mode_sticky` setting) is on, it stays
  locked until `Esc`. Otherwise it ends when the QUILL key times out.
- `QUILL Key` pressed twice locks Quick Nav on until `Esc`, whatever that
  setting says. This is the way most people use it: the first press gets QUILL
  ready, the second locks browse mode.
- `QUILL Key + G` opens **Open From Favorite Folder...**. (Go to Anything is
  `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+A`, and the Quick Nav landmark list is `Ctrl+Shift+Z`.)
- `QUILL Key + M` pastes the rich HTML on the clipboard as Markdown at the
  cursor.
- `QUILL Key + V` opens the browser preview of the current document.
- `QUILL Key + A` opens selection actions when text is selected. With nothing
  selected, it expands an abbreviation by hand in the middle of a word.
- `QUILL Key + Shift+A` opens the abbreviation manager.
- `QUILL Key + Shift+1` to `Shift+9`, then `Shift+0`, `Shift+-` and `Shift+=`
  copy the selection to slots 1 to 12 of the Copy Tray.
- `QUILL Key + ?` shows the QUILL key cheat sheet.
- `QUILL Key + Esc` cancels the QUILL key without running anything.

A few things that once had a QUILL key chord have moved:

- Opening from, saving to and managing remote sites (FTP, SFTP, HTTPS, WebDAV,
  S3 and GitHub) have no key to start with. Find them under
  **File > Open from Remote**, or give them a key of your own. (These were
  `QUILL Key + Shift+O`, `QUILL Key + W` and `QUILL Key + Shift+M`.)
- Turning abbreviation expansion on or off is `Alt+Shift+A`.
- The Copy Tray dialog is `Ctrl+Alt+V`.
- Switching the Tab key between indenting and typing a tab character is
  `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I`.

##### Hearing the QUILL key

When you press the QUILL key, QUILL plays a short double ping that sounds like
nothing else, so you know it is ready before any speech arrives. The sound is in
every sound pack that comes with QUILL, and you can switch it off on its own in
**Tools > Reading and Dictation > Sound Scheme...** (this used to be called
Sound Events).

Some keyboards and drivers report the grave key in unusual ways. QUILL checks
for it three different ways, so it recognises the key on any layout.

On macOS, use the physical **Control** key for the QUILL key, not Cmd.
`Cmd+Shift+Grave` is macOS's own shortcut for cycling windows, and QUILL never
sees it. If you would rather use Cmd, change that system shortcut first in
**System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > Mission Control**.

##### Moving a QUILL key chord

1. Open the Keymap Editor, from
   **Tools > Customize and Support > Keymap Editor...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R`).
2. Find the command you want to move.
3. Type the new chord in the form `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, X`, putting the key you
   want in place of `X`.

The Keymap Editor stores chords in that `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, X` form, and menus
and the cheat sheet show them as `QUILL Key + X`. If the chord you pick is
already in use, QUILL tells you before anything is overwritten.

### The Keyboard Manager

The Keymap Editor, also called the Keyboard Manager, is where you see and change
every key in QUILL. Open it from
**Tools > Customize and Support > Keymap Editor...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R`), or
from the Keymap Editor entry in More Preferences (the QUILL key, then `O`). It is made to be quick
and safe to use, however you think about shortcuts.

- **Search two ways from one box.** Type part of a command's name to narrow the
  list. Or type a *shortcut*, such as `ctrl+alt+m`, `Control + Shift + K`, or
  even a QUILL key chord like `quill, s`. The editor then tells you which
  command that key belongs to, or that it is "unassigned and available". You
  never have to remember whether a key is free. Just ask.
- **Forgiving spelling.** Write the modifiers however you like: `control`,
  `ctrl` or `ctl`, in any order (`shift+ctrl+k` is the same as `ctrl+shift+k`)
  and in any case. QUILL tidies up what you type before saving it. A Mac-style
  `Cmd` stays separate from `Ctrl` and is never mixed up with it.
- **Record Keys.** Would you rather press the keys than spell them? Choose
  **Record Keys**, press the chord, and QUILL fills it in for you.
- **Clear warnings when a key is taken.** If you choose a key that another
  command already has, QUILL tells you that command's name and offers to move
  the key over, taking it off the other command. Nothing is replaced behind your
  back.
- **Diagnostics and repair.** **Run Diagnostics** checks your whole keymap. It
  reports duplicate shortcuts, keys for commands that no longer exist, bindings
  it cannot read, and any key that is "assigned but inert", meaning the editor
  cannot actually use it. For the problems it can fix, one press of **Heal**
  removes the bad entries and reapplies your keymap, so the menus and the
  shortcuts agree again.

### The Main Window

QUILL's main window is kept simple: a menu bar across the top, the editor in the
middle and a status bar along the bottom. When you have several documents open
you can also show a row of tabs, which the Windows and tabs topic, later in this
chapter, covers.

#### The menu bar

The menus run across the top of the window in the order you know from Windows
and Office: File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Navigate, Tools, AI, Window,
QuillVille and Help. There used to be a Search menu as well. Its commands now
live under **Edit > Search Tools**.

Every menu and every menu item can be reached from the keyboard. Press `Alt`
with the menu's underlined letter: `Alt+F` for File, `Alt+E` for Edit, `Alt+V`
for View, `Alt+T` for Tools, `Alt+W` for Window and `Alt+H` for Help.

The menus cover everything. If QUILL can do something, there is almost always a
menu item for it. The menus topic, later in this chapter, says what each one
holds.

#### The editor

The editor is the heart of QUILL. It is where you write, where text taken from
other files lands, and where reports and comparison summaries open, as ordinary
documents you can read and edit like any other.

The editor handles:

- plain text writing
- Markdown-aware writing
- HTML-aware writing
- moving by the structure of the document
- selection helpers
- cleaning up text
- spelling and the thesaurus
- inserting and following links
- reviewing changes after a comparison

#### The status bar

The status bar is something you can work in, not just a strip of text to read.

Press `F6` to move into it. Once you are there, you can move between its cells
and press Enter on one, and most cells open a related window. `Shift+F6` takes
you back to the editor. Depending on your layout and what you are doing, the
status bar can show:

- the current message
- line and column
- word count
- insert or overwrite mode
- tab mode (whether the Tab key indents the line or types a tab character)
- selection size
- encoding
- line endings
- spell-check state
- background tasks
- notifications
- read-aloud state
- autosave timing
- the current search term
- the file path, or that the file is unsaved

You can reorder the cells or hide some of them in
**Tools > Customize and Support > Status Bar Layout...**. **Restore Defaults**
there puts every cell back the way it started.

Open the context menu on a status cell (right-click, `Shift+F10` or the
Applications key) to **Activate** it, **Hide this item**, or open
**Status bar settings...**. On the **Notifications** cell (or the
**Background Tasks** cell) the menu also has **Clear All Notifications**, which
empties the notification list in one go without opening the dialog.

The status bar never says the same thing twice. When the title bar is set to
show the full path, QUILL hides the file path cell. The current message cell
hides itself too, whenever its text is exactly the same as another cell you can
see.

To hide or show the whole status bar, use **View > Status Bar**, described in
View and display, later in this chapter.

#### Moving between regions (F6)

`F6` and `Shift+F6` move you between the main parts of the window. If you write,
check and move around entirely from the keyboard, this soon becomes second
nature.

When **Show Tab Control** is on (in the View menu) and at least one document is
open, the row of document tabs joins the `F6` cycle as **Document Tabs**, so you
can reach the tabs from the keyboard instead of skipping past them. The order is
the editor, then Document Tabs, then the preview (when you have it open beside
the editor), then the status bar. On the tab row, Left and Right Arrow move
between tabs, and Enter, Space or Tab takes you back to the editor on the
document you chose.

#### The Tab key, indent or tab character

Out of the box, the **Tab** key indents. It adds one level of indentation at the
start of the current line, or of every line you have selected, and **Shift+Tab**
takes one level away. On a Markdown list item, Tab and Shift+Tab move the item
in and out a level. QUILL speaks each of these, so you hear that the line moved
even though the cursor stays where it was.

When you indent with Tab, or outdent with Shift+Tab, QUILL says how deep the
line now sits, for example "4 spaces", "8 spaces" or "1 tab". If you would
rather just hear "Indented lines", turn off
**Announce indentation depth on Tab** in Preferences, under **Accessibility**.

Two settings decide what an indent is made of, both in Preferences:

- **Indent size** is the number of spaces per indent level, from 1 to 8. The
  default is 4.
- **Indent with tabs** makes QUILL insert tab characters instead of spaces.

Whichever you choose, the spoken depth follows it.

If you would rather Tab typed a real tab character at the cursor, the way it
does in a plain text editor, switch **Tab Mode** with `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I`, or
with **Format > Tab Key Inserts Tab Character**, which is ticked while the mode
is on. QUILL says the new mode when you switch, and the **Tab Mode** cell in the
status bar shows **Indent** or **Tab char**. Even while Tab types a tab
character, Shift+Tab still outdents, so you can take back a stray indent without
leaving the mode. Tab Mode lasts until you close QUILL.

### The menus

Here is what each menu holds and which chapter tells you more. They are listed
in the order they sit on the menu bar.

#### File

File is where documents begin and end: new, open, save and save as, recent files
and favourite folders, opening from a web address or over SSH and remote sites,
snapshots, publishing, and importing and exporting other formats. Chapter 3,
Opening, saving and converting files, covers all of it.

#### Edit

Edit holds the everyday editing commands, along with selection tools, the Copy
Tray and **Edit > Search Tools**, which has what used to be the Search menu.
Chapter 4, Writing and editing, covers editing and selection, and Chapter 6,
Moving around and finding things, covers Search Tools.

#### View

View changes how your document is shown without changing what is in it: soft
wrap, the tab row, the status bar, text size, previews and Reveal Codes. It is
covered later in this chapter, under View and display.

#### Insert

Insert puts things into your document: headings, lists, the date and time, links
and special characters. Chapter 4, Writing and editing, covers it.

#### Format

Format holds font, size, alignment, colour and paragraph settings, along with
changing case, working on lines, sorting, whitespace, HTML and Markdown, and the
document's language. Chapter 5, Formatting, structure and markup, covers it.

#### Navigate

Navigate gathers the ways to move around a document: go to line, go to heading,
go to an entry in a notebook, the Heading Organizer, the Outline Navigator, back
and forward through places you have been, and next and previous by structure. It
also has bookmarks, folding and sticky notes. When you need to get around a long
document, start here. Chapter 6, Moving around and finding things, covers it.

#### Tools

Tools is QUILL's workshop, for jobs that are more than plain editing. The
Command Palette is here, along with spelling and writing tools (Chapter 7,
Spelling and words), reading, comparison and inspection tools (Chapter 8,
Reading, reviewing and listening), speech and dictation (Chapter 9, Dictation
and transcription), and braille and accessibility (Chapter 11, Accessibility,
speech and braille). **Tools > Customize and Support** is where you make QUILL
your own (Chapter 12, Making QUILL yours), and Story Studio, the Vault and Git
are covered in Chapter 14, Projects, notes and the QuillVille family.

#### AI

AI holds the optional assistant: proofreading, changing the selected text,
translation, reading aloud, transcribing audio and more. Nothing in it runs
unless you choose it. Chapter 10, AI, when you want it, covers it.

#### Window

Window lists your open documents and lets you move between them, open a new tab,
close the others, or send QUILL to the system tray. It is covered later in this
chapter, under Windows and tabs.

#### QuillVille

QuillVille opens the other apps in the QUILL family, each on a key of its own:

- **Open Quill Radio** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F7`)
- **Open Quill Weather** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F8`)
- **Open Quill Cast** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9`)
- **Open Audio Studio** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F10`)
- **Open Quill Converter** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F11`), which changes audio and
  video files from one format to another
- **Open Quill Inkwell** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F12`)

If an app is not on your computer yet, QUILL offers to download it for you.
Chapter 14, Projects, notes and the QuillVille family, says more.

#### Help

Help has help on the control you are on, **What Can I Do Here?**, the tutorials,
the User Guide, the keyboard reference, **Personalise QUILL...**, feature
profiles, checking for updates and ways to get support. Chapter 15, Help,
updates and support, covers it.

### Windows and tabs

QUILL lets you have many documents open at once. Each one gets its own tab, and
QUILL opens things it makes for you as tabs too. The welcome guide, the keyboard
reference and a comparison summary all open as ordinary tabs, right beside the
work that produced them.

#### Tabs and document switching

- `Ctrl+Tab` and `Ctrl+Shift+Tab` move to the next and previous document.
- `Ctrl+W` closes the document you are in.
- The context menu on a tab lets you close that tab, close the other tabs, or
  close the tabs to its right.
- The same menu can show a saved document in File Explorer.

To see the row of tabs, turn on **Show Tab Control** in the View menu
(`QUILL Key + Shift+T`).

#### The Window menu

The **Window** menu is small but handy.

- **New Tab** (`Ctrl+T`) opens a new, empty document tab.
- **Next Document** (`Ctrl+Tab`, also `Ctrl+F6`; on macOS `Cmd+Shift+]`) moves
  to the next open document.
- **Previous Document** (`Ctrl+Shift+Tab`, also `Ctrl+Shift+F6`; on macOS
  `Cmd+Shift+[`) moves to the previous open document. macOS keeps `Cmd+Tab` for
  its own App Switcher, so on a Mac QUILL uses the same tab keys as Safari and
  Xcode.
- **Close Other Documents** (`Ctrl+Shift+F4`) closes every document except the
  one you are in.
- **Send to System Tray** (`QUILL Key + T`) tucks QUILL into the notification
  area without closing it.
- After those come your open documents, numbered, such as
  **1: notes.txt (Alt+1) (active)** and **2: other.md (Alt+2)**. Press `Alt+W`
  to open the Window menu, then the number, to go straight to that document. The
  one you are in is marked active. The list keeps up as you open and close
  files, and an untitled document takes its new name the moment you save it.

You can also jump straight to a document by its position without opening the
menu. **Go to Document 1** to **Go to Document 10** are `Alt+1` to `Alt+9`, and
`Alt+0` for the tenth. If no document is open in that position, QUILL says so
and leaves you where you are. You can change these keys in the Keymap Editor,
like any other.

> **QUILLBee's shortcut:** Juggling notes, extracted files and previews? Keep
> your main document first in the row, and `Alt+1` will always bring you home.

### View and display

The **View** menu changes how QUILL shows your document on screen. Nothing on it
changes what is in the document.

- **Toggle Soft Wrap** (`Alt+Z`) wraps long lines to fit the window without
  changing the file.
- **Show Tab Control** shows or hides the row of document tabs.
- **Status Bar** (`Alt+Shift+B`) shows or hides the **whole** status bar. It is
  the same switch on the same key as in Notepad and QUILL Lite. It is a
  different thing from choosing which cells the bar carries (right-click the
  bar, or **Tools > Customize and Support > Status Bar Layout...**): a bar with every
  cell hidden still takes up a row of the window. The setting is
  **`show_status_bar`** (**Show status bar**). It is on to start with, and QUILL
  remembers your choice. QUILL says which way it went, because your screen
  reader will not tell you a bar has left the window.
- **Increase Text Size** (`Ctrl+=`), **Decrease Text Size** (`Ctrl+-`) and
  **Reset Text Size** (`Ctrl+0`) change how big the editor's text is without
  leaving the document. They are the same three keys as in Notepad and QUILL
  Lite. Chapter 11, Accessibility, speech and braille, has more on the size and
  face of the text.
- **Preview...** (`Alt+Shift+V`), **Preview Side by Side**, **Focus Preview**
  (`Alt+F6`) and **Browser Preview...** (`QUILL Key + V`) show your document
  rendered, the way a reader would see it.
- **Auto Side-by-Side Preview** opens a live preview beside the editor
  automatically.
- **Announce Headings** and **Announce Lists** choose whether QUILL tells you
  when you move onto a heading or a list.
- **What Is This Document?**, **What Changed?** and
  **Undo and Say What Changed** tell you the things a screen reader cannot work
  out for itself.
- **Show Entries Panel** and **Reveal Codes** (`Alt+F3`) show more of the
  document's structure and formatting.

Two switches that used to be on this menu are now in Preferences (`Ctrl+,`):
**Wrap Find Searches** decides whether Find carries on from the top when it
reaches the end, and **Start With No Document Open** makes QUILL open to an
empty workspace instead of a starter document.

Other settings that once lived here are in Preferences too, where they are saved
in one place: the theme and dark mode, system tray mode, how the title bar shows
the path, how the title marks unsaved changes, persistent undo, spell check as
you type, and word prediction as you type. You reach them from
**Tools > Customize and Support > Preferences...**.

#### Live preview while you type

Open the side-by-side preview with **Preview Side by Side**, or turn on Auto
Side-by-Side Preview. `Alt+F6` jumps straight into it, and while it is open it
joins the `F6` cycle too.

As you edit, the preview updates quietly in place. The new content is swapped in
without reloading the page, so your braille display and screen reader are not
interrupted, nothing is read again from the top, and you keep your place. This
is the live preview to use if you read with a screen reader or braille.

The **Browser Preview** in your web browser can also follow your edits. A real
browser has to reload the whole page to do that, so QUILL refreshes it only when
you pause typing, not on every key. Each time, it puts you back at the section
you are editing, or where you had scrolled to, instead of at the top.

#### Jump from the preview back to the editor

Reading the side preview, and want to change what you just heard? Go to a block
(a heading, paragraph, list item, quote, table or code block) and open its
context menu with the **Applications key**, **Shift+F10** or a right-click.
Choose **Go to this location in the editor**. The cursor moves to that block in
your document, focus goes with it, and QUILL tells you where you landed.

Pressing **Enter** on a block does the same, when your screen reader passes the
key through. The context menu is the dependable way, though: in browse mode
there is no way to ask where the virtual cursor is, but a context menu always
belongs to the exact spot you are on. The jump is offered when the preview
matches your document word for word. A preview that expands Vault links does not
offer it, because the places would no longer line up.

### What you learned, and where to go next

You know three ways to reach anything in QUILL: `F1` for help on what you are
on, the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) for any command by name, and the QUILL
key (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave`) for the bigger features and Quick Nav. You have been
round the window with `F6`, heard what each menu holds, moved between documents
and tabs, and seen how View changes what is on screen.

For a guided go at the same ground, open **Help > Tutorials...**
(`Ctrl+Alt+F1`). In the Your first hour track, "Do anything by name", "The QUILL
key" and "Getting unstuck" match this chapter, and "Make QUILL the size you
need", in Living with it, covers text size. On the website, [Own the
keyboard](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/02-own-the-keyboard.html) goes
deeper into keys and the Keymap Editor.

Next, Chapter 3, Opening, saving and converting files, shows you how to bring
documents in and send them out in the format you need.

## Chapter 3: Opening, saving and converting files

This chapter is about getting your words in and out of QUILL. We start with the
everyday things: opening a file, saving it, and what QUILL says when something
about a file changes. Then we look at the kinds of documents QUILL understands,
how to turn one format into another, and how to work with files that live on a
server or on GitHub. Read the first two topics now. Come back to the rest when
you have a Word file to send or a folder of documents to convert.

### Opening files

Most of the time you open a file with **File > Open...** (`Ctrl+O`). The File
menu has a few other ways in, and each one is handy at the right moment:

- **New** creates a blank document.
- **Open...** opens a document from disk.
- **Open Recent** takes you back to files you used lately. At the bottom of
  that list, **Clear Recent Files...** empties it when you want a fresh start.
  It asks first, and pinned files stay. Your files stay where they are; only
  the list goes.
  Just above Clear, **Recent Documents...** (`Alt+Shift+0`) shows the whole
  list in a window of its own. More on that just below.
- **Open from URL...** downloads a document or text resource from the web. QUILL
  checks with you first, naming the host and the expected size.
- **New Document from Clipboard** opens a new document that already holds
  whatever text is on the clipboard. It is on the Edit menu too.
- **Snapshots** saves a group of open documents as one workspace snapshot, so
  you can reopen them all together later. If you know Visual Studio Code, it is
  a little like a lightweight workspace there.

Files on a server or on GitHub have their own commands. They are covered later
in this chapter, under Remote access and GitHub remote files.

#### Opening something you worked on recently

QUILL remembers the documents you open, newest first. There are two quick ways
back to one.

**The first nine.** `Alt+Shift+1` reopens the document you opened most
recently, `Alt+Shift+2` the one before that, and so on up to `Alt+Shift+9`.
They are the first nine rows of **File > Open Recent**, where each row says the
file's name first and then its folder.

**The whole list.** Press `Alt+Shift+0`, or choose **File > Open Recent >
Recent Documents...**. Arrow to a document and press Enter to open it. In the same
window you can:

- **Pin** a document you keep coming back to (`Alt+P`). Pinned documents stay at
  the top, however many others you open. On a pinned one, the button says
  **Unpin**.
- **Remove from List** (`Alt+R`, or the Delete key) takes one off the list. The
  file is not touched.
- **Open Containing Folder** (`Alt+F`) shows the file in File Explorer.
- **Clear Unpinned...** (`Alt+L`) empties the list. It asks first, and pressing
  Enter answers No. Pinned documents always stay.
- **Remember up to this many documents** (`Alt+U`) sets the length of the list,
  from 1 to 50. It is the same setting as **Recent files to remember** in
  Settings.
- **Forget missing files when the app starts** (`Alt+M`) is the same setting as
  **Drop missing recent files automatically**, described below.

A file that has moved or been deleted says "not found" in this window, and
Remove from List tidies it away. QUILL Lite has the same window on the same
key; the two apps keep their own lists.

#### The Simple File Open dialog

QUILL can open files with either the standard Windows file open dialog or its
own **Simple File Open** dialog. The simple one is a short, keyboard-friendly
window: one list of files, a small filter, your recent files and a switch for
hidden files. Both are reached the same way, with **File > Open...** or
`Ctrl+O`. Which one you get is decided by
**Settings > General > Use simple file open dialog**. It is off to begin with.
Turn it on if you would like a plain picker that is easy to use with a screen
reader.

Here is what is in the Simple File Open dialog:

- A **Path** field at the top shows the folder you are in. Type a path and press
  Enter. A folder opens in the list, and a file opens in QUILL. Press `Ctrl+L`
  from anywhere in the dialog to jump back to this field. You can paste a path
  in whatever form you have it: with the quotes File Explorer's "Copy as path"
  adds, with `%APPDATA%`-style environment variables, as a `file://` link, or
  starting with `~`. QUILL tidies it up for you.
- A **Filter** dropdown chooses which file types are shown. The default,
  **Supported files**, shows plain text, Markdown, HTML and Rich Text. Choose
  **Plain text**, **Markdown**, **HTML** or **Rich Text** to narrow it further,
  or **All files** to see everything.
- A **Files** list shows the folders and files where you are. Folders start with
  `[dir]`. To go up to the parent folder, press Backspace in the list or use the
  **Up** button.
- A **Hidden** toggle shows or hides files whose names start with a dot, or that
  Windows marks as hidden. Press `Ctrl+H` in the path field or the file list to
  flip it. On a Mac, use `Cmd+Shift+.` instead, as the Finder does, because
  `Ctrl+H` there is the system's Hide shortcut.
- A **Recent** button pops up your recently opened files, so you can reopen one
  with a single choice.
- A **Use Windows Dialog** button opens the standard Windows dialog just this
  once. Your setting does not change, so the next `Ctrl+O` brings you back to
  the simple dialog. It is there for the odd case, such as a very long path or a
  custom file association, where you want the Windows picker.
- An **Open** button and a **Cancel** button. Enter opens the selected file and
  Escape cancels.

Under the list, a status line tells you the folder you are in, how many entries
are showing, and any error. If a folder is off limits ("permission denied") or a
path is not a folder, the dialog stays open so you can fix the path and try
again.

> **QUILLBee's tip:** Someone sent you a file path in an e-mail? In the Simple
> File Open dialog, press `Ctrl+L` to jump to the Path field, paste it, and
> press Enter. Quotes and all, QUILL tidies it up.

#### When a file is not where it was

Files move. A OneDrive or SharePoint file can be a placeholder whose contents
were never downloaded to this PC. A file on **File > Open Recent** may have been
renamed or deleted since you last used it. A file on a USB stick or a network
share simply is not there when that drive is not connected.

When that happens, QUILL says so in one sentence, in the status bar and out
loud:

> *Bingo3.html is no longer there. It may have been moved, renamed, or deleted,
> or it may live on a drive that is not connected.*

That is all. There is no dialog to close, and QUILL stays exactly where it was,
so you can press `Ctrl+O` and pick something else. If you choose a folder where
QUILL expected a file, it tells you that instead.

Your Recent list keeps the entry. A file that is missing today may be on a USB
stick you plug back in tomorrow, so QUILL does not quietly forget it because one
open failed.

If you would rather lose dead entries, turn on
**Drop missing recent files automatically** in Settings, on the General page
(the setting is `recent_files_auto_clear_missing`, and it is off by default).
Even then, it only removes entries whose file has been deleted from one of this
PC's own fixed drives. Files on USB, removable or network drives are never even
checked, so unplugging a drive never clears its history. "Not connected" is not
the same as "gone".

### Saving files

Saving is three commands on the **File** menu:

- **Save** writes the current document.
- **Save As...** writes it to a new name or place, and converts it to the file
  type you choose in the dialog.
- **Save All** writes every open document that has changes.

**Save As...** really converts. QUILL keeps your text as portable Markdown-style
markup, so choosing **Rich Text Format (\*.rtf)** writes real RTF, **HTML
(\*.html)** writes a standalone web page, and **Text
(\*.txt)** writes your text as a plain file. Choosing **Markdown (\*.md)** keeps
the markup just as it is. The file's extension always decides the format. If you
type a name with no extension, the type you selected supplies one. There is more
on each format under What happens when you save in another format, later in this
chapter.

When Save As changes the format, QUILL can reload the file so the editor matches
it. For example, a freshly saved `.rtf` can reopen in the Rich text editor.
Reloading replaces what is in the editor with the saved file, so by default
QUILL asks first with a Yes or No question. To stop the question, set
**Settings > Editing > Reload after Save As to match the format** to *Reload
automatically* or *Keep current surface*.

**Filename suggestions.** When you save a document that has never been saved,
QUILL fills in the name box from the document's first line. It removes leading
`#` marks, quotes and bullets, and any characters a file name cannot hold. This
is only a suggestion: type over it with anything you like. It never renames a
document that is already saved. It is on by default, and you can turn it off
with **Suggest a filename from the first line** in Preferences.

#### Save As Plain Text

**Save As Plain Text...** saves a clean plain-text copy, with the markup taken
out. Plain text has no links, so
**Settings > Editing > Links in plain-text export** decides what happens to a
Markdown link. You can keep the link text and its URL (the default, so you never
lose where a link pointed), the link text only, the URL only, or the original
Markdown link. The same setting applies whenever Save As writes a `.txt` file.
If your document has hidden formatting such as fonts, colours or alignment,
QUILL offers to keep it in an **Illumination**, which comes next.

#### Keeping formatting in a plain-text file with Illuminations

A plain `.txt` file has nowhere to store fonts, colours or alignment, so saving
formatted text as plain text normally loses the formatting. QUILL gives you a
choice. It is named after the painted decoration a scribe adds to a manuscript:
an **Illumination** is a small companion file, `yourfile.txt.illumination`, that
keeps the formatting beside the clean text. Your `.txt` stays truly plain, so
Notepad, e-mail and every other program can read it. When you open it again *in
QUILL*, the Illumination puts back every font, colour and alignment exactly.

What happens is set by
**Settings > Editing > Saving formatted text as plain text**:

- **Ask each time** (the default). QUILL asks whether to keep your formatting by
  saving as Markdown, Word or RTF instead, to save the plain `.txt` **plus** an
  Illumination, or to save plain text only and drop the formatting.
- **Always save an Illumination sidecar**. QUILL writes the clean `.txt` and the
  `.illumination` companion every time, with no question.
- **Save plain text and drop the formatting**. The classic save that loses
  formatting. The `.txt` is clean, and any old Illumination beside it is
  removed.

Two things to keep in mind. The Illumination is a *separate file*, so if you
copy or e-mail only the `.txt`, the formatting stays behind. Keep the pair
together. And if you edit the `.txt` in another program, QUILL notices the text
no longer matches its Illumination and opens it as plain text, so formatting
never lands on the wrong words. If you want one file that keeps everything, save
as **Markdown**, which keeps the formatting inline, or **Word/RTF**, which turn
it into real formatting.

#### Encoding and line endings (Ctrl+Alt+E)

**File > File Format...** (`Ctrl+Alt+E`) is one window for the two things that
decide exactly how your file is written to disk. QUILL Lite opens the same
window on the same key, under the name
**Tools > File Encoding and Line Endings...**.

- **Encoding.** Choose UTF-8 for anything new. UTF-8 with BOM suits the Windows
  tools that expect one. There is also UTF-16, and Windows-1252 for older `.txt`
  files that use it. A file that arrived in something else, such as UTF-16
  big-endian, shows as a **keep as is** row and stays that way.
- **Line endings.** CRLF is what Windows programs write, and it is what a new
  QUILL document starts with, the same as Notepad, WordPad, Word and QUILL Lite.
  LF is what Unix, macOS and most build tools expect. A file that arrived with
  old-style Mac CR endings keeps them, in its own **keep as is** row.

Nothing changes until you save, and the window tells you so. If the encoding you
chose cannot hold a character in your document, the save names that character
and offers Save As. It never quietly turns it into a question mark.

#### When another program changes the file you are editing

QUILL keeps an eye on the file you have open. When something else writes to it
(Word saving a `.docx`, a build tool regenerating a `.md`, a colleague's sync
client), **QUILL asks** what you want to do. Unless you tell it to, it never
reloads on its own.

You have three answers:

- **Reload from Disk** reads the file again, using the right reader for its
  format, and keeps your cursor where it was.
- **Keep Mine** leaves your tab exactly as it is. The version on disk is ignored
  until you save over it or reload. Escape gives this answer too, because doing
  nothing to your text is the safe choice.
- **Open Disk Version in a New Tab** opens what is on disk as a second,
  read-only tab named `<name> (on disk)`, so you can compare the two and decide.
  Your own tab is not touched.

The question has a checkbox, such as **"Do not ask me again for .docx files."**
Tick it and QUILL remembers your answer for every file of that format. That way
a build that rewrites the file you are reading every few seconds is answered
once, not every time. Reload and Keep Mine can be remembered. Opening the disk
version in a new tab is a one-off comparison, so it never is. To take every
remembered answer back, choose **File > Forget Remembered File-Change Answers**
(`Ctrl+Shift+F11`).

If the file changes while you *do* have unsaved edits, the same question spells
out what is at stake: reloading throws away your edits, and keeping yours
overwrites the disk version the next time you save.

Two related commands are on the File menu:

- **Reload from Disk** throws away your changes in memory and reads the file
  again, after asking you to confirm.
- **Check for External Changes...** asks the same question whenever you want to
  check.

Four settings on the **General** page of Settings shape all of this:

- **Watch the open file for external changes** is on to begin with. Turn it
  off and QUILL stops noticing when another program changes or deletes your
  file.
- **Reload automatically when you have no unsaved edits** is off to begin
  with. Turn it on and, as long as you have not changed anything yourself,
  QUILL reloads a changed file without asking, in every format, and keeps your
  cursor where it was. An answer you asked QUILL to remember still comes
  first.
- **Ask before discarding unsaved edits on a conflict** is on to begin with.
  It is the question above, when you do have unsaved edits, and the question
  about a file that was deleted. Turn it off and QUILL says nothing in those
  cases and leaves your text exactly as it is.
- **External-change debounce (milliseconds)** is how long QUILL waits after
  it notices a change before it reacts, so a program that writes a file in
  several steps is dealt with once. The default is 750.

### The rest of the File menu

The **File** menu covers the whole life of a document. Besides opening and
saving, you will find these:

- **Restore Backup...** brings back a saved backup version.
- **Page Setup...** and **Print...** handle paper and printing.
- **Print Studio...** goes a step further. It first tells you what the printout
  will be, for example "3 pages, Letter, default margins", which is a print
  preview you can hear. Then you can choose **all, odd, or even pages**,
  **print in reverse order**, or **skip the first page** (handy when page 1 is
  pre-printed letterhead) before it hands you to the same print dialog Print
  uses.
- **Header and Footer...** builds a header and footer for the current document.
  Start from a preset such as **Title left, page number right**,
  **Filename and date** or **Roman numerals for front matter**, or make your own
  from a small set of pieces (title, filename, date, page number) placed left,
  center or right. Turn on **Different first page** to give page 1 its own
  header and footer, and choose **numeric or Roman** page numbers with any
  starting number. It is saved with the document and printed on every page, from
  Print or Print Studio.
- **Run Current File** runs the saved file with the program it belongs to, and
  **Open Target at Cursor** opens the path or link under the cursor.
- **Rename Current File...** and **Delete Current File...** rename or delete the
  file on disk without leaving the editor.
- **Close Document** closes the current tab.
- **Exit** closes QUILL.

Anything on this menu that could cost you work, such as reloading, restoring a
backup or opening a web address, asks before it acts.

### Making QUILL your text editor

Installing QUILL tells Windows that QUILL can open your text files, Markdown,
rich text, HTML, Word documents, EPUB books and a few more. It doesn't take
anything over. QUILL simply shows up when you choose **Open with** on a file,
and in Windows Settings under **Default apps**, which is where you decide which
app opens what.

Both of the next steps live in one place: open **Settings**, go to the
**General** page, and find **Windows and your files**. A line at the top tells
you which program opens in place of Notepad right now.

The **Make QUILL My Text Editor...** button takes you the rest of the way. It
tells you what Windows lets an app do and what is up to you, then opens the
Default apps page for QUILL. Choose **.txt**, pick **QUILL**, and choose
**Set default**. Do the same for any other type you'd like QUILL to open.
Anything you leave alone stays with the app that opens it now, and you can
change your mind on the same page. This works from a portable copy of QUILL too.

Some programs still start Notepad by name, and so does typing "notepad" in the
Run box. If you'd like QUILL to open for those as well, check
**Open QUILL instead of Notepad** and press **OK** or **Apply**. It's off to
begin with. Because it changes Notepad for everyone on the computer, QUILL asks
first and Windows asks for administrator approval. The checkbox always shows
whether it's on right now, and clearing it puts Notepad back. On Windows 11,
QUILL then shows you where to turn off the newer Notepad's app execution alias,
which would otherwise go around the switch. Uninstalling QUILL puts Notepad back
for you.

Only one program can open in place of Notepad. If QUILL Lite, or another
program, already does, QUILL tells you who before it takes over. QUILL Lite has
the same two settings in its Preferences.

### Working with Different Document Types

QUILL is at its best with plain text, Markdown, HTML, RTF, EPUB, and text pulled
out of other documents. It can also bring in PDFs and scanned pages, with tools
to check what came through, and it understands the structure of Office files.
Here is what each kind of file gets.

#### Plain text

Plain text stays plain. QUILL never slips hidden formatting into it.

#### Markdown

Markdown gets commands that understand its structure: help with lists, headings,
links and code blocks.

#### HTML

HTML gets tag insertion, help with editing its structure, and link handling.

#### RTF

When an RTF file contains unsafe embedded content, such as OLE objects, QUILL
removes it as the file opens and tells you. Remote fields, which would fetch
something from the internet, are flagged and wait for your consent instead of
being fetched quietly.

Earlier versions had an optional **Rich text lens** for RTF files, switched on
under Settings, Editing (the "Editor surface" choice) and toggled with an
editing-lens shortcut. It has been retired. To move a document between Plain
text, Markdown, HTML, Rich Text and Word, use **Format > Document Format...**
(`Alt+Shift+F`).

#### CSV and TSV

When you open a CSV or TSV file, QUILL asks how: in the CSV grid mode, or in the
normal text editor. You can remember your choice as the default and still switch
modes inside the tab at any time. Grid mode is built for the keyboard and for
screen-reader users who want to edit a table cell by cell without leaving QUILL.

#### Word (.docx and .doc)

Word documents open the same way, with a choice between the structured Word view
and the normal text editor. Again, you can remember a default and switch inside
the tab.

The structured Word view puts readable structure first. Tables are read out in a
straight line, headers and then rows, which is easier to follow with a screen
reader. Normal text mode gives you all of QUILL's editing for making changes
directly.

**Saving to Word.** You can save any document *as* Word. In
**File > Save As...**, choose **Word Document (\*.docx)** (or **Rich Text Format
(\*.rtf)**) in the file type list, and QUILL converts the current content as it
saves. Markdown and HTML structure (headings, lists, emphasis, links, simple
tables) becomes real Word styles, so you can move around the result in Word by
heading, not just look at it. Saving plain text this way gives you a correct but
unformatted document, because plain text has no structure to carry.

#### EPUB

EPUB books get the navigator and reading chapter by chapter.

#### PowerPoint (.pptx and .ppt)

QUILL keeps a presentation's structure when it brings it in. Slide titles become
headings, bullets become nested list items, tables become text tables you can
Tab through, and speaker notes come along when there are any.

#### Excel-style spreadsheets (.xlsx and .xls)

Spreadsheets come in as text, with their structure kept. QUILL lays each sheet
out as readable table text, so you can look through the content quickly. If
optional converters are installed, older and mixed-format files come through
better.

#### PDF and OCR-derived text

PDFs and scanned pages are where QUILL's tools for checking extracted text
matter most. Treat them as a proofreading step, not an extra. The next topics
cover opening PDFs, OCR and those checks.

### What happens when you save in another format

**File > Save As** truly converts your document to the format you pick in the
"Save as type" list. It never just renames the file. QUILL's editor holds your
text in one clean form, and Save As writes that text out in the format you
chose. Here is what each choice does:

- **Markdown (.md)**: your text is written exactly as it is in the editor.
  Markdown is QUILL's own format, so nothing is converted or lost.
- **Text (.txt)**: also written exactly as it is, Markdown markup included, so a
  plain-text file comes back just as it went out. If you want the markup
  *stripped*, with headings and emphasis turned into plain words, use
  **File > Save As Plain Text** instead. That command also offers to keep your
  formatting in an Illumination. A third route is
  **Format > Document Format... > Plain text**, which *asks* which of the two
  you want. Save As leaves your file byte for byte as it was, so a .txt you
  opened comes back unchanged.
- **HTML (.html)**: converted to a complete web page with your document's title,
  ready for a browser.
- **Rich Text (.rtf)**: converted with all its formatting. Fonts, sizes, colors,
  highlights and alignment all carry over.
- **Word (.docx)**: converted to a real Word document. Headings become Word
  heading styles, so Word and screen readers can move by them. Each line in the
  editor becomes one Word paragraph, so your line breaks stay exactly where they
  were. Hidden-codes formatting (font, size, color, highlight, alignment)
  becomes real Word formatting.
- **An extension QUILL cannot write**, for example typing `notes.pdf` in the
  name box: QUILL refuses rather than writing a broken file. For PDF, ODT and
  EPUB it offers to open **File > Export**, which makes them properly with
  Pandoc.

**You keep editing QUILL text.** After a Save As that converts, the file on disk
is Word (or HTML, or RTF), but the editor still holds QUILL's clean text, and
every `Ctrl+S` after that converts it again. QUILL tells you this after the
save: "Saved as report.docx, Word format. You are still editing QUILL text; each
save converts it to Word." The window title and tab title change to the new name
straight away, and from then on `Ctrl+S` saves quietly to the same file.

**Your originals are protected.** If you opened a PDF, EPUB, spreadsheet or
presentation, what you are editing is text taken out of it, and the original
file cannot hold your changes. Pressing `Ctrl+S` on one of these never
overwrites the original. QUILL explains why and opens Save As, so your edits go
into a new file in a format that can hold them.

#### What carries over between formats

QUILL converts everything through one clean form inside, so what survives a Save
As or a conversion depends on the feature, not on the pair of formats. This
table is what QUILL's own tests check. **Yes** means it carries over as that
format's own structure. **Partly** means it carries over, but as text or as
QUILL's portable markup rather than a real object in that format. **No** means
it is not kept. The numbers point to the notes after the table.

| Feature | Markdown | HTML | Word (.docx) | Rich Text (.rtf) | Plain text (.txt) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Headings (1 to 6) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| **Bold**, *italic* | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Underline | Partly (1) | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Strikethrough | Partly (1) | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Superscript / subscript | Partly (1) | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Text colour / highlight | Partly (1) | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Font family / size | Partly (1) | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Links | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Bullet lists | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Numbered lists | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Blockquotes | Yes | Yes | Partly (2) | Partly (2) | No |
| Code blocks | Yes | Yes | Partly (2) | Partly (2) | No |
| Horizontal rule | Yes | Yes | Partly (2) | Partly (2) | No |
| Tables | Yes | Yes | Yes | Partly (3) | No |
| Images | Partly (4) | Yes | No (4) | No | No |
| Paragraph alignment | Partly (1) | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Page breaks | Partly (1) | Yes | No | No | No |

Notes:

1. **In Markdown**, underline, strikethrough, superscript and subscript, colour,
   highlight, font, alignment and page breaks are kept in QUILL's *hidden-codes*
   markup. You don't see it while you edit, and it turns into real formatting
   when you export to HTML, Word or RTF. Markdown itself has no standard way to
   write these, so another Markdown app shows QUILL's `[text]{...}` codes
   instead of the effect.
2. **Blockquotes, code blocks and horizontal rules** belong to Markdown and show
   properly in HTML. In Word and RTF they appear as their Markdown markers (`>`,
   ` ``` `, `---`) rather than a Word quote or code style.
3. **Tables** travel as real tables between Markdown, HTML and Word. A Word
   table you *open* in QUILL becomes a clean Markdown (GFM) table that you can
   edit and move around in. Markdown and HTML tables stay as they are. A table
   you *save to* Word becomes a real, editable Word table with a header row that
   repeats, so a screen reader announces the column headers. The one exception
   is RTF: a table saved to `.rtf` is written as readable pipe text, not a real
   RTF table.
4. **Images**: an image *reference* (`![alt](path)`) survives a trip through
   Markdown and becomes `<img>` in HTML. QUILL does not put image files inside
   Word documents, and images inside a Word document you open are not brought
   into the text.

**Plain text (.txt)** never carries formatting. That is what plain text is for.
Use **Save As Plain Text** when you want the markup flattened on purpose, with
the option to keep your formatting in an Illumination.

#### Choosing a conversion engine

More than one converter can handle a Word document, and each gives a slightly
different result. QUILL lets you choose, and describes what each choice gives
you in plain words. The defaults suit almost everyone. The choices are there for
when they don't.

- **Word document reading engine** (**Settings > Editing**) decides how a
  `.docx` becomes editable text when you open it. **Auto** (the default) tries
  MarkItDown first and falls back to a plain extract. **MarkItDown** is fast and
  reliable: headings, lists and tables come through, but images, comments and
  fonts do not. **Pandoc** keeps more of the structure, so footnotes and complex
  tables come through better. It needs Pandoc installed. If Pandoc is missing,
  this setting quietly acts as Auto, so your file still opens.
- **Word document saving engine** (**Settings > Editing**) decides how your
  text becomes a `.docx` when you save. **Auto** (the default) uses the native
  writer. **Native** keeps QUILL's formatting codes (fonts, sizes, colors,
  highlights, alignment) and makes each line in the editor one Word paragraph.
  It is the best choice for documents written in QUILL. **Pandoc** turns
  structure into Word styles (headings, lists, tables, links and footnotes) but
  drops font, size and color codes.
- In the **Convert File dialog**, the **Conversion engine** choice (Auto, Pandoc
  or MarkItDown) applies to one conversion at a time. As you arrow through it, a
  description under the choice changes, so you hear what each engine will do
  before you convert. MarkItDown only works when the source is Word, PowerPoint,
  Excel or PDF and the result is Markdown or plain text. If you choose it for
  anything else, QUILL says so and offers Pandoc. It never swaps in an engine
  you did not pick.

### Import and Export

QUILL can convert between the formats the people around you use, without you
leaving the editor. **File > Import** brings a document from another program
into QUILL as a new tab. **File > Export** saves the current document as a
different file type. Both use Pandoc and work in the background, so the editor
never freezes. Exports keep your line breaks exactly: one line in the editor is
one paragraph in the exported document, in every format.

**Import (File > Import)** reads Markdown, CommonMark, GitHub-Flavored Markdown,
HTML, Word documents (`.docx`), OpenDocument Text (`.odt`), Rich Text (`.rtf`),
plain text, CSV and TSV tables, EPUB books, and LaTeX or TeX.

**Export (File > Export)** writes the same set, plus PDF and a
**DAISY Talking Book**, which are export only.

A few examples cover most of what people do:

- Choose **File > Import > Word Document**, pick a `.docx`, and a new Markdown
  tab opens with the document ready to edit.
- Choose **File > Export > EPUB Book**, pick a folder, and QUILL writes an EPUB
  next to your current file.
- Choose **File > Export > PDF** to publish a finished document.

**Getting there by keyboard.** `File > Import` and `File > Export` are ordinary
menus: open the menu, arrow down and press Enter. There is no single key for the
whole list, because choosing the format is the point of the command. The
quickest way is the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`): type `import` or `export`
and pick the format from the list.

**After the conversion.** When the new file is one QUILL can edit (Markdown,
CommonMark, GFM, HTML, plain text, CSV or TSV), QUILL asks whether to open it in
a new window. Press **Yes** to open it, or **No** to carry on where you were.
PDF, DOCX, EPUB, ODT and RTF don't ask, because QUILL cannot edit those
directly. Instead a message tells you where the file was saved and copies the
path to the clipboard, so you can paste it into File Explorer.

**Other formats.** Both menus end with **Other Pandoc Format...**. It shows a
list of every other format Pandoc can read (on Import) or write (on Export),
such as CommonMark and GitHub-Flavored Markdown. Arrow to the one you want and
press Enter, and the conversion runs just like the named ones above.

**What it does not do.** Importing a PDF this way is not supported, because
Pandoc cannot do it reliably. Use Import / Convert Document, described below,
and for print-to-braille work, the braille and DAISY tools.

#### DAISY Talking Book export

**File > Export > DAISY Talking Book** saves the current document as a DAISY
2.02 text-only talking book. DAISY is the accessible book format read by DAISY
software and by players such as the Victor Reader Stream, Plextalk and APH
units. A DAISY book is a *folder*, not a single file, so the name you choose
becomes a folder holding `ncc.html`, `content.html` and `book.smil`. Your
headings become the player's navigation points, and Markdown styling is
flattened into clean, readable text. The book has no audio, so a player reads it
with its own text-to-speech. You can also open the folder in APH Book Wizard
Producer to record or synthesize a full text-and-audio book. The export reads
what is on screen, so you do not have to save first.

#### Batch Conversion

When you have a whole folder of documents to convert, opening them one at a time
is slow going. **File > Import > Batch Conversion...** (or
**File > Export > Batch Conversion...**, which opens the same wizard) converts a
whole folder in the background. The key is the QUILL key, then `B`
(`Ctrl+Shift+Grave` then `B`).

Use the single-file Import and Export menus for one document. Use the wizard
when you have a folder of documents, when every file needs the same treatment,
and when you are happy to let it run while you keep writing.

##### The wizard, page by page

1. **Introduction.** A short summary, then a check for Pandoc and its version.
   If Pandoc is not installed, the page says so, and Start stays unavailable
   until you install Pandoc 3.x from <https://pandoc.org>.
2. **Folder and options.** A folder picker, an **Include subfolders** checkbox,
   an **Output layout** choice (Same folder as source, or Output subfolder per
   source folder), and an **Overwrite** choice (Ask each time, Never, Always).
   These start from your Settings, and the last folder you used is remembered
   for next time.
3. **Format and profile.** A **Direction** choice (Import into QUILL, or Export
   from QUILL), a list of source formats and a list of target formats from the
   main Import and Export set, and a picker for the seven built-in conversion
   profiles.
4. **Review and start.** A plain-text summary of the whole plan. Press **Start**
   to begin the batch and close the wizard.

QUILL keeps each file's name and changes only the extension: `report.docx`
becomes `report.md` (or `report.html`, `report.epub`, and so on). With
**Output subfolder per source folder** (the default), the results go into a new
`Output/` folder inside the source folder. With **Same folder as source**, they
go next to the originals.

##### Profiles

The profile picker offers seven ready-made profiles. Each one comes with a plain
description that your screen reader reads before you press Start.

- **Clean Word Document**: `report.md` becomes a polished Word document, with no
  Markdown left showing.
- **Accessible HTML Page**: a single HTML page with a title block and `lang`
  metadata, ready for an accessibility check.
- **EPUB Book**: an EPUB ready for publishing yourself, with a table of contents
  and EPUB-3 metadata.
- **GitHub README**: GitHub-Flavored Markdown with no wrapper, ready to paste
  into a repository.
- **Print PDF**: a PDF with standard PDF metadata. Pandoc picks the right engine
  for your computer.
- **Instructor Handout**: a print-ready PDF with 1-inch margins and numbered
  top-level sections.
- **Plain Text for Screen Readers**: plain text with no HTML wrapper, no smart
  quotes and a fixed 80-column width. The right choice for feeding a
  text-to-speech engine.

##### Overwriting existing files

The three overwrite choices save you from answering a question for every file:

- **Ask each time**: QUILL lists every result that would replace an existing
  file and asks once, with a single Yes or No. If you say No, those files are
  skipped.
- **Never**: existing files are skipped automatically. The Status Page counts
  them under *skipped*, so the totals still add up.
- **Always**: existing files are replaced without asking. Useful when you run
  the same batch again.

##### Following progress

To watch the batch, open the Status Page (**Help > Status Page**). The Tasks &
Downloads tab shows a row for it as it works. The first row is
`Batch conversion: scanning <folder>`, followed by one row per file.

When the batch is done, QUILL says one line, through the announcement backend
you have set up, with the converted, skipped and failed counts and how long it
took:

> "Batch conversion complete. 12 of 14 files converted in 4.2 seconds. 2
> skipped."

That line follows your verbosity settings under **Settings > Accessibility and Announcements**.
