The Status Page row updates either way, so sighted and low-vision users see the
same result. A short report then lists every file that gave a warning or failed,
with the exact error.

##### Batch settings

Three Settings choose what the wizard starts with:

- **Include subfolders in batch conversion**: on or off, on by default (`True`).
- **Overwrite behaviour for batch conversion**: Ask each time (the default),
  Never or Always.
- **Default output layout for batch conversion**: Output subfolder per source
  folder (the default) or Same folder as source.

You can change any of them in the wizard for one run. To change what it starts
with every time, use Preferences.

### Import / Convert Document (OCR)

**File > Import > Import / Convert Document (OCR)...** (also on
**Tools > Reading and Dictation > OCR and Document Conversion**) is QUILL's rescue tool for documents that are
hard to read: locked-down Office files, EPUBs, scanned PDFs and photos of pages.
It follows one rule: **free first, local first, and nothing is ever uploaded**
without your say-so.

Here is how a conversion goes:

1. **The free local converter runs first.** Word, PowerPoint, Excel, HTML, EPUB,
   and PDFs that already contain text convert straight away on your computer and
   open as clean, editable text. No account, no key, no upload and no cost.
2. **A scanned document is noticed, not dumped on you.** If a PDF comes back
   nearly empty, QUILL says "It looks scanned or image-based" and *asks* whether
   to run free OCR on your computer. Yes runs it. No opens the empty result
   anyway. Cancel imports nothing. QUILL never opens a blank result without
   telling you, and never runs OCR without asking.
3. **OCR on your computer rescues the scan.** The local Tesseract engine reads
   each page on your own computer (it uses only the processor and works
   offline). It marks where each page begins with a searchable `<!-- Page N -->`
   marker and tells you how it is going ("Recognizing page 3 of 12..."). When it
   is not confident about what it read, QUILL tells you plainly, so you know to
   check the result.

Other problems get their own clear message instead of the scanned-PDF question.
A file that is really corrupt is reported as *damaged*, with a note that OCR
won't help (repair it or export it again from where it came from). A PDF on a
computer with no text extractor points you to
**Help > Download Optional Components > "PDF and Office text extraction"**
instead of claiming it is scanned. The installed apps come with a PDF reader, so
this only happens with a pip or source install. A *password-protected* PDF is
handled separately, as described next.

#### Opening a password-protected PDF

When you open a PDF that is locked with a password, QUILL asks for the password
and reads the document. You don't need to remove the password in another program
first. Type the password and the PDF opens. If it is wrong, QUILL tells you and
lets you try again. Press **Cancel** to stop opening it.

**The password is used only to open that one file for reading.** QUILL
**never stores, logs or remembers it**, so if you close the file and open it
again, it asks again. PDFs that are technically locked but open with an empty
password (they only restrict permissions) open with no question, as before.

#### A PDF's bookmarks come across

If a PDF has an outline, the chapters and sections you would see in Adobe
Reader's bookmarks pane, QUILL adds those entries to its own
bookmark list (**List Named Bookmarks...**, `Alt+Shift+G`) when you open the file, as it does for
Word and EPUB structure. Each bookmark takes you exactly where **Go To Page**
for that page would. This happens once, the first time you open the PDF. If you
later rename or delete some of those bookmarks, opening the file again will not
bring them back or make duplicates. A PDF with no outline opens as usual.

#### The text from a PDF is repaired before you read it

A PDF does not store sentences. It stores where each letter was printed on the
page. So what comes out is a picture of the page rather than the words the
author typed, and read aloud that can be rough going. QUILL fixes four things as
it opens the file, page by page:

- **Words split across lines are joined again.** Print layout breaks long words
  with a hyphen at the end of a line, so "inter-" on one line and "national" on
  the next would be read as two words, and a search for "international" found
  nothing. QUILL joins them. A hyphen that belongs to the word stays:
  **Anglo-Saxon** and **2018-2019** are left exactly as written.
- **Paragraphs are put back together.** Every printed line arrives as its own
  line of text, so speech would stop at the edge of the page instead of the end
  of the sentence, and moving to the next paragraph moved one printed line.
  QUILL joins lines that were only broken because the page ran out of room.
  Blank lines, list items, headings, short deliberate lines and finished
  sentences keep their breaks, so lists stay lists and paragraphs stay separate.
- **Spaced-out headings are closed up.** A designer's letter-spaced title comes
  through as "C H A P T E R  O N E", which a screen reader spells one letter at
  a time and a search never matches. It becomes "CHAPTER ONE". Ordinary text is
  left alone: a line such as "A B testing" is not a heading and is not touched.
- **Missing joined letters are restored.** The joined "fi", "fl" and "ff" shapes
  a typesetter uses are often stored as characters that mean nothing outside the
  document's own font, so a screen reader reads *nothing* where they were, and
  "office" is announced as "o ce". QUILL turns them back into letters, and
  removes any leftover meaningless character so speech doesn't stumble over it.

These repairs are careful. When a case could go either way, QUILL leaves the
text as it found it, and a PDF whose text is already clean comes through
unchanged. They never cross from one page to the next, so **Go To Page** and the
page count stay exact.

#### Installing the OCR engine

The OCR engine is a free, one-time download of about 48 MB:
**Tools > Reading and Dictation > OCR and Document Conversion > Install Local
OCR Engine (Tesseract)...**. QUILL
fetches the official installer from its own verified release, checks it byte for
byte, and opens it for you to finish. It never installs anything silently. If
Tesseract is already on your computer (or installed with Homebrew on a Mac),
QUILL finds it and uses it.

#### The optional Datalab Chandra OCR cloud service

Some documents are too hard even for OCR on your computer: complex tables,
forms, handwriting, crowded columns, very poor scans. For those, QUILL supports
an optional paid cloud service, Datalab Chandra OCR, using your own key. QUILL
only offers it *after* the OCR on your computer comes back weak (or when you
turn down installing the free engine).
**Every single upload requires your explicit consent** in a window that names
the service, reminds you to think about private, medical, legal or financial
content, and notes that Datalab deletes results from its servers about an hour
after processing. A file whose name suggests sensitive content (tax, medical,
legal and similar) gets an extra CAUTION line. QUILL decides that from the name
only and never looks inside the file to decide. There is no "don't ask again".

To set it up, choose
**Tools > Reading and Dictation > OCR and Document Conversion > OCR Service Settings...**.
This opens the **AI Hub Services tab**. Turn the service on, paste your Datalab
API key (it is kept in the Windows credential vault, never in a settings file),
choose the default mode (Fast, Balanced or Accurate) and output (Markdown is
recommended), and press **Test Connection**. The test checks your key and the
address and uploads no document. Other buttons open the provider's website, key
page, pricing, privacy documents, API documents and list of supported file types
in your browser, and **Copy Service Summary** copies a description with no
secrets in it, for support requests.

#### Checking and tidying up after OCR

**Review Last OCR Result...** opens a checklist for your most recent conversion:
which service made it, the page count, how confident the recognition was, and,
for OCR on your computer, every line it was unsure of, listed as
`Page N: [confidence] text`. Arrow through the flagged lines, then search the
converted document for the page marker (for example `<!-- Page 3 -->`) to jump
to the trouble spot. That way you check by ear exactly where it is needed,
instead of proofreading everything again.

**Delete OCR Temporary Files** clears any leftover job files from QUILL's data
folder and tells you what it removed. The local tools normally clean up after
themselves. Converted results live only in the open, unsaved document until you
choose to save.

**OCR and Conversion Services...** explains each service in plain words: the
free local converter, the local OCR engine and the optional Datalab cloud
service. For each it tells you what it does, what it is best at, whether it runs
on your computer or in the cloud, what it costs and how it is set up right now.

Two settings are there for unusual setups: the OCR recognition language
(`ocr_language`, English by default) and a path to the engine if QUILL cannot
find it (`tesseract_path`). The cloud service's other options, apart from the
key, are on the Services tab.

### Remote access

QUILL can open files from a server, save to it, and copy to it, much as it works
with files on your own computer. You can use FTP, SFTP, HTTPS, WebDAV, and
Amazon S3 (or any S3-compatible service). Every remote action is something you
choose, QUILL tells you what is happening, and nothing is written to disk before
you confirm. The commands are on **File > Open from Remote**:

- **Open from Remote...** lists every site you have saved, lets you look around
  a folder on the server, and downloads the file you choose. QUILL tells you the
  host and the expected size, saves the download to a temporary file, and opens
  it in a normal tab whose title ends with `(from site:path)`. The document is
  **read-only** until you save it back with **Save Copy to Remote...** or copy
  it to your own computer.
- **Save to Remote** writes the current document to a path you choose on one of
  your saved sites, and keeps a tilde backup next to the original.
- **Save Copy to Remote...** writes a copy to the server and leaves your local
  file as it is.
- **Manage Remote Sites...** adds, edits and deletes saved sites for all five
  kinds of server. Each site's password goes into **Windows Credential Manager**
  when it is available, or otherwise into a file protected by Windows (DPAPI).
  On a Mac, the Keychain is used.

All remote traffic uses a **verified TLS context**, a checked and encrypted
connection. Cloud addresses (S3, HTTPS, and WebDAV over HTTPS) must use HTTPS.
FTP is allowed because you chose it, usually for a computer on your own network
or an older server. Every remote connection is listed in QUILL's record of the
places it connects to, and file listings from S3 and WebDAV servers are read in
a way that a booby-trapped listing cannot take advantage of.

These commands have no keys of their own out of the box. Reach them from the
menu or the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`), or give them keys in the Keymap
Editor.

#### Editing a file over SSH

If you look after a Linux server, a Raspberry Pi or a web host, you can edit
its files over SSH as though they were on your own computer. The commands are
on **File > Open over SSH**.

1. Choose **File > Open over SSH > Quick Connect...**. The **Connect to SSH
   Server** window opens.
2. Fill in **Host or IP address**, **Port** (22 unless your server says
   otherwise) and **Username**.
3. Choose how you sign in under **Authentication**: **Password**, **Private
   key file** or **SSH agent**. For a password, type it in **Password / key
   passphrase**. For a key, type its path, or press **Browse...** to find it.
   OpenSSH, PEM and PuTTY (`.ppk`) keys all work. If your key has a
   passphrase, type that in the same box.
4. Press **Connect**. QUILL says "Connecting to" and the server's name, and
   then opens the **Open Remote File** window on your home folder.
5. Arrow through the list. Folders say "dir" in front of their names.
   Press Enter on a folder to go into it, or on **.. (parent directory)** to go
   back up. Press Enter on the file you want, or choose **Open**.

The file opens in a normal tab, and the status bar says that saving uploads it
back. Press `Ctrl+S` as usual, and QUILL sends your changes to the server,
keeps a backup copy of the old version next to it with a tilde on the end of
its name, and keeps the line endings the file already had.

If you connect to the same server often, save it once in **File > Open over
SSH > Site Manager...**. The **SSH Site Manager** window lists your **Saved
sites**, with **New**, **Edit** and **Delete** buttons beside the list. Pick a
site and press **Connect**. A saved site never keeps your password: QUILL asks
for it each time you connect.

QUILL is careful about which servers it trusts. It only connects to a server
whose identity your computer already knows, from the same list OpenSSH uses,
or one you have already told QUILL to trust. A server it has never seen is
turned away, so a server pretending to be yours cannot slip in. If you really
do want QUILL to accept a new server the first time it sees it, turn on
**Trust SSH hosts on first connection** on the **Administration** page of
Settings. Leave it off unless you have a reason.

### GitHub remote files

QUILL can browse GitHub repositories, open files from them and save your changes
back, without Git, the GitHub CLI or GitHub Desktop installed.

#### Getting started with GitHub

The first time you use a GitHub feature, QUILL asks you to confirm that it may
connect to GitHub. You are asked once, and QUILL remembers your answer.

You do not need a GitHub account to browse public repositories. For private
repositories, and for anything that changes GitHub, you need a Personal Access
Token (PAT).

##### Creating a Personal Access Token

1. Go to github.com and sign in.
2. Open Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens > Tokens
   (classic).
3. Choose Generate new token.
4. Give it a name such as "QUILL" and select the `repo` scope (or `public_repo`
   if you only need public repositories).
5. Copy the token. You will only see it once.

QUILL keeps your token safely in **Windows Credential Manager**. It is never
saved in a text file.

##### Managing your GitHub account

Use **File > Open from Remote > Manage GitHub Accounts...** to:

- See which GitHub account you are signed in as.
- Add or replace a token.
- Sign out and clear your stored token.

##### If the GitHub commands are missing

GitHub access is the feature called GitHub Remote Access (`core.github_remote`).
If you can't find it, open **File > Open from Remote** and check whether the
GitHub items are there. If PyGithub is not installed, QUILL shows a message
explaining how to install it: `pip install "quill[github]"`. The GitHub commands
are also unavailable in Safe Mode.

#### Opening and saving GitHub files

##### The repository browser

Open **File > Open from Remote > GitHub Repository...**. The browser has these
parts:

- **Account** shows your GitHub username, or "Anonymous" if no token is stored.
- **Repository**: type an owner/repo name such as `microsoft/vscode` and press
  Enter or choose Load.
- **Branch or tag** chooses which version of the repository to browse. It starts
  on the repository's default branch.
- **Current path** shows where you are in the folder tree.
- **File list** lists folders and files, folders first.
- **Status** shows progress messages and item counts.

To move around:

- Press Enter on a folder to open it.
- Press Enter on a file to open it (the same as choosing Open File).
- Press Backspace to go up one level.
- Press `F5` to refresh the current folder.
- Tab through the buttons: **Open File**, **Go Up**, **Refresh**, **Copy URL**,
  **Cancel**.

##### Opening a file from its address

If you have the web address of a file on GitHub, perhaps from a colleague, use
**File > Open from Remote > GitHub File URL...**. Paste an address like
`https://github.com/owner/repo/blob/branch/path/to/file` and press Enter. QUILL
fetches the file directly.

GitHub's file service only handles files up to 1 MB. A larger file has to be
downloaded by hand from github.com.

##### Saving back to GitHub

When you have opened a file from GitHub and made changes, use
**File > Open from Remote > Save to GitHub...**. QUILL asks for a commit
message. Type a short description of your changes and press Enter. QUILL commits
your changes to the same repository, branch and file path.

- You need a token with permission to write (`repo` scope).
- If the file changed on GitHub after you opened it, QUILL tells you to refresh
  and try again.
- Pressing Save never does this for you. You choose Save to GitHub each time.

#### The GitHub Items viewer

**File > Open from Remote > GitHub Items...** opens a viewer for a repository's
issues, pull requests, branches, commits, tags, releases, workflows and workflow
runs. It is the same kind of overview the GitHub website gives you, made for the
keyboard and a screen reader. It owes a great deal to
[GHManage](https://github.com/kellylford/GHManage), Kelly Ford's open-source
GitHub browser for screen-reader users, which QUILL has followed from the start.
QUILL adds its own touches: pull request and branch differences are read through
the same engine as Compare Documents instead of as a raw patch, and the Quick
filter stays quiet while you type.

You can browse without signing in. Signing in adds the **Batch...** menu and the
**Actions...** menu, for things like new issues and pull requests, merging,
deleting branches, running workflows and replying to comments. Your pins,
favorites and column choices are saved on your own computer only.

##### Loading a repository

Type a repository as `owner/repo`, paste a `github.com` address, or paste a
`git@github.com:` remote, and press **Load**. QUILL turns any of those into
`owner/repo` for you. If the document you are editing came from GitHub, or lives
in a git folder whose `origin` remote points at GitHub, the repository is
already filled in.

- **Pinned...** opens a menu of your pinned repositories. Choose one to load it
  straight away, or pin or unpin the repository you have loaded. It is your own
  short list for the few repositories you really work in. It is separate from
  anything GitHub keeps and never synced anywhere.
- **Favorites.** Press `Ctrl+D` on any row (an issue, a pull request, a branch,
  a release) to bookmark it. The **Favorites...** button lists every bookmark
  across every repository. Choose one to open it in your browser. Favorites are
  kept between sessions.
- **View Upstream.** When the repository you load is a fork, the
  **View Upstream** button becomes available. Press it to load the repository it
  was forked from, just as if you had typed its name. The button stays
  unavailable for a repository that is not a fork, or, rarely, for a fork whose
  parent GitHub cannot find.

##### Views and the list

Pick a **View**: Issues & PRs (issues and pull requests together), Branches,
Commits, Tags, Releases, Workflows or Workflow Runs. The list shows one row per
item, and the **Details** box below shows the full text of the selected row. In
Issues & PRs you can also filter by **Show** (Both, Issues, PRs) and **State**
(Open, Closed, All), and **Sort** by number, title, last updated or number of
comments.

- **List mode.** There are two ways to read the list. **Quick** shows short
  cells as they appear in the columns. **Full** says each cell as `field: value`
  (for example `number: 208, type: ISSUE, state: OPEN, title: Fix the thing`),
  so your screen reader reads a line that explains itself instead of bare
  values. Switch with the **List mode** choice, or press `M` in the list.
- **Columns...** lists every field for the current view as a checkbox. Uncheck
  the ones you don't need (at least one always stays). Your choice is remembered
  for each view.
- **View More** loads the next page of results.

##### Searching and filtering

- **Search with GitHub's own syntax.** Press `Ctrl+F` (or Tab to the Search
  box), type any GitHub search, such as `label:bug is:open crash`,
  `author:alice is:pr` or `created:>2026-01-01 no:assignee`, and press Enter.
  The results replace the Issues & PRs list, limited to the loaded repository.
  Clear the box and press Enter to get the normal list back. Loading another
  repository also clears the search.
- **Quick filter.** `Ctrl+Shift+F` moves to the **Quick filter** box, next to
  Search. Instead of asking GitHub, it narrows the list you already have, as you
  type. Nothing goes over the network, so it is instant even on a slow
  connection. It never moves your focus while you type, and it doesn't announce
  a count after every letter, which would talk over your screen reader's own
  typing echo. QUILL only says the count when a real fetch finishes. Press
  Escape in the box to clear it. Switching views or loading another repository
  clears it too.

##### Reading issues, pull requests and comments

When you select an issue or pull request, the details show its text and then
load the comments. Press `Alt+N` for the next comment and `Alt+P` for the
previous one. QUILL selects and scrolls to each and says "Comment N of M" (and
"first" or "last" at either end).

**AI thread summaries.** Select an issue or pull request and press
**Summarize**. QUILL's AI boils the whole discussion, text and comments, down to
a short summary in plain prose: what it is about, where it stands, open
questions and the next step. It goes at the top of the details and is read out.
It uses the same AI connection and consent questions as every other AI feature
in QUILL. If AI is not set up, Summarize offers to set it up instead of failing
quietly.

##### Pull request diffs and branch comparisons

- **Pull request diffs.** Select a pull request and press **Diff...**. A list of
  its changed files opens, each row reading `status: filename +added -removed`.
  Select a file to hear its changes through the same engine as
  **Compare Documents**, for example "Difference 2 of 5. Text changed at line
  41", with both sides labeled (`main:` and `this PR:`) and the changed words
  described. A new file reads as its content, a deleted file says so plainly,
  and a binary or very large file falls back to its change counts and GitHub's
  patch text.
- **Compare two branches.** In the **Branches** view, select a branch and press
  **Compare...** or `Ctrl+Shift+B`. QUILL asks for the base branch, then the
  branch to compare with it (the row you selected fills in the second question).
  It tells you how far ahead and behind the two branches are and lists every
  commit between them. The **Changed Files** tab walks each file's differences
  the same way **Diff...** does. Comparing only reads, so it works without
  signing in.

##### Workflows

Switch to the **Workflows** view to see the repository's workflow definitions,
the `.yml` files themselves. The **Workflow Runs** view below them shows run
history. Select a workflow and press Enter, or use
**Actions... > Run "name" on Branch...**, to run it: QUILL asks for a branch,
confirms, and tells you whether GitHub accepted the run. You need to be signed
in. If the workflow does not accept manual runs, QUILL shows GitHub's own
explanation.

##### Batch operations

The list lets you select several rows: hold Shift or Ctrl to select issues or
pull requests, then press **Batch...** and choose Close, Reopen or Add label.
You must be signed in, because browsing without an account only ever reads. A
confirmation names the exact action and the exact item numbers, and nothing
changes on GitHub until you confirm. If some items fail, QUILL tells you which,
and the rest still go through.

##### Keys in the Items viewer

- Enter on a row opens it in your browser. On a **Branch** row, Enter shows that
  branch's commits. On a **Workflow** row, Enter runs it on a branch you choose.
- Backspace in the Commits view (reached with Enter on a branch) goes back to
  the branch list.
- `Ctrl+R` refreshes the current view. `Ctrl+O` opens the selected item in your
  browser. `Ctrl+G` goes to an issue or pull request by number (in the Issues &
  PRs view).
- `Ctrl+F` moves to the GitHub search box, and `Ctrl+Shift+F` to the Quick
  filter box. `Ctrl+Shift+B` compares two branches (Branches view). `Ctrl+D`
  adds the selected row to your favorites.

The Items viewer follows the same rules as the other GitHub commands: it is off
in Safe Mode, asks for your consent the first time, and works without an account
for public repositories (GitHub allows fewer requests then) or with your stored
token for private ones.

##### Doing more from the Items viewer

When you are signed in, the **Actions...** button opens a menu that changes with
what you are looking at:

- In **Issues & PRs**: **New Issue...** and **New Pull Request...** ask for a
  title (and, for a pull request, the head and base branches) and an optional
  description. If exactly one unmerged pull request is selected,
  **Merge Pull Request #N...** appears too. Merging changes the target branch
  for everyone, so you confirm it by typing the pull request number again, not
  just by pressing Yes.
- With comments loaded: **Reply to Thread...** posts a new comment. (GitHub's
  comments are not threaded, so a reply is simply another comment in the same
  conversation.) Once you have used `Alt+N` or `Alt+P` to land on a comment,
  **Edit This Comment...** and **Delete This Comment...** appear as well. GitHub
  only lets you edit or delete your own comments, so trying it on someone else's
  brings back GitHub's permission error. To delete, you type "delete" to
  confirm.
- In **Branches**: select one branch and **Delete Branch 'name'...** appears.
  Type the branch name again to confirm. It cannot be undone from QUILL.
  **Compare...** is here too, and needs no sign-in.
- In **Workflows**: select one workflow and **Run "name" on Branch...** appears,
  the same as pressing Enter.
- In **Workflow Runs**: select one run and **Re-run Workflow** and
  **View Artifacts...** both appear.

All of these need you to be signed in. Without an account, the viewer only
reads.

##### Downloading workflow run artifacts

Select a workflow run and choose **Actions... > View Artifacts...** to see that
run's build artifacts, each with its size and whether GitHub has already let it
expire (an expired artifact can't be downloaded). From there:

- **Download Selected...** downloads the highlighted artifact, and
  **Download All...** downloads every artifact in the run. Both ask you to
  choose a folder first.
- If a file with that name is already in the folder, QUILL asks before replacing
  it.
- A progress window with a **Cancel** button follows the download. Cancelling
  stops after the artifact that is downloading at the moment.
- **Refresh** fetches the list again, which helps while a run is still producing
  artifacts, and **Open Run in Browser** takes you to the run's page on GitHub.

A note on your token: GitHub hands the actual download to a different,
short-lived address (usually on Azure Blob Storage). QUILL makes that second
request without your token, so your token is only ever sent to github.com.

#### Managing repositories

These commands are on **Tools > Git and GitHub > GitHub**. They let you do
things you would otherwise open a browser for. All of them need you to be signed
in. If you are not, QUILL offers to sign you in right there.

##### Repository administration

- **Create Repository...** asks for a name, a description, private or public,
  and an optional organization. Right after creating it, QUILL offers to set up
  a local folder synced to the new repository in one step, using the same folder
  sync as **Sync Folder with GitHub** (QUILL Sync). Starting a new project never
  means leaving QUILL.
- **Fork Repository...** forks into your account or an organization you choose,
  and offers to sync it locally afterwards in the same way.
- **Rename Repository...** renames it. GitHub sends the old address on to the
  new one, but anything elsewhere that has the old name written into it will
  need updating. You confirm by typing the repository's current `owner/repo`
  name again.
- **Change Visibility...** switches a repository between private and
  public. QUILL tells you which it is now before asking. Making a repository
  public adds a warning line, because its whole history becomes visible. You
  confirm by typing the repository name again.
- **Change Default Branch...** loads the branches and lets you pick the new
  default from a simple list.
- **Configure Branch Protection...** is a short wizard. Pick a branch, then set
  the required approving reviews, required status checks, and whether the rules
  apply to administrators too. Or check "Remove all protection from this branch
  instead" to clear the rules.
- **Delete Branch...** lists the branches (never the default branch, so you
  cannot delete the one everything depends on by accident), then asks you to
  type the branch name again to confirm. It can't be undone from inside QUILL.
- **Commit Multiple Files...** lets you pick one or more files on your computer,
  choose the branch and write a commit message. QUILL commits them all to GitHub
  together in one commit. This is different from **Save to GitHub**, which only
  commits the document you have open. Only plain text (UTF-8) files are
  supported.

The four riskiest actions, renaming, changing visibility, deleting a branch and
(in the Items viewer) merging a pull request, all ask you to type the exact name
or number instead of answering Yes or No. A stray press of Enter on one of these
is much harder to put right than most things in QUILL.

All eight are in the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`). They have no keys out of
the box. You can give any of them one in the Keymap Editor (**Tools > Customize and Support > Keymap Editor...**).

##### Organizations, releases, notifications and security alerts

Five more commands on **Tools > Git and GitHub > GitHub**:

- **Browse Organization Repositories...** lists the organizations your account
  belongs to, then that organization's repositories. Choose one to open it in
  the GitHub Items viewer. This is for browsing only. QUILL does not manage
  organization teams or their permissions.
- **Create Release...** asks for a tag and an optional title, then either your
  own release notes or GitHub's automatic notes (a summary of pull requests
  merged since the last release), and whether to save it as a draft or publish
  it straight away.
- **Dispatch Workflow...** runs a GitHub Actions workflow on a branch or tag you
  choose, the same as "Run workflow" on github.com. It is useful for workflows
  set up to be started by hand.
- **Notifications...** is a real inbox: every notification for your account,
  across every repository, not just the one you have loaded. Each tells you
  whether it is read or unread, which repository it is from and why you got it.
  Choosing one opens your GitHub notifications page and marks it read.
- **Security Alerts...** lists a repository's open Dependabot alerts (severity,
  the package affected and a summary), so you can see what needs attention
  without opening a browser.

##### Codespaces and Copilot CLI

Four more commands on **Tools > Git and GitHub > GitHub** use the `gh`
command-line tool installed on your own computer, instead of QUILL's usual
GitHub connection. If you don't have `gh` yet, see Downloading git and the
GitHub CLI elsewhere in this guide.

- **Codespaces...** lists your active Codespaces (name, repository and state).
  Select one for a menu to **Stop** or **Delete** it.
- **Create Codespace...** asks for a repository and an optional branch, then
  creates a Codespace.
  **Codespaces use GitHub compute and storage minutes and may cost money.** This
  is the one GitHub command in QUILL that says so, and it asks you to confirm,
  naming the cost, before it does anything.
- **Ask Copilot for a Command...** lets you describe in plain words what you
  want to do (for example, "undo my last commit") and shows the command GitHub
  Copilot suggests.
- **Explain a Command...** asks for a git or `gh` command you don't recognize
  and shows Copilot's plain explanation of what it does.

These four are new. They have been tested with a stand-in for `gh`, but not yet
with a real Codespaces repository or real Copilot CLI access. If something looks
wrong, please tell us through **Help > Get Help from Support**.

### Command-line launching

You can start QUILL from a command line, a script or a shortcut, and tell it
which file to open and where to put the cursor. Most people never need this. It
is handy when another tool, such as a search or a list of errors, hands you a
file name and line number.

The command is `quill.exe`, the launcher that comes with both the installed and
the portable copy. During setup, the installer offers an "Add Quill to PATH"
option. Turn it on and `quill` works from any Command Prompt or PowerShell
window without the full path. If you skipped that option, use the full path
instead (usually `"%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Quill for All\quill.exe"` for an
install just for you). From a source checkout, the command is `python -m quill`.

These are the options:

- `--help`: show the command help and exit.
- `--version`: print QUILL's version and exit without opening the window.
- `--safe-mode`: start with optional features switched off.
- `--reset-profile`: reset the feature profile store before starting.
- `--diagnostics`: start with diagnostics tracing on.
- `--dump-stacks`: write a thread-stack dump and exit.
- `--line N`: the line (counting from 1) for the first file you open.
- `--column M`: the column (counting from 1) for the first file you open.
- `--goto FILE[:LINE[:COL]]`: open a file at a line and column in one argument
  (both optional, counting from 1). It is the short form of `--line` and
  `--column`, handy when a linter, a search result or a build error gives you a
  `file:line:column` string. Example: `--goto main.kt:27:5`.
- `--diff LEFT RIGHT`: open two files straight into compare mode, on the first
  difference, without opening each one by hand.
- `--new-window`: start a new copy of QUILL instead of handing the file to the
  one already running.
- `--wait`: when handing the file to a QUILL that is already running, wait until
  that QUILL closes.

Some examples:

- `quill --version`
- `quill notes.md --line 40 --column 5`
- `quill --goto main.kt:27:5`
- `quill --diff old-draft.md new-draft.md`
- `quill --new-window notes.md`

### What you learned, and where to go next

You can now open files, including ones that have moved, and save them in the
format you need. You know what each kind of document gets in QUILL, what carries
over when you convert, and how to convert one file or a whole folder. You can
rescue a scanned PDF, work with files on a server or on GitHub, and start QUILL
from a command line.

To practise with QUILL open, choose **Help > Tutorials...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F1`) and
try "Write and save your first document" and "Open anything, save as anything".
On the website, [Rescue a scanned
PDF](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/03-rescue-a-scanned-pdf.html), [From
document to published
audiobook](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/04-document-to-audiobook.html)
and [GitHub inside
QUILL](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/08-github-inside-quill.html) walk
through the longer jobs.

Next, Chapter 4, Writing and editing, is where you start shaping the words
themselves.

## Chapter 4: Writing and editing

This chapter is about the work you do most: typing, fixing, moving text
around and putting things in. It starts with the keys you already know from
other Windows programs, then shows the extras QUILL adds, such as a tray of
twelve clipboards, abbreviations that type for you, and an emoji picker that
describes every emoji in words. Read the first few topics now. The rest will
keep until you want them.

### Writing and editing

Start with the commands you already know. They work in QUILL exactly as they
do everywhere else:

- `Ctrl+Z` to undo
- `Ctrl+Y` to redo
- `Ctrl+X`, `Ctrl+C` and `Ctrl+V` to cut, copy and paste
- `Ctrl+A` to select everything

Once those feel at home, QUILL has more to offer. You can put text away in a
numbered slot and paste it back with one chord, get back something you
deleted and drop it somewhere else, and run any command twenty times in a
row. Each has its own topic below.

#### Ending a line without a new paragraph (Shift+Enter)

**Line Break** (`Shift+Enter`) ends the line **without starting a new
paragraph**, the same key Word uses. In Markdown a blank line between two
lines makes two paragraphs, while a line break makes two lines of one
paragraph. Use it for an address block, a verse, or a run of short lines that
should sit close together.

QUILL writes the break in the style set in **Settings > Editing >
Markdown line break style** (`markdown_hard_break_style`), and says which one
it used. The default is a **backslash** at the end of the line. The other
style, two spaces at the end of the line, cannot be seen on screen, is not
spoken by a screen reader, and is often removed by other programs when they
save. QUILL reads both styles, so a document written elsewhere with two
spaces still shows its breaks correctly here.

QUILL Lite has the same command on **Edit > Insert > Line Break**, on the
same key.

### The Edit menu

The **Edit** menu holds the commands you use while writing. The standard
clipboard commands come first:

- Undo
- Redo
- Cut
- Copy
- Paste
- **Paste Text Only** (`Ctrl+Shift+V`), which pastes the words on the
  clipboard and leaves behind any fonts, colours or links that came with them.
  If something is selected, the pasted text replaces it.
- **Copy With Attribution** (`Alt+Shift+C`)
- Select All

**Magic Paste** (press the QUILL key, then `Shift+V`) looks at what is on the
clipboard before it pastes, and tells you what it found: plain text, a web
address, Markdown, HTML or an image. Then it offers the ways that kind of
thing can go in. A web address can go in as a Markdown link, Markdown can
keep its formatting, HTML can come in as clean text or exactly as it is, and
an image can go in as a picture reference. Plain text is always one of the
choices. Arrow to the one you want and press **Paste**.

After those come the commands that know about selection and position:

- **Find...**, **Replace...**, **Find Next**, **Find Previous** and **Find All
  Matches**. The Replace dialog has a **Replace All** button, so bulk
  replacement happens in the same place.
- **Word Prediction...** opens inline word and tag suggestions (`Ctrl+.`).
- **Extend Selection Mode** turns selection growth into a mode of its own.
- The **Selection** submenu: Select Word, Select Line, Select Paragraph,
  Select Block, Select to Start or End of Line, Select to Start or End of
  Document, and the mark commands: **Set Temporary Mark**, **Jump to Previous
  Mark**, **Swap Cursor and Mark** and **List Recent Marks**. Selecting text,
  later in this chapter, has the keys.
- **Search Tools**, with Count Occurrences, Multi Replace and the regular
  expression tools (Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 cover them).
- **Paste HTML as Markdown** turns rich HTML from the clipboard into Markdown
  as it pastes.
- **Paste Markdown as HTML** does the opposite. It turns Markdown on the
  clipboard into a clean piece of HTML, using the same renderer as the live
  preview and HTML export, and inserts it at the cursor. It has no key at
  first; give it one in the Keymap Editor.
- **Follow Link** (`Ctrl+Enter`), on the **Navigate** menu, opens the link
  under the caret. Adding a link is on the **Insert** menu.
- The delete group, on **Format > Line**: **Delete to Line Start**, **Delete
  to Line End**, **Delete to Document Start**, **Delete to Document End** and
  **Delete Paragraph** remove text measured from the cursor. Edit > Restore
  Deleted Text, below, brings the last three back.

**Preferences...** and **Customize Menus...** are with the rest of QUILL's
settings, under **Tools > Customize and Support**.

#### Find and Replace

By default `Ctrl+F` and `Ctrl+H` open the standard Windows Find and Replace
dialog. Turn on **Settings > Navigation and QUILL Key > Use QUILL's own Find dialog** and they open
QUILL's own accessible Find dialog instead. It does everything the Windows one
does, and adds these:

- **Extended mode (special characters).** Choose *Extended* in the Mode list
  to search for characters you cannot type: `\n` for a line break, `\t` for a
  tab, `\xNN` or `\uNNNN` by code, or `\N{EM DASH}` by name. The **Insert
  Special Character...** button offers forty named characters, such as the
  non-breaking space, curly quotes, the zero-width space and the soft hyphen.
  Those invisible characters can quietly spoil a document, and now you can
  find them by name. Replacements understand the same codes, so "replace every
  non-breaking space with a plain space" takes two fields.
- **A spoken match count as you type.** Pause for a moment and QUILL says
  "17 matches", so you know the search is right before you go.
- **Peek navigation.** `Ctrl+Down` and `Ctrl+Up` step through the matches
  while you stay in the search field. Each step speaks the match in its
  sentence and selects it in the editor, and you can keep typing at any
  moment. Look around first, then press Enter when the search is right.
- **Spoken match context.** Each match is read as the sentence around it
  ("line 40: ...the quick brown fox..."), not just a position. QUILL always
  tells you when the search wraps past the end of the document.
- **A Direction group with a name.** The Up and Down choice is a labelled
  group, so your screen reader says "Direction" when you reach it.
- **One dialog, always.** `Ctrl+F` while it is open takes you back to the
  search field. `Ctrl+H` switches it to Replace without opening another
  window. `Ctrl+L` jumps back to the search field from anywhere in the dialog.
  Escape closes it and returns you to your text. **Count** tells you how many
  matches there are without moving anywhere.

The setting is off when QUILL is installed, while the dialog is tested with
every screen reader. The Windows dialog is unchanged, and you can switch back
at any time. For now this dialog searches the current document only.
Searching folders or the Vault from it will come later.

Chapter 6, Moving around and finding things, has much more on searching.

### Selecting text

You can select the usual way, holding Shift while you move. QUILL also gives
you ways to select a whole unit at once, to mark where a selection starts and
finish it later, and to leave yourself marks to jump back to.

#### Anchor selection with F8

With anchor selection you drop an invisible anchor, move anywhere you like,
and then select everything between the anchor and the cursor.

| Key | Command | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `F8` | Start selection | Sets an invisible anchor at the cursor. |
| `Ctrl+Alt+F8` | Toggle selection marker | Drops the anchor without moving the cursor, or picks it back up if you change your mind. |
| `Shift+F8` | Complete selection | Selects from the anchor to the cursor and says how much. |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F8` | Reselect | Brings back the last selection you made. |
| `Alt+Shift+F8` | Go to start of selection | Moves to the start of the selection without changing it. |
| `Ctrl+F8` | Copy all | Copies the whole document. |
| `Ctrl+Shift+A` | Unselect all | Drops the selection, leaving the cursor where it is. |
| `Alt+F8` | Read all | Reads the document from the beginning. |

#### Selecting by structure

| Key | Command | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Shift+W` | Select word | Selects the word the cursor is in. |
| `Ctrl+Space` | Select sentence | Selects the sentence the cursor is in. |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Space` | Select token | Selects the run of characters the cursor is in, whatever kind they are. On a word it is the same as Select Word; its real use is a run of punctuation, such as the `::` in a path, or the spaces at the start of a line. |
| `Ctrl+Shift+E` | Select line | Selects the whole line. |
| `Ctrl+Shift+H` | Select paragraph | Selects the paragraph at the cursor and says its size and word count. |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+B` | Select block | Selects the indented block at the cursor. |
| `Ctrl+Shift+X` | Expand selection | Grows the selection one step: line, then paragraph, then block, then the whole document. |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+X` | Shrink selection | Undoes the last expand step. |
| `Alt+Shift+F5` | Select section | Selects the section at the cursor with all its subsections, and says how many sections and lines that is. Cut and paste then move it anywhere. |

The ordinary selection keys are on the **Edit > Selection** menu too, so you
can find them there if you forget: **Select to Start of Line** (`Shift+Home`),
**Select to End of Line** (`Shift+End`), **Select to Start of Document**
(`Ctrl+Shift+Home`) and **Select to End of Document** (`Ctrl+Shift+End`).

Once something is selected, **Duplicate Selection** (`Ctrl+Alt+Q`) puts a copy
of it straight after itself, which saves a copy and a paste when you are
building a list of similar lines. With nothing selected, it duplicates the
line you are on.

You can also run any of these from the Command Palette, and change their keys
in the Keymap Editor.

#### Extend Selection Mode

In Extend Selection Mode, the keys that normally move the cursor grow the
selection instead. Turn it on and off from the Selection menu, or with
`Alt+Shift+F9`. You can change the key in the Keymap Editor. While it is on,
**EXT** shows in the status bar.

#### The mark ring

The mark ring is a short stack of temporary places to jump back to while you
work.

| Key | Command | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Shift+M` | Set Temporary Mark | Puts a temporary mark at the cursor. |
| `Ctrl+M` | Jump to Previous Mark | Jumps to the latest mark and takes it off the ring. |
| `Ctrl+Alt+X` | Swap Cursor and Mark | Swaps the cursor with the top mark. |
| `Alt+M` | List Recent Marks | Shows every mark with its line and column. |

#### Named marks and the review buffer

Named marks last for the whole session. Find them on **Edit > Selection**:

- **Set Named Mark** gives the cursor position a name and remembers it, and
  tells you the line and column.
- **Jump to Named Mark** shows a list of your marks with their positions.
  Choose one and you are there.
- **Review Buffer** opens the current selection in a read-only window, so
  you can read through it with your screen reader without any risk of
  changing it. You need a selection first. Its key is `Alt+Shift+U`.

Set Named Mark and Jump to Named Mark have no keys at first. Give them keys in
the Keymap Editor, or use the Selection menu.

### Getting text back, and doing it again

#### Restore Deleted Text

Undo (`Ctrl+Z`) puts your last edit back exactly where it was. Sometimes you
want something else: you deleted a sentence, and now you want to put it
somewhere *else*. **Edit > Restore Deleted Text...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Z`)
remembers the last three pieces of text you removed with QUILL's delete
commands (delete to start or end of line, delete to start or end of document,
and delete paragraph). Pick one from the list and it goes in at the cursor.

- The list is newest first, with a short preview and the length of each, so
  you can tell them apart by ear.
- If only one deletion is remembered, it comes straight back with no list.
- To change its key, search for "Restore Deleted Text" in the Keymap Editor.

Fans of the classic WordPerfect Editor will know this as its "Cancel" buffer,
except that here you choose where the text lands.

#### Repeat Next Command

When you need to do the same thing many times, such as moving down twenty
lines, deleting ten words, typing forty dashes or replaying a macro, you do
not have to press the key over and over. Choose **Edit > Repeat Next
Command...**, type how many times, and the *next* command you run happens
that many times. Then the count clears itself and editing carries on as
normal.

- It works with nearly any command, including moving, deleting, inserting and
  a recorded macro.
- The most it will repeat is 1000 times, so a slip of the finger cannot run
  away with you.
- It has no key at first. If you use it often, give it one in the Keymap
  Editor (**Tools > Customize and Support > Keymap Editor...**; search for
  "Repeat Next Command").

This is the "Repeat" command from the classic WordPerfect Editor.

### Copy Tray

The Copy Tray is **twelve** clipboards of your own, each with a number. You
put text in a slot on purpose, and it stays there until you replace it or
clear it, even after you close and reopen QUILL. The Windows clipboard is
shared by every program and changes every time you copy. Copy Tray slots
belong to QUILL alone.

#### Pasting and copying with a slot

**To paste from a slot, hold `Ctrl+Alt+Shift` and press a number key.**

| Key | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+1` through `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+9` | Paste from slots 1 to 9 |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+0` | Paste from slot 10 |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+-` | Paste from slot 11 |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+=` | Paste from slot 12 |

**To copy into a slot, press the QUILL key and then the same key with Shift:**

| Key | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+1` through `Shift+9` | Copy the selection to slots 1 to 9 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+0` | Copy the selection to slot 10 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+-` | Copy the selection to slot 11 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+=` | Copy the selection to slot 12 |

A paste chord does more if you press it quickly more than once:

- **Press once** to paste the slot at the cursor.
- **Press twice** to peek. QUILL reads the slot to you without pasting it, so
  you can check what is there first.
- **Press three times** to open the Copy Tray dialog on that slot.

> **QUILLBee's tip:** Can't remember what is in slot 3? Press
> `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+3` twice, quickly. QUILL reads it to you and pastes nothing.

#### Copy to Next Empty Slot, Copy to Tray Slot and Search Tray Slots

**Edit > Copy Tray > Copy to Next Empty Slot** (`Ctrl+Alt+Y`) copies the
selection to the first slot, from 1 to 12, that is empty and not pinned, and
tells you which: "Copied to slot 4 (first empty)." If all twelve slots are
full, QUILL tells you so and overwrites nothing.

**Edit > Copy Tray > Copy to Tray Slot...** (`Alt+Shift+Y`) lets you choose
the slot yourself, from a list. Each row says what is in that slot now, its
label if it has one, and whether it is pinned, so you know what you would be
replacing before you replace it. Arrow to the slot and press Enter. QUILL
says "Copied to tray slot 3", or "Replaced tray slot 3" if something was
there already.

**Edit > Copy Tray > Search Tray Slots...** opens a small search box. Type a
word or phrase and QUILL searches the text and labels of every slot and reads
you the matches. Press the slot's number to paste it, or Escape to cancel.

#### Pinned slots

In the Copy Tray dialog you can pin any slot. A pinned slot:

- Is never filled by Copy to Next Empty Slot.
- Is read with "pinned" in front: "Slot 1 (pinned, signature)".
- Stays pinned after a restart (the pin is saved in `copy_tray.json`).

To pin or unpin a slot, open the Copy Tray dialog (`Ctrl+Alt+V`), choose the
slot, and press the Pin/Unpin button.

#### The Copy Tray dialog

Open it with `Ctrl+Alt+V`, or **Edit > Copy Tray > Open Copy Tray...**. It
lists all twelve slots. Each row has the slot number, a label if you gave it
one, and a preview of the text. Move with the arrow keys. The buttons are:

- **Paste** puts the chosen slot's text at the cursor. Enter or a double-click
  on a row does the same.
- **Paste from Clipboard** stores what is on the Windows clipboard in the
  chosen slot.
- **Pin / Unpin** pins or unpins the chosen slot.
- **Save Changes** keeps edits you typed straight into the content area.
- **Clear Slot** empties the chosen slot.
- **Close** closes without pasting.

To empty every slot at once, choose **Edit > Copy Tray > Clear All Tray
Slots** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y`). QUILL asks first and tells you how many slots
have something in them, with **No** already chosen, because this cannot be
undone. If the tray is already empty, it just says so.

#### Other ways to reach the tray

- **The Paste from Tray submenu.** **Edit > Copy Tray > Paste from Tray**
  lists every slot that has something in it, with its label and a preview:
  "1 signature, Hi, I wanted to follow...". Your screen reader reads both as
  you move through the submenu.
- **The status bar.** The `Slots: X/12` cell shows how many of the twelve
  slots are in use. Click it to open the Copy Tray dialog. If you cannot find
  it, add it in **Tools > Customize and Support > Status Bar Layout...**.
- **The system tray.** QUILL's icon in the system tray has a Copy Tray
  submenu listing every slot in use. Choose one to paste it into the active
  editor, without bringing QUILL to the front first.

#### Copy Tray tips

- Put a signature, a disclaimer or a heading you use all the time in slot 1
  and pin it. One chord pastes it anywhere, and Copy to Next Empty Slot will
  never overwrite it.
- Label your slots for a research session: slot 1 "intro quote", slot 2
  "methodology note", slot 3 "source URL". Copy one piece into each as you
  read, then paste them in order as you write.
- Slots survive restarts, so you can keep a small set of pieces you reach for
  every day.
- You can change every Copy Tray key in the Keymap Editor (**Tools > Customize
  and Support > Keymap Editor...**).

### Clip Library

The twelve Copy Tray slots are for things you chose to keep. The **Clip
Library**, on the **Edit** menu, is a second, bigger store: a searchable
history of up to 200 clips.

- **Edit > Keep Selection in Clip Library** (`Ctrl+Alt+M`) remembers the
  current selection. Keeping the same text again from the same place does
  nothing, because it is already there.
- **Edit > Open Clip Library...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M`) opens the library.
  Search as you type, **Favorite** a clip so it is never pushed out as the
  history fills up, **Remove** one you no longer need, **Copy to Clipboard**,
  or **Promote to Copy Tray...** to give a clip a labelled slot of its own.
- **Rename...** gives a clip a short name, which is much easier to find later
  than its first few words. Leave the name empty to go back to a preview of
  the text.
- **Combine Marked...** joins several clips into one piece of text. Mark them
  with Ctrl or Shift (plain arrow keys still choose just one), choose what goes
  between them (space, comma, full stop, vertical bar, new line or blank line),
  and the joined text goes on the clipboard in the order the clips are listed.
- **Save as Abbreviation...** turns a clip into an abbreviation. QUILL and
  Quill Inkwell share one abbreviation library, so a clip saved this way can be
  typed in every program, not just here.

**Automatic capture.** Turn on **Settings > Editing > "Automatically keep
everything you copy in the Clip Library"** (off at first) and every copy you
make inside QUILL is kept for you, whether you used the menu, its key or a
right-click Copy. It only sees copies made in QUILL, never the system
clipboard in general, and never anything you copied before you turned it on.

**Format.** What Copy to Clipboard puts on the clipboard, and what Send as
Email and Copy as Email Body send, both follow one setting: **Settings >
Editing > "Kept and sent content format"** (plain text, Markdown or HTML).
Change it once and both follow.

**What the Clip Library is not.** It remembers what you keep or copy *inside
QUILL*. It does not watch the system clipboard, and it keeps no history of
what you copy in other programs. For a clipboard history across everything
you do, use a clipboard manager alongside QUILL. The two do different jobs.

### Copy With Source

`Alt+Shift+C` copies the selection and adds a note of where it came from in
the document. With nothing selected, QUILL copies the current line. This is
handy for notes, reviews and gathering evidence.

### Links

`Ctrl+K` adds a link written the right way for the document's format.
`Ctrl+Enter` follows the link under the caret. In Markdown and HTML this makes
citations and cross-references much less work.

### The Insert menu

The **Insert** menu puts structured content at the cursor. QUILL treats
Markdown and HTML as everyday writing formats, so the tag pickers sit here
next to the other inserts.

- **Insert Link...** adds a link in the right form for the document's format.
- The **Heading** submenu: Heading 1 through 6, **Decrease Level** and
  **Increase Level**, and **Style Headings...** (font, size and alignment) for
  the current level or all levels.
- **Body Text** (`Ctrl+Alt+0`).
- The **List** submenu: **Bullet**, **Numbered**, **Task**, **List
  Manager...** and **Structured List Studio...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+L`).
- **Insert Code Block**, **Insert Footnote**, **Insert Table...**, **Insert
  Block Quote**, **Insert Horizontal Rule**, **Insert HTML Tag...** and
  **Insert Markdown Tag...**.
- **Date and Time** (`F5`) and the **Date and Time** submenu.
- **Insert Snippet...** and **Manage Snippets...** for reusable text with
  blanks to fill in.
- **Special Character...** (`Ctrl+Shift+F2`).
- **Line Break** (`Shift+Enter`), described under Writing and editing at the
  start of this chapter.
- **Insert Emoji...** (`Alt+.`).
- **File Content...** inserts the contents of another file at the cursor.
- **Insert Equation...** (`Ctrl+Alt+=`).

The topics below explain the ones that need more than a line.

#### Headings and lists

**Heading N sets the level, it does not add one.** `Ctrl+Alt+2` on a line
that reads `### Notes` gives you `## Notes`, not `## ### Notes`. It works from
anywhere on the line, not just the start. With several lines selected, it
makes **all** of them headings in one change, so a single `Ctrl+Z` puts them
all back. Your screen reader says "Heading 2" either way, so it is good to
know QUILL gets this right.

**Body Text** (`Ctrl+Alt+0`) is the bottom rung of the `Ctrl+Alt+1` to `6`
heading ladder. It takes the heading marker off and leaves the words.

**Next Heading** is `Ctrl+Alt+H` and **Previous Heading** is
`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H`. `Ctrl+Alt+L` opens the **Outline Navigator**, the same key
QUILL Lite uses for List Headings, so either habit works, and `Ctrl+Shift+O`
opens it too. **AI Thesaurus** no longer has a key of its own; reach it from
the AI menu or the Command Palette. The plain **Thesaurus** keeps Word's
`Shift+F7`.

Bullet lists are on `Ctrl+Shift+L` and numbered lists on
`Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+L`.

#### Format-aware inserts

Block quote, horizontal rule, table and image write Markdown in a Markdown
document and HTML in an HTML document. If the document's format is not set yet
(a new or plain document), QUILL asks **"Markdown or HTML?"** the first time,
then remembers your answer for that document and stops asking.

Some have keys of their own:

- **Insert Table** is `Ctrl+Alt+T`.
- **Insert Block Quote** is the same command as **Quote Lines**
  (`Ctrl+Shift+Q`), because both wrote the same `> ` in Markdown.
  **Unquote Lines** (`Alt+Shift+.`, that is Alt, Shift and the period) takes
  the `> ` off again.
- **Insert Horizontal Rule** is `Ctrl+Alt+-`.

You can change all of them in the Keymap Editor.

**Insert Markdown Tag appears only in Markdown documents.** In a plain or
rich text document it is not on the menu at all, and if you press its key
there, QUILL just says "Markdown tags are for Markdown documents."
**Insert HTML Tag** is the same idea for HTML, except that it stays on the menu,
dimmed, in any document that is not HTML. **Navigate > Set Document
Language...** changes what kind of document you are in.

#### Special Character (Ctrl+Shift+F2)

**Special Character...** opens a picker for the 357 characters a keyboard has
no key for. Search by name (`dash`, `euro`, `acute`, `arrow`) or by a word
people use even if Unicode does not (`gbp`, `copyright`, `eszett`). Or clear
the box and browse one of fifteen groups: whitespace, dashes, quotes,
invisibles, typography, legal and reference marks, currency, maths and units,
fractions, superscripts and ordinals, arrows, accented letters (small and
capital), Greek, and punctuation from other languages.

Each row shows the character, its name and its code point, and a description
pane changes as you arrow. **The search box is also the code-point box**:
`2014`, `U+2014` and `d8212` all find the em dash, and a code point that is in
no group still works, so the picker reaches every character Unicode has. When
you insert one, QUILL tells you what it was, in Describe Character's words,
because most of these characters cannot be seen on the page.

QUILL Lite has the same picker on **Edit > Insert > Special Character...**.
Both keys can be changed in the Keymap Editor.

#### Insert Equation (Ctrl+Alt+=)

**Insert Equation...** (`Ctrl+Alt+=`) asks for a LaTeX or MathML equation in
up to two steps.

1. Type the formula in LaTeX, for example `E=mc^2` or
   `\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}`, or paste a MathML fragment.
2. For LaTeX, choose whether it sits inline in the text (`\(...\)`) or as a
   block of its own (`$$...$$`).

If a LaTeX equation is already selected when you open Insert Equation, QUILL
takes off its delimiters and puts the bare formula in the box for you. MathML
(anything starting with `<math`) goes in exactly as typed, with no second
step. Browser Preview and HTML export show equations using MathJax 3. Math
Equations, later in this guide, has the formula gallery, symbol
abbreviations, exploring an equation part by part, and Word export.

#### Word prediction and snippets

Word prediction and snippets are kept apart, so each has its own key.

1. Press `Ctrl+.` to open **Word Prediction** (also **Edit > Word
   Prediction...**).
2. Type, and matching words from your document, HTML tags and Markdown tags
   appear.
3. Arrow to the one you want and press Enter to insert it.

To set up and look after snippets:

- Press `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, S` for **Insert Snippet**.
- Press `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+S` for **Manage Snippets** (create, edit,
  delete, import, export, and starter packs).
- Open **More Preferences > Install Starter Snippet Packs** for sample sets for
  everyday writing, developer work, and support and accessibility notes.
- In **General Preferences**, turn **Word prediction and tag IntelliSense** or
  **Expand snippet triggers while typing** on or off as you like.

Snippets can have blanks such as `${input:name}`, `${choice:a|b}`, `${date}`,
`${time}` and `${cursor}`.

#### Date and time

**Date and Time** (`F5`) types the time and date at the caret and reads it
back to you. It uses Notepad's key and Notepad's layout (`14:07 16/09/2026`),
and QUILL Lite's too. It is built into QUILL, so it works in **Safe Mode**
as well.

**Insert > Date and Time** is also a submenu. The bundled Insert Tools
Quillin (`com.quill.bundled.insert-tools`) adds three items to it:

- **Insert Date** puts today's date at the cursor, in the format `${date}` uses.
- **Insert Time** puts the current time at the cursor, using `${time}`.
- **Insert Date and Time** puts both, with one space between them.

Those three are part of the Insert Tools Quillin, so they switch off with the
rest of it, and in Safe Mode. If you turn the Quillin off, the submenu stays
but its three items go. Turn it on or off in **Preferences > Quillins**, for
example if you would rather use date and time snippets of your own.

#### Insert Emoji (Alt+.)

**Insert > Insert Emoji...** (`Alt+.`) opens the Accessible Emoji Picker. It
is for the opposite case from **Special Character...**: you do not know the
code, and you want help finding the right one. You can browse or search all
3,781 standard emoji by name, keyword, symbol or a typed smiley like `:)`, and
each has a real spoken description of what it looks like. There is no grid of
pictures anywhere in it. It is a category list and a list of named results,
like QUILL's other browse-and-search windows.

There are two ways to find an emoji.

- **Search** (the box at the top) looks, in this order, for: the emoji itself
  if you paste or type one in; an old typed smiley like `:)`, `:D` or `<3`;
  part of the official Unicode name or a keyword (for example "grin", "dog"
  or "heart"); and last, part of the emoji's description. So a half-remembered
  word like "melting" or "puddle" can still find the right one even when it is
  not a keyword.
- **Category** (the list on the left) follows Unicode's own groups, largest
  first:

  | Category | Emoji |
  | --- | --- |
  | People & Body | 2,261 |
  | Flags | 270 |
  | Objects | 264 |
  | Symbols | 224 |
  | Travel & Places | 218 |
  | Smileys & Emotion | 169 |
  | Animals & Nature | 159 |
  | Food & Drink | 131 |
  | Activities | 85 |

  Clearing the search box takes you back to the category you chose last.

As you arrow through the results, the **Description** pane shows the emoji's
category and subgroup, its official name, its keywords, any old typed smiley,
and one or two sentences about what it actually looks like: colours, shapes,
expression and pose, not just its name again. Press **Insert**, or Enter on a
result, to type the emoji at your cursor and close the picker. **Cancel** or
Escape closes it without inserting anything.

**Favorites and Recent** sit above the nine Unicode categories:

- **Favorites** lists the emoji you have starred. Choose any emoji, from a
  category, a search or Recent, and press **Add to Favorites**. Once it is a
  favourite the button reads **Remove from Favorites**.
- **Recent** fills itself with the last 30 emoji you inserted, newest first.

Taking an emoji out of Favorites, or letting it drop off Recent, only changes
those two lists. The emoji is still in the picker, under its category and in
search, as before.

All 3,781 emoji, with their categories, keywords, typed smileys and
descriptions, come in one file installed with QUILL. The picker never goes
online, in Safe Mode or otherwise. The PRD's Accessible Emoji Picker section
explains how the catalogue is kept up to date.

The full list, with every description, is in Appendix C, Every emoji QUILL can
insert.

### Abbreviation Expansion

Abbreviation Expansion types longer text for you, like TextExpander. You type
a short trigger word followed by a space, full stop, comma or other
punctuation, and QUILL quietly replaces the trigger with the full text. For
example, type `btw ` (with the space at the end) and QUILL changes it to
`by the way `.

**It is off by default**, so your text never changes as you type unless you
asked for it. Turn it on when you want it; QUILL remembers your choice.

#### Turning it on and off

Any of these turns it on, and the same again turns it off:

- Press `Alt+Shift+A`, or choose **Insert > Toggle Abbreviation Expansion**.
- Click the **ABR: On / ABR: Off** cell in the status bar, if it is showing
  (add it in the status bar settings).
- Change **Abbreviation expansion** in **Settings > Editing**.

#### The built-in abbreviations

QUILL comes with fifteen abbreviations for common shorthand. You can edit or
switch off any of them, and add your own.

| Abbreviation | Expansion |
| --- | --- |
| `afaik` | as far as I know |
| `afaict` | as far as I can tell |
| `asap` | as soon as possible |
| `atm` | at the moment |
| `btw` | by the way |
| `fwiw` | for what it's worth |
| `imo` | in my opinion |
| `imho` | in my humble opinion |
| `irl` | in real life |
| `omw` | on my way |
| `tbh` | to be honest |
| `tbc` | to be confirmed |
| `tbd` | to be determined |
| `ttyl` | talk to you later |
| `wrt` | with regard to |

#### Managing your abbreviations

Open **Insert > Manage Abbreviations...** (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+A`) to
add, edit and organise your abbreviations. Each one has:

- **Abbreviation**: the short trigger word, such as `btw`.
- **Expansion**: the full text that replaces it, such as `by the way`.
- **Description**: an optional note for yourself.
- **Case sensitive**: when ticked, only the exact capitals match. Otherwise
  any capitalisation of the trigger works.
- **Enabled**: switch one off without deleting it.
- **Category**: any word you like (Work, Personal, Email) to group the list.
  There is a category filter beside the search box, and abbreviations with no
  category are listed under Uncategorised.
- **Expand after**: which keys set it off. A space or punctuation (the
  default), a space only, punctuation only, or never. **Never** means it only
  expands from Quick Insert, which suits a long expansion you would not want
  to appear by accident.
- **Speak**: what your screen reader says when it expands: nothing, the
  abbreviation, or the expanded text. You set this for each one, because a
  short one usually needs no announcement and a long template sometimes does.
- **Sound**: follow the main sound setting, always play, or never play.
- **Add a trailing space after punctuation**: adds a space after the
  punctuation that set it off, so `co.` gives `Company, ` and not
  `Company ,`. It makes no difference after a space, which already leaves one.

The **Search** box at the top of the manager filters the list as you type
any part of a trigger or its expansion. Switched-off abbreviations show
"(disabled)" after their name.

**Import** and **Export** read and write your library as a JSON file. Export
saves the whole library. Import adds a file's abbreviations to yours, skips
any it already has, and tells you how many it added.

#### Other ways to use an abbreviation

- **Expand now.** Press `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, A` (or **Insert > Expand
  Abbreviation**) to expand the word just before the cursor without typing a
  space or punctuation. Useful in the middle of a word or at the very end of
  a document.
- **Quick Insert.** **Insert > Quick Insert...** opens a list of every
  switched-on abbreviation, with the ones you use most at the top and a
  preview of each expansion. Type a few letters, arrow down, press Enter, and
  the expansion goes in at the cursor. It is how you use an abbreviation you
  have not memorised, and the only way to reach one set to expand after
  Never. It has no key at first, but you can give it one in the keyboard
  settings, and it is in the Command Palette.
- **New Abbreviation from Clipboard.** **Insert > New Abbreviation from
  Clipboard...** opens a new abbreviation with the clipboard text already in
  the expansion, so all you add is the trigger. It is the quickest way to turn
  a signature, an address or a block of standard wording into an
  abbreviation.

#### Abbreviations in every program, with Quill Inkwell

Your abbreviations also work in other programs through **Quill Inkwell**, a
small free companion app that sits in the system tray. It uses the very same
library file as QUILL. Add an abbreviation here and it works in your browser;
add one there and it works here. Open it from the QuillVille menu, and see
Quill Inkwell's own user guide for where it will and will not type.

**Abbreviations for certain programs only.** You can limit an abbreviation to
named programs, such as a signature to your mail program or a code snippet to
your code editor, by listing them in its **Applications** field. Leave the
field empty, as it is at first, and it works everywhere. This only matters in
Quill Inkwell, which types into whatever program you are in. Inside QUILL
there is only one program, so the field has no effect there. If Inkwell cannot
tell which program is in front, a limited abbreviation does **not** fire, so
it never types into the wrong place.

#### Variables in expansions

An expansion can include these:

| Placeholder | Inserts |
| --- | --- |
| `${cursor}` | Puts the cursor here after expanding |
| `${date}` | Today's date (for example June 11, 2026) |
| `${time}` | The current time (for example 02:30 PM) |
| `${clipboard}` | The text on the system clipboard |
| `${datetime}` | The date and time together |
| `${day}` | Day of the month |
| `${month}` | Month name |
| `${year}` | Four-digit year |
| `${username}` | Your Windows user name |

#### Fields that ask you something

A signature is the same every time. A letter or a bug report is the same
*except* for a name, a date or a reference number. Put a field in the
expansion and QUILL asks for it before inserting:

- `${field:Label}` asks for a value with that label.
- `${field:Label=something}` offers a starting value you can keep or change.
- The same label used twice is asked once and filled in everywhere, so a name
  in the greeting also appears in the sign-off.
- `${choice:Label|first reminder|second reminder|final notice}` gives you a
  list to choose from instead of a box to type in. Use it whenever the answer
  is one of a few known ones: choosing is one arrow key, and you never have to
  spell "Second reminder" exactly right. The first option is the default.

A small form opens with one labelled control for each field, a box to type in
or a list to choose from, in the order they appear in the text. Tab moves
between them, Enter moves to the next one, Enter on the last one accepts, and
Escape cancels and leaves your text exactly as it was. `${cursor}` still
works alongside fields: the cursor lands where the template puts it once your
answers are in. Quill Inkwell shows the same form, so a template works the
same wherever you use it.

#### Timing and sound

- **Multi-press window.** How quickly you must press a key twice or three
  times to count as a double or triple press is set in **Settings > Editing**
  as **Multi-press time window (ms)**. The default
  is 400 ms, and it can be anything from 100 to 1000 ms. Make it longer if you
  press keys slowly, or shorter if double presses happen by accident when you
  type fast.
- **Sound.** To hear a sound when an abbreviation expands, turn on **Play
  sound on abbreviation expansion** in **Settings > Editing**. You can point
  **Abbreviation expansion sound file**
  at a `.wav` file, or leave it empty for the standard system beep.

#### Abbreviations from Quillins

Installed Quillins can add abbreviations of their own. You can switch each one
on or off on that Quillin's own preferences page: open **Preferences**
(`Ctrl+Comma`) and go to the Quillin by name. For the bundled Smart Insert
Quillin, they are on its **Abbreviations** tab. These are kept apart from
your own library and never saved into it, so removing a Quillin removes its
abbreviations too. Your own abbreviations always win over a Quillin's. If two
Quillins use the same trigger, the one loaded first wins. **They work in
other programs too**, through Quill Inkwell, so a Quillin full of medical
abbreviations or company wording is useful everywhere you type.

The bundled **Smart Insert** Quillin adds four abbreviations that expand as
you type:

| Trigger | Inserts |
| --- | --- |
| `qbug` | A bug report template (Title, Build, Screen reader, Windows version, Steps, Expected, Actual, Notes) |
| `qmeet` | A meeting notes template with today's date |
| `qlog` | A date and time stamp |
| `qtodo` | A three-item to-do checklist |

Only abbreviations with fixed text expand as you type. Ones that build their
text when used, such as Smart Insert's `qbrf`, do not fire from typing the
word. Use the matching smart trigger (`=brftest()`) or the Insert menu
command instead.

#### Abbreviation tips

- Use `${cursor}` to put the cursor inside a template. For example, `sig`
  expanding to `Best regards,${cursor}Jeff` leaves the cursor just after the
  comma.
- Use case-sensitive abbreviations sparingly. Most triggers are lower case,
  and you rarely need it.
- Abbreviations expand before snippets. If a word is both, the abbreviation
  wins.
- Export your library now and then, as a backup and to copy it to another
  computer.

### Insert Automation

Insert Automation ties abbreviations, smart text triggers, `.LOG` files and
append anchors together, all from the keyboard. Everything it does is
announced and can be undone, and it only acts on an exact match. Nothing runs
in the background, and nothing reads through your file unless you asked.

#### Smart Text Triggers

A smart text trigger is a short command that starts with `=`, sits on a line
by itself, and expands when you press Enter. Because it starts with `=`, it
cannot go off by accident in the middle of a sentence.

The bundled **Smart Insert** Quillin comes with these:

| Trigger | Inserts |
| --- | --- |
| `=bug()` | A bug report template |
| `=meeting()` | Meeting notes with today's date |
| `=journal()` | A journal entry with today's date |
| `=todo()` or `=todo(5)` | A to-do checklist (5 items unless you give another number) |
| `=logentry()` | A time stamp at the cursor, in your Log Mode format |
| `=brftest()` | A predictable test document of several braille pages |
| `=rand(3,4)` | Three paragraphs of four readable sentences each |

**How to use one.** Type the trigger on a line by itself and press Enter. If
it matches, QUILL replaces the whole line with the new text and tells you what
it inserted. If it does not match, nothing happens and Enter works as usual.

**Large inserts.** If a trigger would produce more than a set amount of text
(50 paragraphs at first), QUILL asks before inserting anything. Change the
amount in **More Preferences > Smart Insert > General tab**.

**Switching triggers on and off.** Every trigger can be switched on or off in
**More Preferences > Smart Insert > Smart Triggers tab**. A switched-off trigger's
`=name()` text is simply left on the line as you typed it.

#### Log files that stamp themselves
