Numbered bookmarks give you fixed slots you set with one keystroke, no menu
and nothing to type:

- `Ctrl+Shift+1` through `Ctrl+Shift+9` set the bookmark for that slot at the
  cursor.
- `Ctrl+Shift+B` drops a bookmark in the next free slot.
- `Ctrl+Alt+B` clears them all.

To get back to one, use `F2` and `Shift+F2`, the bookmark list
(`Alt+Shift+G`), or **Go To...** (`Ctrl+G`) with Bookmark chosen. They are
stored like named bookmarks, under names such as "Quick 3", so they are kept
with the document. Going to a slot you have not set tells you so plainly.

#### Marks, bookmarks and selecting a block

These three all "mark a spot", so they are easy to mix up. Here is what each
one does.

**Bookmarks are named places that are saved.** They travel with the file, as
described above. Use **Set Named Bookmark...**, **Go To Named Bookmark...** and
**List Named Bookmarks...** when you want to name a place and come back to it
days later.

**The mark ring is a short stack of temporary jump points.** It lasts only
for the current session and is never saved.

- **Set Temporary Mark** (`Ctrl+Shift+M`) drops a point at the cursor. The
  status bar says "Mark ring point set at line ..., column ... (temporary
  jump)".
- **Jump to Previous Mark** (`Ctrl+M`) jumps back to the most recent mark and
  removes it from the ring.
- **Swap Cursor and Mark** (`Ctrl+Alt+X`) moves the cursor to the mark.
- **List Recent Marks** (`Alt+M`) shows the marks in the ring.

These commands only move the cursor. They do not select text and they do not
copy anything. In some other editors you drop a mark, move away, and cut or
copy everything in between. QUILL's mark is not that. It is a breadcrumb you
can jump back to.

**To copy or cut from one point to another, select the text.** Put the cursor
at the start, then either hold Shift while you move to the end (arrows,
`Ctrl` with the arrows, the Page keys, Home and End) or use one of the
selection commands below. Then press `Ctrl+C` to copy or `Ctrl+X` to cut.
There is no separate "copy from the mark to the cursor" command; the
selection is what gets copied.

**Selecting a block, a line or a paragraph.** A block here means the indented
block at the cursor: a run of lines at the same indent, like the inside of a
list item or a code block. The selection commands are on **Edit > Selection**:

- **Select Line** (`Ctrl+Shift+E`) selects the current line.
- **Select Paragraph** (`Ctrl+Shift+H`) selects the paragraph around the
  cursor.
- **Select Block** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+B`) selects the indented block at the
  cursor.
- **Select to Start/End of Line** and **Select to Start/End of Document**.
- **Expand Selection** (`Ctrl+Shift+X`) grows the selection one step at a
  time: word, line, paragraph, block, document, telling you the new size each
  time.

Each one tells you what it selected and how many words, so you know exactly
what you have before you copy or delete it.

### Favorite folders

Favorite folders are a short list of folders you want to reach quickly. They
are different from the recent folders Windows keeps. Recent folders track
what you opened lately; favorites track what you actually want to hand. A
folder you use all the time but have not touched in months still belongs here.

- **Add Current Folder to Favorites** (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave` then `Shift+F`)
  adds the current document's folder. Save the document first if it is new.
- **Remove Favorite Folder...** (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave` then `Shift+X`) lets you
  choose a favorite to take off the list.
- **Open From Favorite Folder...** (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave` then `G`) opens Quick
  Open, described next.

All three are on **File > Favorite Folders**.

#### Open From Favorite Folder

**Open From Favorite Folder...** opens a small window with a text box already
focused, much like Quick Open in Visual Studio Code.

1. Start typing part of a file name. The list below narrows as you type,
   across every favorite folder at once, and capital letters do not matter.
2. Arrow to the file you want. Each entry tells you which favorite folder it
   came from.
3. Press Enter, or choose **OK**, to open it.

By default QUILL looks only at the files directly inside each favorite
folder, not in folders inside them, which keeps the list instant. Check
**Include subfolders** to search every subfolder too. That search stops at a
few thousand files, so even a very large folder cannot hang the window.

### Folding and inline notes

#### Code folding

Folding lets you tuck away a heading section or a fenced code block
(` ``` `...` ``` `) so it is out of your way, without ever hiding it from you.

- **Toggle Fold** (`Ctrl+Shift+[`) folds or unfolds the smallest region around
  the cursor and tells you what happened: "Folded: 14 lines under 'Chapter
  Two'" or "Unfolded: 'Chapter Two'."
- **Next Fold** (`Alt+Shift+]`) and **Previous Fold** (`Alt+Shift+[`) jump
  between regions you can fold, folded or not, and tell you the region's
  name, whether it is folded, and how many lines it has.
- **List Folds** (`Ctrl+Shift+]`) opens a list of every region you can fold,
  with its state and line count. Pick one to jump to it, or fold and unfold it
  from there.

In most editors, folding hides lines and the arrow keys skip right over them,
so a screen reader user cannot tell whether text was folded or deleted. QUILL
never does that. Folding never changes the text, and arrowing by character,
word or line works exactly as before. Arrow through a folded region and you
will read every word of it. Folding only changes where the jump commands take
you.

#### Inline notes

Inline notes are private comments you attach to a line or a selection: a
question, a reminder, a note to yourself while you draft. They are on **Tools
> Writing**, and you can change any of their keys in the Keymap Editor.

- **Add Inline Note...** (`Alt+Shift+I`) attaches a note to the selected text,
  or to the current line if nothing is selected. Type the note and choose
  Save.
- **Next Inline Note** (`Alt+Shift+J`) and **Previous Inline Note**
  (`Alt+Shift+K`) move to the next or previous noted text, and QUILL reads the
  note.
- **Speak Inline Note** (`Alt+Shift+H`) reads the note at the cursor. Press it
  twice quickly to open the note so you can read, change or delete it.

Each note remembers the exact text it was placed on, plus a little around it,
so it follows that text as you edit. Notes are kept with each document between
sessions, just like bookmarks. If the text a note was on is deleted, the note
is kept, not lost. A new document keeps its notes until you close it; save it
and they are kept. Notes are yours alone and are never written into the
document.

### Working in code

#### Code-aware editing

When you open a source file, QUILL loads a language profile based on the file
extension. It knows HTML, Markdown, CSS, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C,
C++, C#, PHP, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Shell, YAML, JSON, TOML and SQL, and treats
anything else as plain text. The profile tells QUILL how the language is put
together, so moving and announcements make sense for code.

- **Next Token** and **Previous Token**, on the Navigate menu, move by code
  token instead of by word. You land on the next name, keyword, operator or
  value, which is much easier to follow by ear than moving by character or
  word.
- Token movement goes well with the optional indentation tones described
  under [Sound notifications and earcons](#sound-notifications-and-earcons),
  so you hear the structure as pitch while you move.

#### Setting the document language

QUILL normally goes by the file extension, but you can set the language
yourself for the current document. That helps with an unsaved document, an
unusual extension, or code you pasted into a plain `.txt` file. You get the
whole of that language's editing support:

- **Bold** and **Italic** insert the right markup (`<strong>`/`<em>` for HTML,
  `**...**`/`*...*` for Markdown).
- The **heading, table, list, and tag** menu items become available for HTML
  and Markdown.
- **Toggle Line/Block Comment** uses the language's comment style (`#`, `//`,
  `<!-- -->`, `-- `).
- Heading and structure navigation, the outline, link insertion and live
  preview all follow the language you chose.

There are three ways to set it, and they all do the same thing:

- **Key:** `Ctrl+Alt+F6` opens the language picker. Type to find a language;
  the current one is already selected.
- **Menus:** **Navigate > Set Document Language...** opens the same picker.
  **Format > Document Language** is a checkable list where you can switch with
  one key press and hear which language is active.
- **Status bar:** the **Language** part shows the current language, with
  **(set)** after it when you chose it yourself. Press Enter on it to open the
  picker.

Choose **Auto-detect from file** to go back to following the file name.
Setting a language never renames the file. If you set HTML on a `.txt` file,
QUILL reminds you to use **Save As** to save it as `.html`. The choice applies
to the current tab and is forgotten when you close the file.

#### Automatic language detection

QUILL can guess the language when you paste or type code into a plain `.txt`
or new document. This is off by default. Turn it on in **Settings > Editing >
Auto-detect document language**, which has four choices:

- **Off**: never guess. This is the default.
- **Hint in the status bar only**: the status bar quietly shows something like
  "Looks like HTML". Nothing changes and nothing is spoken.
- **Suggest and announce, you confirm**: QUILL tells you which language it
  thinks this is ("This looks like HTML") and you decide whether to set it.
- **Switch automatically**: QUILL sets the language and tells you.

QUILL waits a moment after you stop typing or pasting, then looks at the
first several thousand characters. It is careful: it only acts when it is
confident, never guesses on ordinary prose, and never overrides a real file
extension or a language you set yourself. It also learns a little from the
languages you use during a session. In every mode you either stay in control
or hear what changed. Braille files and pasted braille are not affected,
because braille has its own Braille Mode.

#### Abbreviation expansion

If you write HTML or CSS, three commands on the **Edit** menu turn short
Emmet-style abbreviations into full markup. You can type
`ul>li.item$*3>a[href]{Item $}` instead of a whole three-item list.

- **Expand Abbreviation** expands the selection, or, with nothing selected,
  the word just before the cursor. It is one undo step, so one Undo puts it
  all back.
- **Preview Abbreviation...** asks for an abbreviation (filled in from your
  selection, if you have one) and shows the result in a new tab without
  touching your document. It is a safe way to try something.
- **Explain Abbreviation...** gives you a plain, indented breakdown of what an
  abbreviation means (tag, id, classes, attributes and how many times it
  repeats) before you expand it. It is the quickest way to learn the grammar
  by ear.

The usual Emmet operators work: child (`>`), sibling (`+`), climb-up (`^`),
grouping (`(...)`), multiplication (`*N`) and numbering (`$`, with `$$` for
zero-padded numbers). So do ids (`#id`), classes (`.a.b`), attributes
(`[attr="value" bool-attr]`) and text (`{...}`). Common tags get sensible
attributes if you leave them out: `a` gets an empty `href`, and `img` gets
`src` and `alt`. Elements like `br` and `img` never get a closing tag.

Some ready-made snippets expand as they are:

- `!` gives a full HTML5 page.
- `!a11y` gives an HTML5 page with a skip link and `header`/`main`/`footer`
  landmarks in place.
- `skiplink` gives just the skip link.
- `form:a11y` gives a labeled form field inside a fieldset.
- `table:a11y` gives a table with a caption and properly scoped header cells.

When the document is a `.css` file, all three commands work with CSS
shorthand instead, such as `d:f` for `display: flex;`, `pos:a` for `position:
absolute;`, `m10-20` for `margin: 10px 20px;` and `mt-10` for `margin-top:
-10px;`.

If QUILL cannot make sense of an abbreviation, the status bar tells you what
it expected and where.

### Quill Eraser

Quill Eraser (**Tools > Writing & Language > Quill Eraser...**) tidies the
small mechanical slips in your text: extra spaces, spaces at the ends of
lines, a missing space after punctuation, too many blank lines, and sentences
that start with a small letter. It offers a fix for each one. It follows
fixed rules, so there is no AI and nothing goes over the network.

To check only part of the document, select it and use **Quill Eraser on
Selection...**. If nothing is selected, it offers to check the whole
document.

#### What Quill Eraser checks

Each finding comes with a confidence level (High, Medium or Low) so you can
decide what to fix first.

| Rule | Confidence | What it catches |
|------|-----------|-----------------|
| Multiple spaces between words | High | Two or more spaces where one space belongs |
| Trailing spaces at end of line | High | Spaces or tabs at the end of a line |
| Space before punctuation | High | A space immediately before `,`, `.`, `!`, `?`, `;`, or `:` |
| Excessive blank lines | High | More consecutive blank lines than your configured maximum (default: 2) |
| Missing space after sentence punctuation | Medium | A sentence-ending `.`, `!`, or `?` directly followed by a letter |
| Missing space after comma, semicolon, or colon | Medium | A `,`, `;`, or `:` directly followed by a letter |
| Sentence starts with lowercase letter | Medium | A sentence or paragraph that begins with a lowercase character |

Quill Eraser leaves web addresses, email addresses, file paths, code,
decimal numbers and times alone. In a Markdown file it also skips fenced code
blocks, inline code, front matter and link addresses.

#### Code files

If you run Quill Eraser on a code file (`.py`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.html` and so
on), it asks first. You can check only for spaces at the ends of lines, which
is safe in code, or skip the check. The prose rules are never used on code
files.

#### The review dialog

When Quill Eraser finds something, it opens a review window that stays open
while you keep working in the editor.

- The **findings list** shows each issue in order: confidence, type and line
  number.
- Select a finding and the pane below tells you what was found, what the fix
  is, and what it means in plain English.
- **Apply Fix** makes the fix and moves on to the next issue.
- **Ignore** hides the finding for this session without changing anything.
- **Go to Issue** takes you to the exact place in the editor with the text
  selected, so you can decide for yourself.
- **Previous / Next** move through the list.
- **Rescan** checks again after you have made changes by hand.
- **Close** closes the window.

QUILL tells you the result of every action.

#### Quill Eraser settings

Four settings at the end of the **Spelling** page in Settings (`Ctrl+,`) control
Quill Eraser. Each one's name starts with "Quill Eraser", so typing eraser in
**Find a setting** lists all four:

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---------|---------|--------------|
| `hygiene_min_confidence` | `high` | Minimum confidence level to report. Set to `medium` or `low` to see more findings. |
| `hygiene_allow_double_space_after_period` | off | Suppresses the "multiple spaces" rule when exactly two spaces follow `.`, `!`, or `?` (two-space-after-period style). |
| `hygiene_max_blank_lines` | 2 | Maximum consecutive blank lines before a finding is raised. |
| `hygiene_rules_disabled` | (empty) | Comma-separated list of rule IDs to disable (e.g. `prose.lowercase_sentence_start,prose.missing_space_after_comma`). |

The rule IDs you can put in the disabled list are
`prose.multiple_spaces`, `prose.trailing_spaces`,
`prose.space_before_punctuation`, `prose.excessive_blank_lines`,
`prose.missing_space_after_sentence_punct`,
`prose.missing_space_after_comma` and `prose.lowercase_sentence_start`.

### What you learned, and where to go next

You can now find text in one document or many, jump by line, page, heading or
bookmark with `Ctrl+G`, and get back with `Alt+Left`. You know what QUILL says
about headings, lists and tables, how Quick Nav moves you with single letters,
and the difference between bookmarks, marks and a selection. Favorite folders,
folding, inline notes, the code tools and Quill Eraser are there when you want
them.

To practise with QUILL guiding you, open **Help > Tutorials...**
(`Ctrl+Alt+F1`) and try "Get around a long document", "Find, replace, and
search across files", "Select, mark, and move text", "Tables, by ear" and
"Quick Nav: single-letter movement". On the website,
[Own the keyboard](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/02-own-the-keyboard.html)
covers much of the same ground.

Next, Chapter 7, Spelling and words, shows you how to check spelling and find
the right word.

## Chapter 7: Spelling and words

This chapter is about getting the words right. You will check spelling a
whole document at a time or one word at a time, hear exactly how a misspelled
word is spelled, find a better word in the thesaurus, look up what a word
means, and count what you have written. Near the end you will also find how to
quieten QUILL's sounds, or choose new ones. Everything here works on your own
computer, with no AI and no internet connection, unless you choose otherwise.
AI spelling and grammar help is in Chapter 10, AI, when you want it.

### Spelling

QUILL checks spelling on your own computer. Nothing you write is uploaded, and
no AI provider is involved. The everyday commands are on the **Tools** menu:

- **Spell Check...** (`F7`) opens the Spelling Review, which walks you through
  every misspelling.
- **Spell Check Word** (`Alt+Shift+F7`) checks only the word you are on.
- **Next Misspelling** (`Ctrl+F7`) moves straight to the next one in the
  document, and `Ctrl+Shift+F7` goes back to the previous one.

#### Spelling Review (F7)

Press `F7` to start a guided spelling review.

- **What it checks.** If you have text selected, QUILL checks only the
  selection. With nothing selected, it reviews the whole document, starting at
  your caret.
- **Where you land.** The **Spelling Review** dialog opens with focus in a
  read-only **Context** field. The misspelled word is selected inside its
  sentence, so you hear it in context. You can arrow through it letter by
  letter or copy the text, just as you would in a read-only document.

The controls, in Tab order, are: Context, Change to, Suggestions, the **Review
most-frequent words first** checkbox, then the buttons Change, Change All,
Ignore Once, Ignore All, Read Sentence, Add to Dictionary, Undo Last and Close.

- **Suggestions** lists the corrections QUILL has for the word. Arrow through
  them; choosing one fills **Change to** for you.
- **Change** replaces this occurrence and moves to the next problem. Pressing
  **Enter** in the **Change to** field does the same.
- **Change All** replaces every remaining occurrence in the part you are
  checking, and keeps the capitals as they were (`teh` becomes `the`, `Teh`
  becomes `The`, `TEH` becomes `THE`).
- **Ignore Once** skips this occurrence. **Ignore All** skips every
  occurrence, for this session only.
- **Add to Dictionary** adds the word to your personal dictionary for good.
- **Undo Last** takes back your last spelling action without closing the
  dialog. It is unavailable until you have done something.
- **Read Sentence** (`Ctrl+R`) reads aloud the whole sentence around the
  misspelling, so you can hear the word in context without leaving the
  dialog. The **Read Sentence** button does the same thing.
- `Alt+W` takes you back to Context and selects the current word again, at
  any point. It is handy after you have been arrowing around the context.

When every problem has been dealt with, QUILL tells you how many words were
changed, ignored and added to the dictionary, and puts you back in the
document.

##### Review most-frequent words first

Normally the review goes from top to bottom. Tick **Review most-frequent words
first** in the dialog and it walks the misspellings by how often each word
turns up instead, with the most common first. It is the same dialog and the
same buttons (Change, Change All, Ignore Once, Ignore All, Add to Dictionary,
Undo Last); only the order changes.

This is for really messy documents: a rough scan that came through OCR, or a
document with one mistake repeated many times. Press **Change All** on the top
word and the order is worked out again straight away, so whatever is now most
common among what is left comes to the front. You clear the worst offenders
first, without hunting for them in reading order. QUILL remembers the
checkbox for next time.

##### How much the review says

**Spelling review announcement verbosity**, on the **Spelling** page of
Settings, chooses how much the review tells you:

- **Concise**: progress numbers and the result of each action, and nothing
  else.
- **Balanced** (the default): the kind of problem, the current word, your
  progress and the results.
- **Detailed**: all of that, plus hints about the controls and reminders of
  what you are checking.

Three more settings on the same page belong to the review:

- **Spell out the misspelled word letter by letter**: after telling you the
  misspelling, QUILL reads it letter by letter. On to begin with.
- **Pause before spelling the word (milliseconds)** is how long it waits
  before spelling starts, from 100 to 3000. The default is 800.
- **Wrap spelling review to the beginning**: when the review reaches the end
  of the document, it offers to carry on from the top back to where you
  started. On to begin with.

#### Spell Check Word (Alt+Shift+F7)

If you are used to checking just the word under the cursor in another word
processor, **Spell Check Word** (`Alt+Shift+F7`) is that. It checks only the
word at your cursor and leaves the rest of the document alone.

- If the word is spelled correctly, QUILL says so and that is all. No dialog
  opens.
- If it is misspelled, a small list opens with the same choices as the
  right-click spelling menu: suggested corrections, **Add to Dictionary** and
  **Ignore**. Pick one and you are back to typing.

Use `F7` when you want to work through a whole document or selection. Use
`Alt+Shift+F7` when you only want to check the one word in front of you.

#### Moving between misspellings

Sometimes you would rather stay in the document and hop from one problem to
the next. `Ctrl+F7` moves to the next misspelling and `Ctrl+Shift+F7` to the
previous one. When you land on one, QUILL says the word and then spells it
(see How a misspelling is said, later in this chapter).

> **QUILLBee's shortcut:** Coming from Word? `Alt+F7` also jumps to the next
> misspelling, just as it does there.

To hear them all in one place, open the **Misspelling List** (`Alt+Shift+L`).
It lists every misspelling in document order. Arrow through it and press
Enter to jump to any one.

##### Ranked spelling

**Tools > Misspelling List (Ranked by Frequency)...** (`Alt+Shift+R`) shows
the same list in a different order. The word that turns up most often comes
first, and each entry carries its count, for example "teh (Ln 12, Col 4, 8
occurrences)."

A repeated typo or a single OCR misreading is usually the quickest thing to
fix first. Deal with one entry, by correcting it or with **Add to
Dictionary**, and you have dealt with every occurrence of that word at once.
Arrow through the list and press Enter to jump to any occurrence, exactly as
in the regular list. The document-order list on `Alt+Shift+L` stays as it
was, and it is still the default.

#### Spell check as you type

With **spell check as you type** turned on, finishing a word the dictionary
does not know plays a soft spelling sound, and the status line shows "Possible
misspelling" with the word. The sound comes from your current sound pack; if
the pack has no spelling sound, you hear the Windows beep instead. QUILL uses a
sound here, not speech, so it never talks over your screen reader in the
middle of a sentence.

The check waits until you have **finished** a word, with a space, a comma or a
new line. It does not judge a word you are still typing, so "recie" on the way
to "receive" never sets it off.

Some places are full of things that look like misspellings, so the live check
stays quiet there: web addresses, email addresses, Markdown inline code
(between backticks) and fenced code blocks. The F7 review still covers the
whole document; only the alert as you type skips them.

You can switch the spelling sound on or off by itself in **Tools > Sound
Scheme** (look for "Possible misspelling as you type"). The spell check as you
type toggle turns the whole live check on or off.

##### Quiet in code files

In source and configuration files the live check says nothing at all. That
covers `.py`, `.json`, `.js`, `.css`, `.ps1`, `.log`, `.yml` and the other
coding file types. Almost every name and setting in a file like that is a word
no dictionary knows, so you would hear nothing but wrong alerts.

Markdown is writing, so `.md` files **are** checked. Only the code blocks,
inline code, web addresses and email addresses inside them are skipped.

The setting is **`spellcheck_skip_code_files`**, and it is on by default.
Turn it off if you want the live check everywhere, whatever the file type.

`F7` is never affected. The Spelling Review checks whatever document you run
it on, a code file included. Pressing `F7` is you asking for a check.

#### Spell check a document before saving

Turn on **Settings > Editing > Spell check a document before saving** (off by
default) and QUILL opens the Spelling Review for you each time you save, so
you can fix misspellings before the file is written. Fix or skip them as
usual; the save then goes ahead with your corrections. This applies to
**Save** and **Save As** for the document you are working on.

#### Spell-check language

**Tools > Spell Check Language...** chooses the language the spell checker
uses. It affects both the `F7` review and the check as you type.

**English (United States)** is built in and works offline straight away. Other
languages are downloaded when you first choose them. Pick **Spanish (Spain)**
or **French (France)**, for example, and QUILL fetches that dictionary from
its own verified source. The download is checksum-checked, and a progress
window lets you cancel it. After that the language works offline, just like
English.

QUILL remembers your choice between sessions. If you are offline, or you
cancel the download, English keeps working and nothing else changes. The
downloaded dictionaries are kept in your QUILL data folder, so reinstalling or
upgrading QUILL never makes you fetch them again.

### How a misspelling is said

Speech alone cannot tell you what is wrong with a misspelled word. "receive"
and "recieve" sound the same, so hearing the word tells you nothing. **The
letters are the answer.** So when you land on a misspelling, with Next or
Previous Misspelling or in the `F7` review, QUILL says the word, pauses, and
then spells it.

The spelling comes as a second, separate announcement, so you can cut it off.
Press your next key and the spelling is cancelled before you hear it. If you
are moving fast you lose nothing, and if you want the letters they are there.

Twelve settings under **Spelling** in Settings control all of this. Both
editors also gather them in a window of their own. In QUILL it is **Spelling
Announcements**, on `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F6`, or type its name in the command
palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`). In QUILL Lite it is **Tools > Spelling >
Announcements**. They are the same twelve settings in the same file, so
setting them up once sets up both editors.

#### While you are typing

- **Play a sound when you type a misspelling** (`spelling_alert_sound`)
  plays the falling blip when you finish a misspelled word. Turn it off for
  silence.
- **Also say the word when you type a misspelling** (`spelling_alert_speech`)
  speaks the word as well. It is off by default, because being interrupted
  while you are writing costs more than it tells you.
- **Shortest gap between two alerts for the same word (milliseconds)**
  (`spelling_alert_repeat_ms`) is the shortest time before the same word is
  reported again, so one stubborn name does not become a drumbeat. Zero means
  every time. The default is 750.

Whichever way you set those two, the status bar always shows the word, for
example "Possible misspelling: teest", so you can read it with your screen
reader whenever you like. QUILL does not speak that status line on its own;
it is spoken only when **Also say the word when you type a misspelling** is
on, which is what the setting means in QUILL Lite too.

#### Spelling a word out

- **Spell misspelled words out letter by letter** (`spell_aloud_enabled`)
  is the main switch.
- **How letters are spoken** (`spell_aloud_style`) chooses how the letters
  are said. Plain **Letters (R, E, C)** are fastest. The **Phonetic alphabet
  (romeo, echo, charlie)** is clear where B, D, E, P, T and V all sound alike.
  **Letters, then the phonetic alphabet** is for learning a word rather than
  checking one.
- **Say which letters are capitals** (`spell_aloud_capitals`) says "cap"
  before a capital letter, so you can tell MacDonald from Macdonald. It is
  worth having, because letters are always spoken as capitals, whatever the
  word does (several voices read a single lower-case letter as a word).

#### When the letters follow

There are three pauses, because the right wait is different in each place.

- **Pause before spelling a word (milliseconds)** (`spell_aloud_delay_ms`)
  is the pause in the `F7` review, where you have stopped to decide. The
  default is 800 ms.
- **Spell the word when you move to a misspelling**
  (`spell_aloud_on_navigation`) and **Pause before spelling when moving
  between misspellings (milliseconds)** (`spell_aloud_navigation_delay_ms`)
  cover Next and Previous Misspelling. There you may just be passing through,
  so the default pause is shorter, 600 ms.
- **Spell each suggestion as you arrow through them**
  (`spell_aloud_suggestions`) and **Pause before spelling a suggestion
  (milliseconds)** (`spell_aloud_suggestion_delay_ms`) spell whichever
  correction you arrow onto in the suggestions. Choosing between two
  spellings by ear is as hard in a list as it is in the document.
- **Spell the first suggestion on arrival** (`spell_aloud_first_suggestion`)
  also spells the top suggestion when the review reaches a new word. It is
  off by default, because it doubles what you hear each time you arrive.

### The thesaurus, Look Up and other word tools

The rest of the writing and language commands on the **Tools** menu are about
words themselves: finding a better one, finding out what one means, and
counting them. Chapter 4, Writing and editing, gives a short introduction;
this is the fuller story.

#### Thesaurus (Shift+F7)

**Tools > Thesaurus...** (`Shift+F7`) opens a two-pane picker for the word you
are on. It finds the word even when it is in another form, so "running" finds
"run", and when you choose a replacement it goes back in the form your
sentence needs.

#### Look Up Word (Alt+F10)

**Look Up Word...** (`Alt+F10`) is a dictionary with no AI. Out of the box it
uses the thesaurus, which works offline. Tick **Use online sources** in the
window and it also brings definitions, more words, and a Wikipedia summary
from three free online services. Nothing goes online until you tick that box.

#### Say Word Summary and Dictionary Status

- **Say Word Summary** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+[`) says what the thesaurus knows
  about the word you are on, without opening a window.
- **Dictionary Status...** (`Alt+Shift+;`) shows which spelling engine QUILL
  is using, how many words are in your personal, document and project
  dictionaries, and whether the thesaurus is installed.

#### Document Statistics (Ctrl+Shift+G)

**Tools > Document Statistics...** (`Ctrl+Shift+G`) gives you the number of
words, characters, lines and paragraphs, and the reading time. It used to be
called Word Count. It now has the same name and key as in Word and QUILL Lite.

### Sounds, and turning them off

QUILL plays short sounds, called earcons, for things your screen reader does
not mention, like a misspelling or a paste. Here is how to silence them all at
once, change one, or build a set of your own.

#### Quiet mode

`Alt+Shift+M` silences every sound at once. Press it again to bring them back.
It is one key so you can reach it while the noise is happening: on a call, in
a quiet room, or when you have simply heard enough for today. The setting is
shared with QUILL Lite, so silencing one editor silences both.

#### The Sound Scheme window

**Tools > Reading and Dictation > Sound Scheme...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+O`) lists every sound QUILL can
make, and lets you hear them.

As you arrow through the list, each event plays as you land on it. That turns
a list of about a hundred and forty sound names into something you can
browse by ear. It is a checkbox under the list, so if you are hunting for one
row you can turn it off and pass the rest in silence.

Each row tells you everything about itself: its group, the event, whether it
is switched on, which file it plays and how long that file is. Your screen
reader reads it all as you arrive, so you never have to Tab away to find out.
The buttons underneath work on the row you are on:

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Play** | Play this event now, even when the event is switched off |
| **Switched on** | Silence this one event without changing which sound it has |
| **Browse...** | Use a WAV file of your own |
| **No Sound** | Remove the sound from this event entirely |
| **Use Default** | Put this one event back to the sound the scheme ships |

QUILL refuses a file that is not a WAV, is longer than ten seconds, or is
bigger than two megabytes, and tells you why when you choose it. Better to
hear about it then than to have the event go silent later with no clue why.

- **Save As Scheme** saves the whole set under a name you choose, as an
  ordinary folder with the sounds copied into it. It keeps working after you
  tidy your Downloads folder, and you can zip it up and send it to a friend.
- **Delete Scheme** removes one of your own schemes. The schemes that come
  with QUILL cannot be deleted.
- **Restore All Defaults** puts every event back and switches them all on.
  It always works completely, because QUILL never overwrites the sounds it
  ships.

QUILL Lite opens the same window over the same schemes, so a scheme you make
in one editor is offered in the other.

#### The sounds themselves

The **Ink** pack that comes with QUILL has a sound for every event. That
includes the ones desktop programs have had for decades: open, close, cut,
copy, paste, delete, undo, redo, print, information, question and task
finished. Those are the moments a screen reader says nothing about; nothing
is announced when a paste lands, for example.

Related sounds share a tone and differ by direction, so you learn a family
once instead of one sound at a time.

- **Undo and redo are the same figure, played backwards from each other.**
- Open and close are one pair of bells, rising and falling. App start and app
  exit are the same pair, one note longer.
- Cut, copy and paste are one dry wooden tick in three gestures. Delete is
  that tick dropped an octave and a half, with a breath of noise underneath.
- Nothing to undo does not move in pitch at all, because nothing moved.

### Starting with a blank document, or not

When you start QUILL without opening anything, it gives you an empty
**Untitled** document, as most editors do. If you always open an existing
file and would rather not close a blank one every time, turn off
**open_blank_document_at_startup**, under **General** in Settings.

Turning it off changes only that one case. A file you double-clicked, a file
named on the command line, the documents from your last session and recovered
unsaved work all still open. QUILL Lite has the same setting, with the same
name, in **Preferences**.

### Spelling keys at a glance

These work straight from the document, without opening a dialog first.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `F7` | Open the Spelling Review |
| `Alt+Shift+F7` | Spell Check Word, the word at the cursor |
| `Ctrl+F7` | Jump to the next misspelling |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F7` | Jump to the previous misspelling |
| `Alt+Shift+L` | Misspelling List |
| `Alt+Shift+R` | Misspelling List, ranked by frequency |
| `Shift+F7` | Thesaurus |
| `Alt+F10` | Look Up Word |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+[` | Say Word Summary |
| `Alt+Shift+;` | Dictionary Status |
| `Ctrl+Alt+F9` | Add Word to Dictionary, the word at the cursor |

**Add Word to Dictionary** (`Ctrl+Alt+F9`) teaches your personal dictionary
the word at the cursor, so a name or a word from your work stops being called
a misspelling, in this document and every other. If the word is already
there, QUILL tells you and changes nothing.

### What you learned, and where to go next

You can now check a whole document with `F7`, or one word with
`Alt+Shift+F7`, and hop between misspellings with `Ctrl+F7`. You know how to
put the most common mistakes first, how QUILL spells a word out and how to
tune that, and how to pick a spell-check language. You met the thesaurus,
Look Up Word and Document Statistics, and you can silence QUILL's sounds with
`Alt+Shift+M` or change them in the Sound Scheme window.

To practise with QUILL open, try the lesson "Spelling, words, and the
thesaurus" in **Help > Tutorials...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F1`).

Next, Chapter 8, Reading, reviewing and listening, shows you how to have your
work read back to you and how to check a document before you share it.

## Chapter 8: Reading, reviewing and listening

This chapter is about taking things in rather than typing them. You will
have QUILL read your document to you, look closely at text you did not write,
see the formatting that normally stays hidden, and compare two versions of a
file. Later on it covers turning documents into audiobooks, and keeping your
place in everything you listen to. Start with Read Aloud. The rest is there
when you need it.

### Read Aloud

Read Aloud speaks your document in a voice of your choosing, separate from
your screen reader. It is handy for proofreading by ear, for resting your
ears from a fast screen reader voice, or for simply listening to a long piece.
You can start, pause, stop, preview, and choose a voice.

#### Starting and stopping

Everything for listening lives on **Tools > Reading and Dictation**:

- **Read Aloud** is a submenu:
  - **Start / Pause** (press the QUILL key, then `R`) starts reading from the
    cursor, and pauses or carries on when you press it again.
  - **Voice...** and **Settings...** choose the voice and how fast, how loud
    and how high it speaks.
  - **Generate Audio...** saves the reading as a sound file instead of
    playing it, described below.
  - **Announcement Backend...** chooses how QUILL's own short messages reach
    you: automatically, through your screen reader, or on the status bar only.
  - **Announcement Trace (in Settings)...** opens Settings at the switch that
    keeps a record of QUILL's announcements. It is only useful when support
    asks you for it, and it never records your document.
- **Stop Reading** (press the QUILL key, then `Shift+R`) stops the current
  reading straight away.
- **Say Selected** (`Ctrl+Shift+Y`) reads the text you have selected.
- **Read All** (`Alt+F8`) reads from the cursor to the end of the document.
- **OCR Image...**, **OCR Clipboard Image** and **OCR Screen Capture...** turn
  a picture of text into text you can read. There is more on them under OCR
  Image, later in this chapter.

**Generate Audio...** makes a recording of your document in your Read Aloud
voice. It uses the selection if you have one, and the whole document if you do
not. Choose a name and a type in the save window: a Wave file always, and MP3,
M4A, M4B audiobook, OGG, Opus or FLAC as well when the free ffmpeg tool is on
your computer. Making audio from your documents, later in this chapter, covers
the bigger jobs.

There is one setting worth knowing about. **Move cursor to follow Read
Aloud** (in **Settings > Read Aloud**) makes the cursor select each sentence
as it is read, so the caret tracks what you hear and stops where the reading
stopped. It is **off by default**. With a screen reader running, moving the
selection makes the screen reader say "selected" over the Read Aloud voice.
If you are sighted or have low vision and want the cursor to follow along,
turn it on.

The rest of the **Read Aloud** page in Settings tunes the voice:

- **Read Aloud engine** chooses which speech engine reads. Choosing a voice,
  below, explains them.
- **Read Aloud rate** is the speed of the Windows voice in words per minute,
  from 80 to 450. The default is 200.
- **Read Aloud volume** runs from 0 to 100. The default is 100.
- **Read Aloud pitch** runs from 0 to 100. The default is 50.
- **Read Aloud sentence pause (milliseconds)** adds a pause between
  sentences, up to two seconds. The default is no extra pause.
- **ElevenLabs Read Aloud voice** and **ElevenLabs Read Aloud model** are used
  when the engine is ElevenLabs. Pick a voice in the Voice Browser rather than
  typing one; left blank, ElevenLabs uses its default voice and model.
- **AI Voice provider**, **AI Voice model** and **AI Voice** choose the cloud
  voice used by Read Aloud with AI Voice and by audio export: **OpenAI** (the
  default), **Google Gemini**, or **ElevenLabs (export only)**. Leave the
  model and voice on **Provider default** unless you have a favourite.

#### Choosing a voice

Read Aloud uses voices on your own computer. The Windows system voice runs on
**SAPI 5**. It is always there, works offline and needs no download, so Read
Aloud works the moment QUILL is installed. **DECtalk**, **eSpeak NG**,
**Piper**, and **Kokoro** (neural, offline) are extra downloads from Speech
Center, which keeps the installer smaller. Before any download starts, QUILL
tells you what is available right now and what it suggests you do next. For
cloud voices, see Read Aloud with AI Voice, which covers OpenAI and Google
Gemini voices.

The **Kokoro** voice models (about 120 MB), the classic **DECtalk** runtime
(about 2 MB), and the **eSpeak NG** engine with its voice data (about 40 MB)
are not in the installer. The first time you choose one of these voices,
QUILL downloads it for you from its own verified source. The download is
checksum-checked and has a progress window you can cancel. Your other voices,
including the SAPI 5 system voice, keep working while it downloads. If you
are upgrading from a version that bundled these, your existing copies are
kept and keep working, so there is nothing to download.

**Manage Voices** is the **Speech (Offline)** tab of the Speech Settings
dialog. It lists SAPI 5, DECtalk, Piper, Kokoro, and eSpeak NG. ElevenLabs,
the only cloud voice, has its own **Speech (Online)** tab, so local and cloud
voices are never mixed in one list. The **Set as Default** button (also on
the voice list's right-click menu) applies your engine and voice choice at
once, without closing the dialog with OK.

To hear a voice before you choose it:

1. In **Manage Voices**, select the voice.
2. Press the **Preview** button.

If the voice is already downloaded, QUILL speaks the preview phrase with that
voice's real model. If it is not downloaded yet (a Kokoro voice, for
example), QUILL plays a short pre-recorded sample so you can still hear it
before you decide. The rate, volume, pitch, and speed controls only apply to
real speech, so they stay dimmed until the voice is downloaded.

Starting a new preview stops the one already playing, so previews never
overlap. Some neural voices take a moment to get going. While they do, QUILL
plays a short earcon and, by default, says "Generating preview, please wait".
You can turn either off on its own: the earcon in **Tools > Reading and
Dictation > Sound Scheme...**, and the announcement in **Settings >
Accessibility and Announcements**. While a preview is generating or playing, the Preview/Test
button becomes a Stop button, so you can cancel it at any time.

#### Voices in other languages

Read Aloud speaks more than English. The Windows engine lists every voice
installed on your PC, in any language. Add one in Windows Settings under
**Time & language > Speech > Manage voices** (Italian's Elsa, say, or a
Spanish, French, German, or Japanese voice) and it appears in QUILL's voice
list, ready to use, with nothing to download from QUILL.

The offline neural voices go further too:

- **Kokoro** includes **Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian, and Brazilian
  Portuguese** voices. They are part of the voice pack you already
  downloaded, so picking one just works.
- The **Piper** catalog includes Italian voices (Paola and Riccardo) that you
  download like any other.
- **eSpeak NG** offers those languages from its built-in data.

Pick the voice whose language matches your document, and Read Aloud,
audiobook export, and batch speech all speak it correctly.

#### Text cleanup for speech

Real documents are full of typography that trips up speech engines. The
optional **text cleanup** pass (turn it on in Read Aloud settings) fixes
curly quotes, em and en dashes, ellipses, invisible spaces, ligatures,
bullets, symbols, fractions, and emoji, the same way every time. It also
speaks **phone numbers, emails, and URLs** clearly. For each type you choose
whether to announce it, speak it, or speak it and then repeat it, which makes
an address easy to catch. Cleanup runs first, before anything else, so live
Read Aloud and batch export sound the same.

#### Teaching QUILL how to say a word

**Tools > Speech > Manage Pronunciations...** teaches QUILL how to say
particular words: names, brands, acronyms, and technical terms. Each entry
is a substitution, either literal or a regular expression, and can be
case-sensitive. QUILL applies it silently to the text just before speaking,
so a correction is heard everywhere speech happens, in batch export and live
Read Aloud alike.

- A dictionary can be **global** (all projects) or belong to one **project**.
- An entry can target a specific engine.
- You can **preview** an entry to hear the result.
- A small **starter dictionary** already covers common terms.

#### SSML Builder and SSML playback

For fine control over how a passage is spoken, the **SSML Builder** dialog
writes `<speak>` markup for you from ordinary controls: emphasis, pauses
(`<break>`), say-as, phonemes, and prosody. A read-only preview shows the
markup it made, so you never type the tags yourself. Read Aloud plays this
markup **natively on SAPI 5 and eSpeak NG**, so the pauses and emphasis
happen instead of being read out.

#### Read Document in Browser (experimental)

Your web browser has voices QUILL's own engines cannot reach, including
Microsoft Edge's "Online (Natural)" voices. This optional feature reads your
document with them.

To turn it on:

1. Open **Settings > Experimental**.
2. Tick the acknowledgement box.
3. Turn on **Read the document aloud in your browser**.
4. Apply Settings. It works straight away, with no restart.

A **Read in Browser (Experimental)** item then appears under **Tools > Reading
& Dictation > Read Aloud**, and the command palette gains **Read Document in
Browser (Experimental)**.

When you use it, QUILL writes a self-contained, accessible reader page and
opens it in the browser you chose under **Settings > General > Preview browser**. The page
has:

- a labelled **Voice** picker. Each voice is marked "on this device" or
  "online", and the list is filtered to your QUILL display language. Tick
  **Show all languages** to see the rest.
- a **Speed** slider.
- **Play** and **Stop** buttons.

Focus lands on Play, changes are announced through a live region, and
**Escape** stops. Reading goes section by section, so even a book-length
document stays reliable. **Pause** keeps your place and tells you where you
are ("Paused at section 12 of 300"), and resuming carries on from that
section. **Stop** goes back to the top. Your voice and speed are remembered
between sessions, and the document text carries your display-language tag so
a screen reader reading the page pronounces it correctly.

About privacy: QUILL itself makes no network call, and no audio file is made.
Voices marked "on this device" speak locally. The browser's "Online
(Natural)" voices are made in the voice company's cloud, so choosing one
sends the text being read to that service. Pick an on-device voice to keep
everything local. The reader page holds your document text. It is written to
QUILL's app-data folder and deleted when you close QUILL, so no plain copy is
left behind.

#### Voice commands on the same menu

The Speech menus also hold QUILL's voice commands. They are listed here so
you know what they are when you meet them. Chapter 9, Dictation and
transcription, covers them properly.

- **Voice Command (Offline)** (**Tools > Speech**) is push-to-talk for QUILL.
  Run it, speak one command such as "save file", "word count" or "next
  heading", then run it again to stop and act. Recognition happens entirely
  on your computer with the offline speech engine, and only a safe list of
  non-destructive commands can ever run, so a misheard phrase cannot do
  damage. Say "cancel" or "never mind" to give up. Turn it on with the
  **Voice commands (push-to-talk)** setting. It is off by default and always
  off in Safe Mode.
- **Voice Conversation Mode** (**Tools > Speech**) is the hands-free version.
  Run it once and QUILL listens for a command, then keeps a short
  **follow-up window** open after acting, so you can chain commands ("next
  heading", then "read aloud", then "word count") without arming it again.
  A sound marks every state: a rising chime when conversation mode starts, a
  soft two-note when the microphone opens, a gentle rise when your command is
  recognized (with a brief moment to say "cancel" before it runs), a sparkle
  when the action finishes, a quiet tick while QUILL is working, and a calm
  falling tone if nothing matched. Run it again, or say "stop", to turn it
  off. The nine cues are **Sound Events** you can retune or replace in any
  sound pack. Four settings let you pace it to your own rhythm: the pause
  that ends a command, the cancel window, the follow-up window, and the
  "still working" tick interval. Set any of them to 0 to switch that part
  off. It uses the same on-device recognition and the same safe list as
  Voice Command, and is also off in Safe Mode.
- **Listen for Hey QUILL** (**Tools > Speech**) turns on always-listening.
  QUILL listens continuously, on your computer, for the phrase "Hey QUILL".
  Say "Hey QUILL, save file" to run a command straight away, or just "Hey
  QUILL" to start one. The status bar shows that the microphone is live and
  plays a reminder now and then, so an open microphone never takes you by
  surprise. Run the command again, or say "stop", to end it. It turns itself
  off when QUILL closes, unless you turn on **Keep listening for "Hey QUILL"
  across restarts**. Off in Safe Mode.
- **Speak Voice Status** (**Tools > Speech**) tells you what the voice
  features are doing right now: whether QUILL is listening for "Hey QUILL",
  whether conversation mode is on, and whether it is listening for a command.
  When none of them is, it says "Voice is not listening right now", which is
  the quick way to be sure the microphone is closed.
- **Ask a question by voice.** In conversation or wake mode, if you speak a
  question rather than a command (starting with "ask", or shaped like a
  question, such as "how do I save my document"), QUILL opens **Ask QUILL**
  with the question filled in and ready to send. You press Enter to send it,
  so a person always decides what reaches the AI. This needs AI set up.
  Questions are the only thing voice ever sends to a network service, and
  never on their own.

For the complete reference (every voice mode, every spoken command, and the
privacy rules) see [Voice Interaction](voice-interaction.md).

### Tools for Reading, Review, and Inspection

These tools help when a file is hard to read, or when you need to know
exactly what is in it. They answer questions like "which kind of space is
that?", "where does the bold end?" and "did this scan come through
properly?"

#### Describe Character at Cursor

Some characters sound the same but are not: a curly "smart" quote and a
straight apostrophe, a no-break space and an ordinary space, an invisible
zero-width space that quietly breaks a search, or a stray byte-order mark
pasted from the web. **Tools > Advanced > Describe Character at Cursor**
(`Ctrl+Shift+C`) tells you exactly what sits under the cursor. It says the
answer where you are and leaves it in the status bar, so you can read it
again.

When you want to study a character, **Character Details** (`Ctrl+Alt+C`)
opens the full description in a read-only window, the same kind F1 help
uses, so your screen reader can read it all in one pass or line by line. It
gives:

- the character's name (for example "No-break space" or "Right single
  quotation mark"),
- its Unicode code point in both hexadecimal and decimal,
- its category in plain words (uppercase letter, dash punctuation, control
  character, and so on), and
- a note for the invisible characters that are easy to miss, plus a flag
  when the character is not ASCII.

If the cursor is at the very end of the document, it tells you so instead of
guessing.

#### Reveal Codes (Alt+F3)

QUILL keeps formatting codes hidden, so your editing text stays clean and
fast. Reveal Codes lets you see and hear every one of them when you ask. If
you used WordPerfect, you will know it: this is the same idea, built for a
screen reader.

Press `Alt+F3` (or tick **View > Reveal Codes**) to open a pane below the
editor. It shows your document as an ordered stream of bracketed codes and
text: `[Bold On]`, `[Font: Arial]`, `[Size: 14]`, `[Center]`, `[Heading 2]`,
`[Link: ...]`, `[Tab]`, `[¶ Hard Return]`, `[No-Break Space]`,
`[Smart Quote]`, and so on. The editor itself does not change. Reveal Codes
is a window onto the hidden formatting, not a different way of editing.

Reveal Codes is **hidden by default** and costs nothing until you open it.

> **QUILLBee's tip:** Not sure whether a word is really bold, or where the
> bold stops? Press `Alt+F3`, arrow to it, and you will hear "bold on" right
> where it starts. Press `Alt+F3` again to close the pane.

##### Moving between the panes

`F6` moves through the regions (Editor, then Reveal Codes when it is shown,
then the Status Bar), and `Shift+F6` goes back, just like switching windows.
The two carets stay in step however you move: arrow keys, word jumps, Home
and End, Page Up and Page Down, a mouse click, or a jump from Find. Move in
the editor and the pane follows to the same spot. Move in the pane and the
editor's cursor follows to the matching place. Sit in whichever you like and
your place in the document comes with you.

##### Moving through the codes

In the default **Flowed** view the pane reads like your document with the
hidden formatting showing, and the caret moves the way it does in the
editor:

- `Left Arrow` and `Right Arrow` move one character at a time, but step over a
  whole code in one go. One press moves you across `[Bold On]` and your
  screen reader just says "bold on". It is never spelled out letter by
  letter.
- `Ctrl+Left` and `Ctrl+Right` move by word, stopping at each code.
- `Up Arrow` and `Down Arrow` move by line and read the new line, as in the
  editor.
- `Home` and `End` go to the start and end of the line. `Ctrl+Home` and
  `Ctrl+End` go to the top and bottom of the document.
- Land on a code and you hear it named as one thing: "bold on", "tab",
  "centred", "font Arial". An opening code also tells you how far its
  formatting reaches ("bold on, 12 characters").

While you arrow through the pane, your screen reader does the talking. The
region is named once when you arrive, and after that you hear the character,
word, line, or code your screen reader reads. QUILL puts its fuller phrase
(for example "italic on, 15 characters") quietly in the status bar, where
you can read it whenever you want it. Jumps you ask for (next or previous
code, go to the matching pair) and mouse clicks are still spoken by QUILL.

If you would rather hear QUILL's own phrase on every arrow press, turn on
**Reveal Codes: Speak Codes Aloud** in the command palette. It is off by
default.

In either view you can also jump code to code, skipping the plain text, and
from an opening code to its matching close.

##### Editing a run in place (F2)

1. Move onto text that sits between a pair of formatting codes, for example
   the words inside `[Bold On] ... [Bold Off]`.
2. Press `F2`. The pane limits you to just that stretch of text, and you can
   edit it freely.
3. Press **Enter** to put your change back into the document, or **Escape**
   to cancel.

The codes around it are left exactly as they were. The whole stretch edits as
one piece, so a run that contains a `[Tab]` or a code inside it (bold text
with one italic word, say) comes along together. The inner codes appear as
their markup and are put straight back when you press Enter. If you press F2
on plain text with no formatting around it, QUILL tells you there is nothing
to edit there.

##### Views and how much it says

In **Settings > Editing** (or on the View menu) you can choose:

- **Flowed** (the default): the interactive pane described above, with codes
  shown inside the running text (`[Bold On]Hello[Bold Off]`), movement by
  character, and F2 editing. It is the closest to the classic WordPerfect
  look and the most natural layout on a braille display.
- **Structured**: one item per code in a list. It is clear and labelled, and
  good for scanning structure. Your screen reader reads each item as you
  arrow through it. Movement by character, word and line, and F2 editing,
  belong to the Flowed view only.
- **Verbosity**: *quiet* (just the code name), *balanced* (adds how far an
  opening code reaches), or *detailed* (adds Unicode notes for invisible
  characters).

QUILL remembers your view and verbosity between sessions.

#### EPUB Navigator

When you open an EPUB, the navigator lets you move chapter by chapter
instead of scrolling blindly through one long block of text.

Chapter headings are also placed in the text itself, so single-key heading
navigation (`H` and `Shift+H`) walks every heading in the book, not just the
chapter breaks. Many older or home-made EPUBs never used real headings at
all. For those, QUILL works the headings out from the book's layout (a
paragraph styled as a title or chapter, or a short bold line on its own), so
heading navigation and the chapter outline still work where they would
otherwise be empty.

Equations are spoken, not skipped. When a chapter contains mathematics
(MathML, or LaTeX written as a `math` span or between `$$...$$` or `\(...\)`
delimiters), QUILL turns each equation into plain words and places it in the
text as "Math Equation: ..." so you hear the formula as part of its
sentence. It uses the same math speech as the editor: the MathCAT engine
when it is installed, and QUILL's built-in reader otherwise. A formula QUILL
cannot understand is read as its plain source instead of being dropped, and
a book with no math reads just as before.

#### OCR Image

**OCR Image...** (on **Tools > Reading and Dictation**) reads the text out of
a picture, using optical character recognition on your own computer. Nothing
happens behind your back: you choose the image, confirm, and hear progress
as it works.

Two more commands on the same menu skip the file altogether:

- **OCR Clipboard Image** reads the picture you have just copied, for example
  with the Print Screen key or Copy Image in a web browser. If there is no
  picture on the clipboard, QUILL tells you so.
- **OCR Screen Capture...** takes a picture of the screen and reads it. QUILL
  asks whether you want **The whole screen** or **The active window**, with
  the active window already chosen.

Both show you the recognised text to review, just like OCR Image.

#### Document intake and extraction quality

When you bring in a scanned PDF or another hard-to-read file, the text QUILL
pulls out may not be perfect. These commands help you check. Instead of
assuming every import is right, QUILL helps you ask whether the extraction is
good enough, what may have been lost, and whether you should quote from it
directly.

### Comparing documents

When you have two versions of something (a draft and the edited copy, or
your file and the one that came back by email), comparing them tells you
exactly what changed. Everything happens on your own computer. You can
compare one file with another, review several open documents, move through
the differences one at a time with both documents following along, and make
a summary of what changed.

#### The Comparison menu

**Tools > Comparison** holds:

- **Compare with File...**
- **Compare Open Documents**
- **Next Difference** / **Previous Difference**
- **Announce Current Difference**
- **Difference List...**
- **Toggle Synchronized Navigation**
- **Toggle Ignore Whitespace**
- **Compare Options...**
- **Generate Accessible Report**
- **Create Difference Summary**
- **Copy Current Difference** / **Copy All Differences**

**Toggle Ignore Whitespace** decides whether spaces count as a change. Each
press moves one step and says where you are: exact (every space counts),
ignore trailing (spaces at the ends of lines do not count), then ignore all
(no difference in spacing counts), and back to exact. Use it when one copy
went through a program that tidied the spacing and you only care about the
words.

**Generate Accessible Report** writes every difference into a new Markdown
document, under a heading that names the two files and says how many
differences there are. Because it is an ordinary document, you can read it
at your own pace, search it, and save or send it.

#### Moving through the differences

Once a comparison is open, these keys do most of the work:

- `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+.` moves to the next difference.
- `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+,` moves to the previous one.
- `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D` reads the current difference.

The compare dialog is a list you can review with your screen reader, one
difference at a time, entirely from the keyboard.

#### Compare sounds

If you use a sound pack, compare mode plays short earcons: one when a
comparison opens, one when it closes, separate ticks for moving to the next
or previous difference, and a soft "blocked" tone when you reach the first or
last difference and there is nothing further. You can turn each one on or
off in **Tools > Reading and Dictation > Sound Scheme...**
(`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+O`), under the Compare section. The topic on sound notifications and earcons has more about
sound packs.

### Making audio from your documents

QUILL can turn your writing into audio files: a single document, a whole
folder, or a chaptered audiobook ready to publish. This section is for when
you want something to keep, share or put on a phone. Live listening is Read
Aloud, earlier in this chapter.

#### Audiobook and Batch Speech

**Tools > Speech > Audiobook & Batch Speech...** (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave` then
`Y`) is the guided home for audio production. It turns a whole folder of
documents into speech audio in one pass, and it builds chaptered audiobooks
from documents, from a folder of recordings, or from both. It is a wizard
that asks one thing at a time. It is listed in the command palette under
"Audio Studio...". It replaced the old single-page Batch Export to Speech
Audio dialog; every option is still there, spread across clear steps, and
your saved project settings still fill everything in.

##### What do you want to make

The first page asks what you want to make. It remembers which one you chose
last time and selects it for you.

- **Narrate documents into an audiobook or speech audio.** The steps are:
  What should I read? (folder, file types, filters); Who should read it?
  (engine, voice with a preview button, pace, round-robin voices, voice
  casting rules, translated editions); How should chapters work? (chapter
  mode, spoken headings, the transition sounder and its volume, pauses);
  Output and diagnostics (format, existing-file policy, loudness,
  incremental-rebuild reuse, dry run, temp folder); the book page
  (optional, to put everything together into one audiobook); and a summary
  in plain words.
- **Combine audio files into one chaptered audiobook.** A shorter path: pick
  the folder of recordings, describe the book (title, author, narrator,
  cover, M4B or MP3, ACX loudness), review the summary, and Start. Each file
  becomes one chapter, and you always review the chapter list before the
  book is built. There is more on this under Build an audiobook from a
  folder of recordings, below.
- **Edit an existing audiobook.** Pick a finished MP3 or M4B and it opens in
  the Chapter Workbench, described below. A file with no chapter markers
  opens as one chapter, ready to split up.

##### Moving through the wizard

Each step is announced as you arrive ("Step 2 of 7: What should I read?").
**Back** and **Next** move between steps. **Skip to summary** jumps ahead
when your saved project profile already fills every page, so a repeat run
is three keystrokes. The work runs in the background with progress for each
file, and you can cancel it. It uses the same speech engine as live Read
Aloud, so the voice you audition is the voice you get.

The source pages offer a list of **recent source folders**, and the edit
path's file picker remembers **recently opened audiobooks**. Both lists are
kept between sessions, are separate from your recent documents, and never
grow without limit.

##### What should I read

- **Source folder**, and whether to include subfolders.
- The **file types** to include: `.docx`, `.md`, `.html`/`.htm`, `.txt`.
- Optional **include/exclude filters**: patterns separated by semicolons or
  commas, matched against the file name and its path.
- **Skip files larger than (MB)**: a **maximum file size**, in megabytes
  (`0` means no limit). One accidental 400 MB export in a folder can no
  longer take over an overnight run. Any file over the limit is left out,
  and the live document count on the same step changes as you change the
  limit. Press **Count documents** to hear the settled count.

##### Who should read it

- **Engine, voice, and pace.** Any offline engine (SAPI 5, DECtalk, Piper,
  Kokoro, eSpeak NG), with a **Preview** button to hear the voice first.
- **Round-robin voices** read each article or heading in a different voice,
  cycling through a list you build:
  1. Pick a voice from the **Round-robin voices** combo box.
  2. Press **Add voice**.
  3. Repeat for each voice, and use **Move Up**, **Move Down** and
     **Remove** to set the order.

  Article 1 uses the first voice, article 2 the second, and so on, starting
  again at the top when the list runs out. The list uses voices from the
  engine you selected, so the sound quality stays consistent, and changing
  the engine clears it. Leave the list empty to use the single chosen voice.
- **Voice casting** lets you say exactly who reads what, on top of the
  rotation. On the same page, add rules: a pattern plus the voice that should
  read every matching chapter. A pattern matches the heading title as a
  wildcard (`Chapter *`, `*interview*`, or an exact title, ignoring case) or
  a section number (`#1` for the opener). The first rule that matches wins;
  chapters no rule matches go to the rotation or the single voice. Rules use
  voices of the selected engine (switching engines clears them) and are
  saved in job files. A dialogue-heavy drama or an interview show can cast
  its voices on purpose instead of by rotation order.
- If a voice ever **fails to speak** (a broken system voice, a missing model,
  or a cloud voice the provider rejects), QUILL notes it and **skips it on
  later runs**, so one bad voice in a rotation cannot keep stopping your
  batches.

Your combine and round-robin choices are remembered for each project.

##### Translated editions

**Also export in other languages (translated)** makes a translated audiobook
alongside the original.

1. Choose a **language**.
2. Pick a **voice** for it.
3. Press **Add language**. Repeat for as many languages as you want.
   **Remove language** drops one.
4. Choose **Translate with**: **AI provider** (any AI provider you have set
   up) or **LibreTranslate** (runs locally).

Voices are offered local ones first (eSpeak speaks nearly every language
offline, plus any Windows voice installed for that language), then the
**premium multilingual cloud voices: OpenAI, Gemini, and ElevenLabs**. Those
need the matching provider API key, the same key the AI Voice feature uses.
When you press Start, each document is translated and written as
`<doc> (<Language>).<ext>` next to the original, with the same chapters,
page-turn cue, and loudness. A pronunciation dictionary can be limited to
one language, so it only affects that language's narration. If a cloud
voice you chose has no key set up, that language is skipped with a note and
the run carries on.

You see the cost first for cloud runs. Cloud translation and cloud narration
are paid by use, so if your choices would use a paid cloud service, QUILL
shows a **combined cost estimate** and asks you to confirm before it starts.
Runs that use only local engines and LibreTranslate start straight away.

##### How should chapters work

- **Chapters** turn a long document into a **chaptered** file you can move
  around in. Choose **MP3** (ID3 chapter markers) or **M4B audiobook** (native
  MP4 chapter atoms, the Apple and audiobook format). Apple Podcasts,
  Overcast, VLC, foobar2000, and others recognize both.
- A **transition sound** plays between articles: a natural page-turn by
  default, or a different earcon from your active sound pack. Whichever you
  use is matched to the audio format automatically, so it always joins
  cleanly.
- You choose whether each heading is spoken, and set pauses between articles
  and between sentences, plus a short silence at the end that stops clipping.
- A very long section is split automatically at a safe sentence boundary, so
  no single passage runs past the engine's time limit. The run report lists
  how many chapters each document got.
- **Chapter mode**: keep the whole document as **one chaptered file**, or
  choose **Separate file per article** to write each section under a heading
  as its own `NNN - <heading>` audio file, in a folder for that document.
- **Combine empty headings**: when a heading has no text of its own (a "Part"
  heading followed straight away by a "Chapter" heading), fold it into the
  next article that does have text and join their titles ("Part One: Chapter
  1"), so you do not hear an empty chapter. Off by default. Turn it on with
  the **Combine empty headings into the next article** checkbox.

##### Output and diagnostics

- **Output format**: **WAV** (always available) or, when `ffmpeg` is
  installed, **MP3, M4A, M4B (audiobook), Opus, FLAC, or OGG**. When `ffmpeg`
  is missing, compressed formats fall back to WAV with a note for each file,
  instead of failing. MP3 has a quality setting, and WAV can be made to one
  sample rate and channel count throughout.
- **Normalize loudness**: tick **Normalize loudness to audiobook (ACX)
  level** to bring every exported file to the same audiobook loudness, the
  standard the Build Audiobook tool uses. QUILL measures each file and
  re-levels it in two passes, without touching the chapters or their timing.
  Needs ffmpeg; without it, the file is saved as it is, with a note.
- **If a file already exists**: **Skip** (a cheap way to resume),
  **Overwrite**, or **Rename** so both are kept (`name (2).mp3`).
- **Output layout**: mirror the source folders or **flatten** everything into
  one folder. You can also rename outputs with a **template** such as
  `{index:03d} - {stem}`, which gives `001 - chapter-one`.
- **Audiobook metadata**: album, author or narrator, genre, and year are
  written into compressed files. Each file's title comes from its heading or
  name, and its track number from its position.
- **Dry run**: instead of speaking, write a `<doc>.preview.txt` for each
  document with the exact text that would be spoken (after cleanup,
  pronunciation fixes, and polish) and how many pronunciation substitutions
  were made. You can proofread what will be said before waiting on slow
  speech.
- **Audition**: tick **Audition** on the output step to convert only the
  first document. You can judge the voice, the pace, and the loudness in a
  couple of minutes before you commit to an overnight run.
- **Run report**: optionally write a `manifest.json` and `manifest.csv`
  listing every file's status, output path, length, and any error.

##### Incremental rebuilds

With **Reuse unchanged audio from the last run** ticked (the default), QUILL
takes a fingerprint of each document's text together with every setting that
shapes its audio. On the next run, documents that have not changed, and
whose audio is still on disk, are reused instead of spoken again, and you
hear "Reused ... (unchanged since last run)". Edit one chapter of a
forty-document book and only that chapter is narrated again. Change the
voice or any audio setting and everything rebuilds by itself. Untick the box
to force a full rebuild. The fingerprints are kept in the source folder's
`.quill/speech-cache.json`; deleting that file also forces a fresh run.

##### The book page

- **Look up book details.** Type the title (and the author, if you know it)
  and press **Look up book details**. QUILL searches **Open Library** and
  **MusicBrainz**, two free public catalogs, and the match you pick fills in
  the author, genre, and year. QUILL asks before the first contact, and only
  the title and author you typed are sent. If the match has a cover image on
  Open Library and you have not set one, QUILL offers to download it as
  `cover.jpg` next to your audio and fills the cover field. Say no and
  nothing is fetched.
- **Spoken credits.** Tick **Add spoken opening and closing credits** and
  QUILL narrates the usual audiobook frame ("My Book. Written by Jane Doe.
  Narrated by Sam Reader.") in the run's own voice, as the first and last
  chapters.
- **Polish during the build.** The audio source page's **Trim silences from
  each recording** and the book page's **fade-in / fade-out / tempo**
  controls are applied while the audiobook is built. Each chapter file is
  prepared first (silence trimmed from the start and end, fades added, and
  the tempo changed without changing pitch) and then joined into the master.
  The prepared copies live in the build's temporary folder, so your source
  recordings are never overwritten. If polishing one file fails, the build
  keeps going with that file as it was. The defaults (no trim, `0` ms fades,
  `1.0` tempo) leave the audio unchanged.

##### Settings that stay with the folder

A folder remembers its whole speech setup in
`<folder>/.quill/speech-project.json`: engine, voice, output format,
chapters, text cleanup, pronunciation dictionaries, metadata, and run policy.
Set up a project once and run it again whenever you like. When you open the
wizard on a folder you have set up before, those settings **fill in by
themselves**, and your choices are **saved when you press Start**. Anything
you change this run beats the folder's saved settings, which beat your
global defaults.

**Job files** go one step further. On the summary page, **Save a job file**
writes a small `.quilljob` file that pins this exact run: folder, voices,
chapters, mastering, and book details. You can edit it by hand. **Load a job
file** on the first page brings everything back, filled in. Keep one per
project, or edit it in Notepad between runs.

##### Running it without you

- **Library mode** (a checkbox on the combine-audio path) builds every
  subfolder as its own audiobook in one unattended run. Point it at a folder
  of book folders and come back to a shelf of finished masters, each titled
  after its folder.
- The watch action **"Build audiobook from the folder"** keeps a drop folder
  working for you. Whenever new recordings land in a watched folder, its
  chaptered master is rebuilt automatically. A batch of files arriving
  together causes one rebuild, not many.

#### Export to Translated Speech Audio (one document)

**Tools > Speech > Export to Translated Speech Audio** is the one-document
version of the translated export above. It translates and narrates just the
document you are editing, with no folder involved.

1. Pick the output format.
2. Choose **Translate with**: any AI provider you have set up, or local
   LibreTranslate.
3. Add one or more **language + voice** targets, the same way as in the
   wizard. Local voices are listed first, then the premium cloud voices.
4. Press **Export**.

QUILL writes `<doc> (<Language>).<ext>` next to your document. If the
document has unsaved changes, QUILL offers to save first, so your latest
edits are the ones translated. As with the wizard, a **combined cost
estimate** appears before any paid cloud run.

The dialog also has an **"Open in Audio Studio"** button. It closes the
dialog and opens the Audiobook and Batch Speech wizard with your document
already filled in, for when you want chapters and the rest.

#### Build an audiobook from a folder of recordings

The wizard's **Combine audio files** path (**Tools > Speech > Audiobook &
Batch Speech...**, the second choice on the first page) joins a folder of
existing audio files into one chaptered audiobook, the kind your audiobook
or podcast app moves through track by track. Where the narrate path turns
