documents into speech, this one stitches a folder of audio (your own
recordings, or speech QUILL exported earlier) into a single master.

- Point it at a **folder of audio files**. Each file becomes one
  **chapter**, in natural sort order, titled from the file name (a leading
  track number such as `01 - ` is removed).
- **Edit the chapters before building.** The dialog lists the chapters, and
  works fully from the keyboard. You can **rename** the selected one (type a
  new title and press Rename or Enter), **move** it **up** or **down**,
  **merge** it into the chapter above (the two files then play as one
  chapter with one marker), or **remove** it from the book. **Restore
  original** undoes every edit in one press.
- **Bring your titles with you.** **Import titles...** reads chapter names, in
  order, from an Audacity label track, a CUE sheet, plain timestamp lines,
  Podcasting 2.0 chapters JSON, or a **CSV spreadsheet**. Any sheet with a
  "Title" column works, and so does a simple `number,title` list, so a
  chapter list you keep in Excel can name your MP3 files in one step.
  **Export titles...** writes the current list back out as text.
- **Honest numbers, before and after.** The run log starts with a
  **pre-flight check**. It names files whose sample rate, channels, or format
  differ (the build still works; it re-encodes them) and gives an estimated
  length and size. After the build, QUILL **re-reads the finished book** and
  tells you what a player will actually see: "verified 24 chapters", or
  exactly what went wrong. A plain-text **chapter report** and a
  **Podcasting 2.0 `...chapters.json`** file are written next to the book.
- Choose **M4B audiobook** (native MP4 chapter atoms, the Apple and audiobook
  format) or **MP3** (ID3 chapter markers). You can move by chapter in both
  in Apple Podcasts, Overcast, VLC, foobar2000, and others.
- Tick **Normalize loudness to ACX (Audible/audiobook) spec** to bring the
  master into the loudness range audiobook platforms require (RMS between
  -23 and -18 dB, peak under -3 dB). After the build, QUILL measures the
  result and says in the status bar whether it met the ACX range.
- Fill in the book's **title, author, narrator, genre, and year**. A **cover
  image** in the folder (named like `cover.jpg`, `folder.png`, and so on) is
  picked up automatically, or you can browse for one.
- The build runs in the background, and the status bar tells you when it is
  done.

#### The Chapter Workbench

The Workbench is where you fix a finished audiobook by ear. Reach it from the
wizard's **Edit an existing audiobook** path.

##### The chapter list and the player

The chapter list reads each row in full ("3. The Long Road, starts 1:02:03,
runs 12:40"). Press Enter on a chapter to hear it.

The built-in **player** has Play/Pause, Stop, Previous and Next chapter,
Rewind and Forward, a position slider that speaks minutes and seconds, and a
volume slider. The current chapter is announced as playback moves into it.

- It **remembers where you stopped** in each book and picks up there next
  time.
- It has a **playback speed** control, from 0.75x to 2x, with the pitch kept
  natural.
- It answers **"Where am I?"** with the whole picture: "Chapter 4 of 24: The
  Long Road. 3:12 into the chapter, 9:28 left in it. 1:02:03 of 7:41:00 in
  the book, 6:38:57 remaining."

Playback normally uses Windows' built-in media engine, with nothing to
install. For gapless audio, exact seeking, and instant chapter jumps even in
8-hour books, download the **mpv player engine** from **Help > Download
Optional Components** (about 44 MB, checksum-verified; its licenses and a
source offer come inside the download). The player switches to **libmpv**
the next time it opens. If you prefer, you can instead put a
`libmpv-2.dll` into the data folder's `engine-packs\mpv` folder, or set the
`QUILL_LIBMPV` environment variable to point at one. If the DLL is missing
or broken, QUILL quietly stays on the built-in engine.

##### Fixing the chapters

- **Split at playhead**: listen for the spot where a chapter should begin,
  pause there, and press the button. The chapter is cut in two exactly at
  that point. This is how you fix a book whose chapters landed in the wrong
  places.
- **Set start to playhead**: move an existing boundary. Select the chapter,
  park the playhead where it should start, and press. The previous chapter's
  end moves with it, so there are never gaps.
- **Merge into previous**, **Rename** (type and press Enter), and **Restore
  original** (one press undoes every edit).
- **Add chapter...** puts a marker at the playhead, or at a time you type,
  and asks what to call it. Past the end of the last chapter it adds a new
  one at the end instead of refusing.
- **Delete chapter** removes a marker only. The audio joins its neighbour,
  and unlike Merge it works on the first and last chapters too.
- **Edit chapter...** opens a small window for the title and the exact start
  and end (and a chapter link and image, if you publish with Podcasting
  2.0).
- **Preview chapter** plays just that chapter and stops at its end.

##### Nudging a boundary until it sounds right

**Nudge back** and **Nudge forward** move the selected chapter's start by one
step. From the chapter list, `Alt+Left` and `Alt+Right` do the same, and
adding Shift moves ten steps at once.

- The **Step** box goes from 100 milliseconds up to 10 seconds, and
  remembers your choice for next time (`audio_studio_chapter_nudge_ms`, half
  a second to start with).
- **Hear boundary** plays three seconds before the marker and two after it,
  then stops. It is the quickest way to tell whether a boundary falls in the
  middle of a sentence.
- Tick **Hear after each nudge** to have that happen automatically after
  every press. It is off by default, so you only get sound on every keypress
  if you ask for it.
- Each nudge speaks only the new time ("0:00:09.500"), so it keeps up when
  you hold the key down. The full sentence follows about half a second after
  you stop.
- Push a marker into its neighbour and it stops there and says "Cannot move
  further" once.

##### Finding chapters for you

- **Propose chapters from silences...** listens for silences in the
  recording, using ffmpeg's `silencedetect`. A small dialog asks for the **noise threshold** (dB, default
  -30) and the **minimum silence** length (seconds, default 0.8), and QUILL
  suggests chapter boundaries in the middle of each silence. The suggestions
  land in the chapter list for you to review; nothing is applied without
  you. Press **Restore original** to undo. So one long recording is no
  problem: open a single 80-minute file (it opens as one chapter), press one
  button, review, and save.
- **Propose AI titles...** names a folder of `track07`-style chapters by
  listening to them. The first minute of each chapter is transcribed on this
  computer by the local speech model, so the audio never leaves your
  computer. Only that text goes to the AI you have set up (a local model
  keeps even the text on your computer). A short suggested title for each
  chapter lands in the list for you to review, and **Restore original**
  undoes the lot. Needs AI set up; not available in Safe Mode.

##### Checking, importing and splitting

- **Check against ACX** measures the file with ffmpeg's loudnorm and shows a result with
  integrated loudness, true peak, and noise floor, plus a plain suggestion
  for each thing that fails ("Integrated loudness is -14.2 LUFS, target -20
  plus or minus 3; make the recording 5.8 dB quieter"). The result is
  announced when the measurement finishes, however you close the dialog.
- **Import chapters...** replaces the whole list from Audacity labels, a CUE
  sheet, timestamp lines, Podcasting 2.0 JSON, or CSV. **Export chapters...**
  writes the list in any of the same five formats.
- **Split into files...** goes the other way: one audio file per chapter,
  named `NN - Title`, in a folder you pick. That gives you podcast episodes
  straight away, or tracks for players without chapter support.

##### Book details and tags

**Book details** (title, author, narrator, genre, year) are edited right in
the Workbench. **All tags...** opens the full **Tag Editor** for everything
else: twenty-six fields over five pages (main, details, publishing, sort
order and cover art). They include track and disc numbers, composer,
publisher, copyright, BPM, ISRC, language, grouping, the compilation flag,
the four sort-order fields, and cover art you can load, save out or remove.
`Ctrl+Tab` moves between pages. The five quick fields and the editor always
agree with each other, in both directions.

You can also open the Tag Editor on its own, without the Workbench: tick
**Edit the tags only** on the Studio wizard's *Open a book* page.

The same editor is in podHarvest. A file edited in one reads back exactly as
you left it in the other, with the same fields, operations and keys. If you
use both, you only learn it once.

##### Saving

**Save** writes an MP3's edits **in place**: only the tags are rewritten and
the audio is left alone. An M4B depends on what you changed. Tag edits alone
also save in place and finish at once. A chapter change needs **Save As**,
which copies the audio into a new file without re-encoding, so there is no
loss of quality. Long saves run in the background, so QUILL stays
responsive.

##### Publishing

**Publish...** offers ways to get the finished book out into the world. Each
one is something you choose to do:

- **Podcast feed**: QUILL writes a complete `.rss` file next to the book
  (RSS 2.0 with iTunes and Podcasting 2.0 tags; chapter navigation uses the
  `chapters.json` file beside it). Upload the feed and audio wherever you
  like. Making the feed never touches the network.
- **Folder feed (all episodes)**: run a whole show from one folder. Every
  MP3, M4B, or M4A master becomes an episode (the oldest file is episode 1),
  with its title from its tags or your own, your description for each
  episode (edited in an accessible episode list), its real publication date,
  length, and chapter link. The show settings are kept in the folder, so
  after each new build, one press of **Write feed.rss now** makes the
  complete feed again. **Write show notes page** makes an accessible
  `show-notes.html` beside it, with a heading for each episode, the
  descriptions, and chapter lists, ready to upload with the feed.
- **SFTP upload**: save a destination (host, folder, and the public web
  address that matches it), and QUILL uploads the book and its companion
  files over SSH, with the same strict host-key checking as editing over
  SSH. The password is kept in the **Windows Credential Manager**, never in
  QUILL's settings.
- **Auphonic**: send the book to your own Auphonic account for professional
  post-production. QUILL uploads it, waits for the production to finish, and
  downloads the results into a folder next to the book. Your API token is
  also kept in the credential vault, and you can manage it in **AI > AI Hub >
  Services** with QUILL's other service keys. Press **Check account and load
  presets** first: QUILL tells you whose account the token belongs to and
  how many processing credits remain, and fills the **preset picker** with
  your saved Auphonic presets. The confirmation then names the preset and
  your balance before anything uploads. QUILL asks before anything is
  uploaded.

Publishing is not available in Safe Mode. Every upload runs in the
background and tells you when it is done. SFTP uploads and Auphonic
transfers show a progress dialog that speaks whole-percent steps as the file
moves ("Uploading book.m4b: 42%") and has a real **Cancel** button. What
cancelling does depends on when you press it, and QUILL tells you which
happened:

- Cancelling an SFTP upload stops in the middle of the file. Files that
  already finished stay on the server.
- Cancelling Auphonic before the upload finishes means no production starts.
- Cancelling Auphonic after that leaves the production running in your
  Auphonic account and skips the download.

#### The Universal Audio Converter

Apart from the audiobook wizard, QUILL has a general **audio converter**. It
changes audio files from one format to another, and pulls the sound out of
video files, entirely on your computer using the bundled ffmpeg. It works in
Safe Mode and never uploads anything. There are three ways in:

- **Voices > Convert Audio...**: the dialog, from the audiobook and batch
  speech wizard.
- **`quill convert`**: a command for scripts, for example
  `quill convert *.wav --to mp3 --preset podcast --out ./done`. Add
  `--dry-run` to see the plan first, `--list-presets` or `--list-formats` to
  see what is available, and any of the Advanced options (`--bitrate`,
  `--sample-rate`, `--channels`, `--loudness`, `--gain`, `--high-pass`,
  `--trim-silence`, `--speed`, `--compress`, `--level`, `--fade-in`,
  `--fade-out`).
- **Convert from URL...**: paste a link (YouTube, and the many sites yt-dlp
  supports) and QUILL downloads the best audio and hands it to the
  converter. This is the only part that uses the internet. yt-dlp is **not**
  bundled, so the first time you use it QUILL asks once, shows a rights
  notice ("only download content you have the right to use"), and installs
  the small yt-dlp component. It is not available in Safe Mode.

##### Building a batch

1. Add single files or whole folders. A folder is searched, and its layout
   of subfolders is copied into the output folder.
2. Choose the output **format**. Only formats your ffmpeg can actually make
   are offered, so a conversion never fails halfway for lack of an encoder.
3. Pick a **preset**: *Just convert* (change the container only), *MP3
   128/192/320*, *Podcast*, *Audiobook*, *Voice memo*, *Web Opus*,
   *Archival FLAC*, or *Hearing-aid mono*.
4. Choose an output folder, or leave it to make a `Converted` folder beside
   the source.
5. Choose what happens when a file already exists: **auto-number** (never
   overwrites an original), **skip**, or **overwrite**.

The batch runs in the background on several files at once, so the window
stays responsive. Progress shows in the status bar and, when QUILL is
minimized, in the tray tooltip. The final summary is spoken and always names
any files that failed, so a problem is never hidden behind "done".

##### Advanced options

Tick **Advanced options** to show more controls on top of the preset:

- exact **bit rate**, **sample rate**, **channels** (keep, mono or stereo),
  and **bit depth**
- loudness normalized to an **audiobook** (-20 LUFS, ACX) or **podcast**
  (-16 LUFS) target
- **gain** in decibels
- a **high-pass** filter to remove low rumble
- **trim silence** from the ends
- **speed**, a tempo change from 0.5x to 2x with no change in pitch
- a **compressor** and a volume **leveler**
- **fade in** and **fade out**, in seconds

Each control leaves the preset alone until you change it, so Advanced only
overrides what you set on purpose. The effects are the same ones QUILL uses
elsewhere, so the results match the rest of the app.

### Media

QUILL also plays podcasts, recorded programmes and audiobook chapters. This
part is about keeping your place in all of it, even across computers, and
about letting it stop by itself when you fall asleep.

#### Continue Listening

**Continue Listening...** (in the Command Palette) is one list of everything
you started and did not finish, newest first, with the kind named on every
row: a podcast episode you are twenty minutes into, a recorded programme or
LibriVox chapter you were halfway through. It answers the question "what was
I in the middle of?" in one place.

- **Resume** starts the highlighted row where you left off.
- **Forget This One** drops the saved place and removes the row. The episode
  stays unplayed, because "I am not going back to this" and "I finished it"
  are different things. Clearing what you have given up on keeps the list
  worth opening.

#### Carry My Place Between Machines

If you listen on more than one computer, **Carry My Place Between
Machines...** makes your place follow you. It needs two things: a folder both
computers can see, and a recovery phrase.

The folder is yours. Point it at somewhere inside OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud
Drive, a network share, or even a memory stick you carry between the two.
QUILL runs no server of its own and never holds your listening history.
Everything is encrypted before it reaches the folder, so whoever runs that
folder learns nothing but file sizes and times.

The recovery phrase is eight ordinary words, made up for you, something like
*earth dock hollow iris farm laser daisy amber*. Write it down. It is the
key, and QUILL cannot get it back for you if you lose it. **Read My Phrase
Aloud** says it back numbered, one word at a time, which is just what you
want while writing it on paper.

To set up the second computer, use the same window:

1. Open **Carry My Place Between Machines...** on the second computer.
2. Point it at the same folder.
3. Type the phrase from the first computer.

QUILL notices the folder is already set up and says so. If the phrase is
wrong it tells you at once ("that recovery phrase does not match this
folder; nothing was changed") instead of half-syncing and failing later.
Typing is forgiving about capitals, spacing and punctuation, and a word that
is not on the word list is named, so you only need to check that one.

**Sync Now** runs it and tells you in a sentence what happened: what came
back, what went out, and whether two computers disagreed about a place (the
most recent wins, and you are told). It can also run when playback stops, if
you like. If both computers remembered a different place in the same thing
and they are more than a few minutes apart, QUILL treats that as a real
disagreement and tells you, instead of quietly picking one.

Everything works normally with no sync at all. Nothing ever waits on the
folder before playing.

#### Sharing your place with apps that are not QUILL

The sync above carries your place between two copies of QUILL. It is
encrypted from end to end, which is right, and which is also why no other
app can read it. If you listen on a phone with a podcast app that is not
ours, it does not help you.

**Listening Places** is the other half, and it is a separate checkbox in the
same window. In the folder you already chose, QUILL also writes a small,
plain file in a published format that any podcast app is free to read and
write. There is no account, no server, and no signup. The format is written
down publicly, so another app can simply support it.

What that means for you:

- **Turn on only the half you want.** The encrypted QUILL-to-QUILL sync and
  the shared plain file are separate switches, because they reveal different
  things. You can use either, both, or neither.
- **No recovery phrase is needed for this half.** The shared file cannot be
  encrypted and still be readable by another app, so setting it up is one
  checkbox.
- **Titles are left out unless you say so.** Every show and episode is
  identified by a scrambled fingerprint instead of its name, so a folder you
  share with a family member does not become a list of what you listen to. A
  third checkbox, off by default, adds readable titles if you want them.
- **Each device writes its own file.** That stops a cloud drive ever making a
  "positions (Jeff's conflicted copy)", and it means a third and fourth
  device work with no extra setup.
- **The most recent place wins, not the furthest.** If you jumped back twenty
  minutes on purpose and then opened the episode somewhere else, that jump is
  kept.
- **It reads at launch and when you press Sync Now, and at no other time.**
  So a position from another device never moves the playhead under you in
  the middle of an episode.

**Sync Now** covers both halves in one press and reports on each.

#### Sleep Timer

**Tools > Media > Sleep Timer...** stops whatever is playing after a while,
from one place.

1. Choose a preset (15, 30, 45, 60, or 90 minutes), or type your own number
   of minutes.
2. Press **Start**.

Over the last 20 seconds, playback fades gently down and then stops. Your
volume is then set back to what it was before the fade, so pressing play
later is not suddenly quiet. Open the dialog again while a timer is running
to hear how much time is left, or press **Cancel Sleep Timer** (also in the
Command Palette as **Media: Cancel Sleep Timer**) to stop the countdown
early.

### What you learned, and where to go next

You can now have QUILL read to you in the voice and language you like, and
teach it how to say the words it gets wrong. You can inspect a character,
hear the hidden formatting with Reveal Codes (`Alt+F3`), read an EPUB by
chapter, and step through the differences between two documents. You know
where QUILL makes audiobooks, fixes their chapters and publishes them, and
how to keep your place in what you listen to.

To practise with QUILL beside you, open **Help > Tutorials...**
(`Ctrl+Alt+F1`) and try "Have it read to you", "See the formatting that is
normally hidden" and "Inspect a document you did not write". On the website,
[Rescue a scanned PDF](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/03-rescue-a-scanned-pdf.html)
and
[From document to published audiobook](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/04-document-to-audiobook.html)
walk through the longer jobs.

Next, Chapter 9, Dictation and transcription, turns things around: you speak
and QUILL writes.

## Chapter 9: Dictation and transcription

This chapter is about turning speech into text. You will learn to talk
straight into a document, to turn a recording into a transcript, and to have
QUILL make meeting minutes or notes out of that transcript for you. Most of it
runs entirely on your own computer, with no account and nothing uploaded. If
you would rather speak than type, or you have a pile of recordings to get
through, this chapter is for you. The parts about speech models, optional
downloads and memory come last, for when you want to tune things.

### Dictating into a document

QUILL gives you three ways to dictate. **Live Dictation** writes each phrase
as you pause, which suits most people most of the time. **Locked Dictation**
records a whole passage and writes it when you finish. **Dictate (Offline)**
is the simple start-and-stop toggle on the Speech menu. All three put the
words at your cursor, and all three work without an internet connection.

> **QUILLBee's tip:** Can't remember what you are allowed to say? While Live
> Dictation is running (`Ctrl+F11`), just say "what can I say" and the whole
> list opens in a window.

#### Live Dictation (Ctrl+F11)

This is the dictation QUILL Lite has, in QUILL too, on the same keys. It lives
at **Tools > Speech > Live Dictation**.

1. Put your cursor where you want the words.
2. Press `Ctrl+F11`.
3. Talk, then pause. Each phrase is written at the cursor when you pause. A
   soft tone tells you it arrived, and the words are read back to you.
4. When you are done, press `Ctrl+F11` again, or say "stop dictation".

Nothing leaves your computer, nothing is downloaded, and no recording is kept.
Unlike **Locked Dictation**, which records a passage and transcribes it
afterwards, Live Dictation writes as you go.

The same submenu has two more windows:

- **Recent Phrases...** (`Shift+F11`) lists the last twenty phrases of the
  session, with Insert Again and Copy.
- **My Words and Phrases...** (`Alt+Shift+F10`) is a window with Add Word, Add
  Phrase, Add Correction, Edit and Remove. It edits your `dictation.md` file for
  you.

A few things that are good to know while you talk:

- **Escape** throws away the phrase being heard.
- Pressing `Ctrl+F11` in a second document moves dictation there.
- If your microphone goes away, dictation pauses, and it picks up again when
  the device is back.
- If the engine has a problem, QUILL quietly restarts it once before it tells
  you about a failure.

The full list of everything Live Dictation understands is its own page,
**[Dictation commands](dictation-commands.html)**, built from the same table
QUILL itself reads. While dictating, say **"what can I say"** to open that list
in a window.

##### Punctuation

**You do not need to say punctuation.** The built-in engines add full stops,
commas, question marks and capitals by themselves. When you want a particular
mark, say it ("comma", "new paragraph") and your word wins. If a pause splits a
sentence and the next part begins with a word like *and* or *which*, the full
stop the pause put in is taken back out.

**Punctuation and layout, anywhere in a phrase.** You can say "period",
"comma", "question mark", "open quote" and "close quote", brackets, "hyphen",
"dash", "slash", symbols like "at sign" and "percent sign", "new line", "new
paragraph" and "tab". Say "literal" first to write one of them as a word.

##### Voice commands

**Commands, as a whole phrase after a pause:**

- "scratch that" removes the last phrase
- "undo that"
- "select that"
- "capitalize that", "all caps that", "no caps that"
- "delete word", "delete sentence"
- "read that"
- "go to beginning of line", "go to end of line", "go to top", "go to end of
  document"
- "stop dictation"

If you have typed into the last phrase since you said it, the commands that
change it leave it alone, and tell you so.

**Spelling.** Say "start spelling", then the letters. The phonetic alphabet
(alpha, bravo, charlie...) is the reliable way. Say "capital" before a capital
letter and "space" for a space. Say "stop spelling" when you are done.

##### Speech engines for Live Dictation

**Speech engines.** You have four to choose from:

- **Moonshine**, the default. It is fast even on a modest computer.
- **Whisper**, a little slower. Try it if Moonshine often mishears you.
  Moonshine and Whisper are both built in, and both are English. This
  Whisper comes with QUILL; it is not the whisper.cpp engine that
  transcription uses, which downloads the first time you need it.
- **Windows speech recognition** works in any speech language installed in
  Windows, but adds no punctuation of its own.
- **Windows voice typing** hands over to `Windows+H`, where none of the
  commands apply.

##### The wake phrase

**The wake phrase.** Switch on **Listen for the wake phrase while dictation is
off** in Dictation Settings, then say **"Quill dictate"** (or a phrase of your
own, at least two words) to start without touching the keyboard. Anything you
say after it in the same breath is written.

While the wake phrase is on, the microphone is open whenever QUILL is the
window in front. Nothing it hears is written, kept or sent unless it begins
with the wake phrase, and the microphone closes when another program comes to
the front. It never listens in the background.

##### Your own words and phrases

**Your own words and phrases.** **Edit My Words and Phrases...** in Dictation
Settings opens your `dictation.md`, the same file Locked Dictation reads.
**Vocabulary** entries correct near misses to your spelling. **Replacements**
(`say => write`, with `\n` for a new line) are spoken phrases of your own.

##### Dictation Settings (Alt+Shift+F6)

**Dictation Settings -- Alt+Shift+F6** (press `Alt+Shift+F6`) is where Live
Dictation is set up. Each choice is listed here with its setting name in
brackets:

- The **speech engine** (`windows_dictation_engine`).
- The **dictation language** (`windows_dictation_speech_language`): English,
  or Spanish. See "Dictating in Spanish" below.
- The **language** for Windows speech recognition
  (`windows_dictation_language`).
- The **microphone** (`windows_dictation_microphone`, saved by name).
- **What you hear after each phrase** (`windows_dictation_phrase_feedback`): a
  sound, the words read back, both (the default), or neither.
- What **"dash"** writes (`windows_dictation_dash`): em dash, spaced en dash,
  or two hyphens.
- The **start, stop and error tones** (`windows_dictation_cue_sounds`).
- **Saying "Dictation on" and "Dictation off"** (`windows_dictation_announce`).
- The **wake phrase** (`windows_dictation_wake_enabled`,
  `windows_dictation_wake_phrase`).
- The **stop phrase** (`windows_dictation_stop_phrase`). It is "stop
  dictation" until you choose your own words, said on their own after a pause.
  "stop dictation" always works too.

Five finer choices sit beside them:

- **Automatic punctuation** for Moonshine and Whisper
  (`windows_dictation_auto_punctuation`). Turn it off and you say every mark.
- The **pause before a phrase is written** (`windows_dictation_pause`): short,
  normal or long.
- **Remove filler words** such as um and uh
  (`windows_dictation_remove_fillers`).
- **Stop dictation after silence** (`windows_dictation_silence_minutes`):
  never, 1, 5 or 10 minutes.
- **Just write what I say** (`windows_dictation_continuous`), for talking in
  one long run. A pause then puts in no full stop, plays nothing and reads
  nothing back, and voice commands are written as words. Only spoken marks and
  the stop phrase are still obeyed.

**Test Microphone** records four seconds and tells you how loud it was and what
the engine heard.

A failure is always spoken, whatever these settings say. If the read-back
plays through speakers, the microphone can hear it, so use headphones or choose
a sound only.

##### Dictating in Spanish

You can dictate in Spanish. This is new, so treat it as something to try, and
tell us how it goes.

**To switch it on**, open Dictation Settings (`Alt+Shift+F6`), move to
**Dictation language**, choose **Spanish**, and press Enter. That's
all. To go back, choose English the same way.

**What works now:**

- **Your words come out in Spanish**, accents and all. With Moonshine or
  Whisper, QUILL uses Whisper's multilingual speech model, which comes with
  QUILL, so there is nothing to download. Moonshine only knows English, so in
  Spanish you get Whisper either way.
- **With Windows speech recognition**, Windows needs Spanish installed: add
  Spanish (Spain or Mexico) in Windows Settings, Time and language, Speech. If
  it isn't there, dictation tells you so when you start.
- **The wake and stop phrases** become "Quill dicta" and "deja de dictar". If
  you have typed your own, yours are kept.

**Commands stay in English for now.** "Scratch that", "select that", "new
paragraph" and the rest work exactly as they do in English. Spanish commands
are on the way, once a native speaker has checked them.

**Punctuation.** With automatic punctuation on (the usual setting), Whisper
puts in the commas, full stops and question marks for you, so just speak.
Spanish punctuation words only work when automatic punctuation is off, or with
Windows speech recognition. That's because "coma" and "punto" are everyday
words too, and we don't want "que coma" turned into a comma. When they are
on, you can say:

- "coma" for a comma, "punto" (or "punto y seguido") for a full stop, and
  "punto y aparte" for a full stop and a new paragraph
- "punto y coma", "dos puntos" and "puntos suspensivos"
- "abrir interrogación" and "cerrar interrogación" for the question marks at
  each end, and "abrir exclamación" and "cerrar exclamación" the same way
- "abrir paréntesis", "cerrar paréntesis", "abrir comillas", "cerrar comillas"
- "guion", "guion largo" and "arroba"
- "nueva línea", "nuevo párrafo" and "tabulador"

Say "literal" first to write the word itself: "literal coma" writes *coma*.
Say "what can I say" while dictating to see the whole list.

**This is new, and we'd love to hear from you.** If a word keeps coming out
wrong, or something doesn't work the way you expect, use Help > Get Help from
Support and tell us what you said and what was written.

##### Where the words go

**Where the words go.** Into the document you started in, replacing any
selection. Each phrase is one step for `Ctrl+Z`. If you move to another tab,
window, program or dialog and speak, nothing is written: dictation stops and
tells you why. Closing the document stops it too.

If dictation will not start, it tells you why: no microphone, microphone
access turned off for desktop apps in Windows Settings, Privacy and security,
Microphone, or (for Windows speech recognition) no speech language installed.

Live Dictation and Locked Dictation each keep their own microphone choice.

#### Locked Dictation (Ctrl+F9)

Locked Dictation is a keyboard-only way to dictate a longer passage without
opening a dialog or leaving the editor. It uses the same on-device Whisper
engine and microphone as **Dictate (Offline)**, so nothing is uploaded.

1. Put your cursor where the text should go.
2. Press `Ctrl+F9`. QUILL says "Locked dictation on."
3. Speak as long as you like, across sentences and paragraphs.
4. Press `Ctrl+F9` again to finish. QUILL transcribes what you said and
   inserts it at the cursor as one undoable edit.

There used to be a press-and-hold `F9` mode. It was removed, because a held
key repeats and announces itself endlessly under a screen reader.

##### Stopping, pausing and checking

- **Stopping safely.** While recording, `Escape` stops and keeps your speech
  for transcription. `Shift+Escape` cancels and throws it away. A session also
  stops by itself after five minutes, and it stops and keeps your audio if
  QUILL loses focus.
- **Pause and status.** `Ctrl+Shift+F9` pauses or resumes the session.
  `Alt+F9` speaks the current state without changing anything.
- **Distinct sound, one-time hint.** Locked Dictation plays its own sounds, and
  the very first time you dictate, QUILL speaks a short hint about the keys.
- **Remappable.** `Ctrl+F9` and the rest are only the defaults. Change them in
  the Keymap Editor (**Tools > Customize and Support > Keymap Editor...**).

To use Locked Dictation you need an offline speech model installed (**Tools >
Speech > Manage Speech Models**) and the optional microphone-capture support.
In Safe Mode, dictation is turned off.

##### Nothing is lost

**Nothing is lost.** Your audio is saved to a recovery folder before
transcription starts, and a transcript that cannot be safely inserted is kept
for you to review.

**Dictation History & Review.** **Tools > Speech > Locked Dictation >
Dictation History & Review...** lists every recording whose transcript was
never inserted: ones left behind by a crash, and ones that could not be placed
safely. For each you can **insert** it at the cursor, **copy** it, or
**discard** it. `Enter` inserts the selected row. If anything is waiting for
review when QUILL starts, QUILL tells you and points you here, so dictated
speech is never silently lost.

##### Locked Dictation settings

**Dictation Settings.** **Tools > Speech > Locked Dictation > Dictation
Settings...** holds the choices the dictation engine reads:

- the session time limit
- stop and keep speech when QUILL loses focus
- intelligent insertion spacing
- a reset that brings back the one-time first-use hint

##### Parakeet 3 and silence

**Parakeet 3: the most reliable dictation engine, and QUILL prefers it once
you install it.** Whisper has a well-known flaw for dictation. Give it silence
(a pause while you think, a breath before you stop) and it sometimes invents
text, most famously a phantom "thank you". Parakeet 3 only writes words when it
actually hears them, so silence produces nothing.

Parakeet 3 is an NVIDIA model. It knows 25 languages, detects the language by
itself, runs on the CPU only, and is about a 650 MB download from **Manage
Speech Models**. Once its model is installed, dictation switches to it
automatically. If you have chosen an engine yourself, that choice is always
respected, and removing the model simply returns you to Whisper. Nothing else
changes: same keys, same review, same recovery.

**Silence is trimmed before transcription.** QUILL removes the quiet lead-in
and tail from each dictation take before the engine hears it. A recording with
no speech in it at all gets the "no speech" sound, so no engine gets the chance
to make something up. This applies to every engine, Whisper included, and
there is nothing to set.

##### Teach dictation your words

**Teach dictation your words.** A small file called **`dictation.md`** in your
QUILL data folder holds your own vocabulary (so names and jargon come back
spelled right), spoken-to-written replacements (such as "new line" becoming a
real line break), and spoken command phrases of your own. It applies to Locked
Dictation and the Dictate (Offline) toggle.

Your vocabulary is used twice. Engines that accept a hint, such as Whisper, are
steered toward your words before they transcribe. Then every engine, including
Parakeet 3, which takes no hints, gets a **fuzzy correction pass afterwards**.
It recognises near misses by spelling and by sound, so "charge b" comes back as
"ChargeBee" exactly as you wrote it, capitals and all. Names split in two,
words run together, and "R&D" heard as "r and d" are all repaired. Ordinary
words are left alone.

The **Voice Interaction** guide ([voice-interaction.md](voice-interaction.md)),
in its section "Teaching dictation your words," explains the file format and
how to choose a speech engine (Whisper's small models, Parakeet 3, or
Nemotron).

##### Filler words

**Filler words can be removed, but only if you ask.** This option is off by
default. Turn it on with the `dictation_remove_fillers` setting, and
hesitations like "uh" and "hmm" are taken out of your transcripts. It pays
attention to language: "um" is only removed when your dictation language says
that is safe, because in Portuguese "um" means "a" or "an", and in German it
means "at" or "around". When QUILL cannot tell the language, it only removes
sounds that are fillers in every language.

#### Dictate (Offline)

**Dictate (Offline)** on **Tools > Speech** is a simple toggle that speaks
straight into your document.

1. Choose it, or press the QUILL key (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave`) then `Shift+D`.
   QUILL plays a start tone and the status bar shows "Dictation listening".
2. Speak.
3. Choose it again to stop. QUILL plays a stop tone, transcribes what you said
   in the background, and inserts the text at your cursor as one undoable edit.
   The status bar shows the word count.

**Dictation Microphone...** on the same menu chooses which microphone this
dictation uses, or the system default.

### Transcribing a recording

When you have a recording rather than a live voice, QUILL can turn it into
text. You can do it entirely on your computer from **Tools > Speech**, or send
it to a cloud service from the **AI** menu. Either way you get a draft to read
and correct. Automatic transcription is never perfect.

#### Transcribe on your computer

QUILL can transcribe **entirely on your computer**, with no cloud account and
without uploading your audio. **No AI account or key is required**, and you
do not need to turn on Artificial Intelligence to use it.

1. Choose **Tools > Speech > Transcribe Audio or Video (Offline)...**.
2. Pick an audio or video file.
3. Choose a transcript format: **plain text, Markdown, or HTML**.
4. Keep working while it runs in the background. QUILL tells you when it is
   done and how many words it produced, and opens the result as a draft
   document you can edit.

The first time you transcribe or dictate offline, QUILL may need to fetch its
speech engine and a model. It offers to do that for you. The Speech section
later in this chapter explains models and engines.

##### Supported formats and FFmpeg

**Supported formats.** You can pick MP3, M4A, AAC, FLAC, OGG, Opus, WMA, WAV,
MP4, M4V, MOV, MKV, WebM, or AVI.

If **ffmpeg** is installed, QUILL converts the file for you before
transcribing, so you never have to make a WAV yourself. QUILL does not ship
ffmpeg, but it can fetch it:

- **Tools > Speech > Download FFmpeg...** downloads the official build (about
  110 MB, with a progress bar you can cancel) and sets it up.
- Or install it yourself once (for example, `winget install Gyan.FFmpeg`) and
  QUILL finds it on your PATH.

ffmpeg is open source (GPL/LGPL) and comes straight from the official builder.
QUILL never bundles or redistributes it. Without ffmpeg, the whisper.cpp engine
needs a 16 kHz mono WAV, while the Faster Whisper engine can handle the other
formats by itself.

##### Captions and speaker labels

- **Generate Captions (Offline)...** on **Tools > Speech** transcribes a file
  with timestamps and saves the result as **SRT** or **VTT** caption files.
- **Speaker attribution.** If you download the "Small English with speaker
  detection" model (in Manage Speech Models), QUILL marks **who is speaking
  when**. Each turn is labelled "Speaker 1", "Speaker 2", and so on in the
  transcript, in bold in Markdown and HTML. It tells the turns apart; it does
  not name the people.

#### Transcribe Audio File

If you have AI set up, **AI > Transcribe Audio File...** sends a recording to
OpenAI Whisper in the cloud.

1. Choose **AI > Transcribe Audio File...**. A file picker opens.
2. Pick the audio file. Supported formats: MP3, MP4, M4A, WAV, WEBM, OGG, FLAC
   (maximum 25 MB).
3. Choose your options:
   - **Language**: detect it automatically, or pick a language for better
     accuracy.
   - **Speaker diarization** (uses Deepgram): works out who is speaking when.
     Each turn is labelled Speaker 1, Speaker 2, and so on, with timestamps.
     This needs a Deepgram API key set up in AI Hub.
   - **Translate to English**: transcribes audio in any language and gives you
     an English translation in one step (Whisper translation mode).

When the transcript is ready, QUILL asks **"What would you like me to make of
this?"** and offers a short list of **Transcript Actions**, chosen to suit the
recording. Pick one and QUILL turns the transcript into a finished document,
such as meeting minutes, action items, study notes or a clean draft, and opens
it for you to review and edit. Or choose **"Just keep the transcript"** to go
to the viewer, where you can copy it, insert it at the cursor, or open it as a
new document. If AI is turned off, you go straight to the viewer.

**AI > Translate Audio File to English...** goes straight to the Whisper
translation, skipping the language step.

#### Transcript Actions

A transcript is rarely what you actually need. You want the minutes, the
action items, or a clean draft. **Transcript Actions** make that last step one
choice away. You can reach them in two places:

- **Right after transcription**, in the "What would you like me to make of
  this?" chooser described above.
- **Any time**, on text you already have, with **AI > Transcribe Audio >
  Transcript Actions...**. Paste in a transcript or notes (or select part of
  your document) and pick an action.

The built-in actions are:

- **Meeting Minutes**: attendees, decisions, action items with owners,
  follow-ups.
- **Action Items**: every task and commitment as a numbered list you can act
  on.
- **Executive Summary**: a short briefing for leadership.
- **Interview Notes**: questions, answers, strengths, concerns and an
  assessment.
- **Study Notes**: a lecture or talk turned into organized notes.
- **Q&A Extraction**: every question and its answer in clean Q&A format.
- **Clean Up & Draft**: spoken rambling turned into a clean, readable draft.
- **Follow-Up Email**: a warm, ready-to-send recap with next steps.
- **Key Quotes**: the most notable quotes, word for word, with who said them.
- **Decisions Log**: just the decisions made, each with its reason and owner.

QUILL puts the most likely ones first for the recording in front of you. A
meeting with several speakers starts with Minutes and Action Items; a single
voice starts with Clean Up & Draft. Every action is always there, though. The
finished document opens in a new window, so your original transcript is never
overwritten. Transcript Actions use whichever AI provider you have set up in
the AI Hub.

### Automate transcription with watch folders

A watch folder lets you set a rule once: drop a file in this folder, and QUILL
deals with it. You will find the commands on **Tools > Watch Folder**.

#### The Watch Folder menu

- **Watch Folder Monitoring (in Settings)...** turns on or off the automatic
  opening of supported files dropped into a folder you have chosen.
- **Watch Folder Profiles...** sets the folder path, whether subfolders count,
  what happens at startup, and how often the folder is checked.
- **Watch Folder Queue...** shows what is happening right now and the settings
  in use.

Watch folders are good for "drop and open" work: copy supported files into one
folder and let QUILL open them in the background. They respect Do Not Disturb
and run quietly.

#### Transcribing arriving audio

Each watch profile runs one action on every file it picks up. As well as
opening, moving, copying, converting, running a macro or a sandboxed
transform, and OCR, a profile can **transcribe arriving audio**. Any audio or
video file dropped into the folder is transcribed on your machine with the
offline speech engine, and a transcript is written next to it. Nothing is
uploaded.

Choose the **Transcript format** in the profile:

- plain **Text** (`.txt`)
- **SubRip captions** (`.srt`)
- **WebVTT captions** (`.vtt`)
- **Markdown** (`.md`)

The caption formats carry timestamps. If the engine returns no timed parts,
they fall back to plain text, so you never get an empty caption file. This
needs no consent. If no speech model is installed yet, the profile tells you to
download one from **Tools > Speech > Manage Speech Models**.

There is also a separate **Transcribe audio (OpenAI Whisper)** action for
cloud transcription, once you have turned on AI and set up a key.

#### Making minutes automatically

A transcribe profile can also **chain an AI Action onto each recording**:

1. In **Tools > Watch Folder > Watch Folder Profiles...**, point a profile at a
   folder (for example, *Meetings*).
2. Choose a transcribe action (offline or OpenAI Whisper).
3. Under **Then make**, pick a Transcript Action, such as *Meeting Minutes*.

From then on, every recording that lands in that folder is transcribed, and the
minutes document is written next to it, with a name like
`standup-meeting-minutes.md`. If AI is off or no provider is set up, you still
get the transcript. The action step is skipped with a note, never an error.

#### The Watch Folders page in Settings

- **Enable folder watching by default** starts watching your enabled
  profiles each time QUILL starts. It is off to begin with. **Watch Folder
  Monitoring (in Settings)...** brings you to Settings so you can turn it on.
- **Poll interval (seconds)** is how often a watched folder is checked, from
  2 to 300 seconds. The default is 5.
- **Watch folder: play a sound on each check** plays a short tick every time
  the folder is checked, so silence means the watcher has stopped rather than
  found nothing. Off to begin with.
- **Watch folder: let results interrupt speech** announces a newly opened
  file straight away, cutting across whatever is being said. Off means the
  notice waits its turn.

### Speech

**Tools > Speech** is where QUILL keeps its on-device speech tools: the
transcription and dictation commands you have already met, and the speech
models and engines that make them work. You do not have to understand any of
this to dictate. Come here when you want a more accurate model, a lighter one
for an older computer, or a different engine.

#### Manage Speech Models

**Manage Speech Models...** lists local speech models with their download size,
accuracy and speed, and helps you pick one that will run well on your computer.

- The dialog opens with a one-line summary of your machine: its RAM, and
  whether a GPU was found.
- Each model shows roughly how much memory it needs. A model too big for your
  RAM is flagged.
- The best fit for your computer is marked **"Recommended for your
  computer."**
- A larger model warns you when there is no GPU, because it will be slow on
  the CPU.

**Choosing what to do.** Pick a model, then choose an action: **Download this
model** if it is not installed, or **Remove this model from my computer** if it
is. Before a download starts, QUILL warns you if there is not enough free disk
space.

**Downloads run in the background and show progress.** You can keep working.
A progress window shows a **percentage** and has a **Cancel** button you can
press at any time, and QUILL announces progress as it goes. Cancelling cleans
up the partial file. Models come over a secure connection from the Hugging Face
Hub and are stored on your computer. Downloading is turned off in Safe Mode.

**Manage Speech Models** is the **Dictation (Offline)** tab of the Speech
Settings dialog. When more than one local engine is available, it asks which
**Speech Engine** to use. A **Set as Default** button (or a right-click option)
chooses which downloaded model QUILL uses without switching engines. QUILL
remembers your choice and uses it for transcription, captions and dictation.

#### Choosing a speech engine

**Choosing a speech engine.** QUILL uses the **whisper.cpp** engine by default.
You can add two more optional engines, each by installing what it depends on:

- **Faster Whisper** (`fasterwhisper` dependency): a faster engine for many
  languages. It runs inside QUILL and uses your **GPU** automatically when you
  have one.
- **Vosk** (`vosk` dependency): a **very low-resource, CPU-only English**
  engine that runs on a ~40 MB model with no GPU. It is ideal for older or
  smaller machines where the other engines are impractical. Its models download
  from alphacephei.com (verified HTTPS, integrity-checked) through Manage
  Speech Models.

Each engine has its own models, so download a model after switching. All of
them run **entirely on your computer**. Faster Whisper does not label
speakers; for speaker attribution, use the whisper.cpp speaker-detection model.

#### Getting the offline engine

**Download Offline Speech Engine...** The private, on-device speech engine
(whisper.cpp) is not bundled in the installer. The first time you use offline
dictation or transcription, QUILL **offers to download it for you**: about 8
MB, checksum-verified, with a progress bar you can cancel. It is turned off in
Safe Mode. You can also fetch it any time from **Tools > Speech > Download
Offline Speech Engine...**, or from the all-in-one **Help > Download Optional
Components** list described below. If you are **upgrading** from a version
that bundled the engine, your existing copy is kept and keeps working, with
nothing to download.

The installer does not include it and has no option to add it. In a
portable copy you can also place the executable under
`tools\speech\whispercpp` yourself. You do not need to install anything else or change
your PATH. Then download a model from Manage Speech Models.

Offline **dictation** also needs microphone-capture support (the optional
`sounddevice` package). If it is missing, QUILL tells you, and you can still
use Windows dictation.

**Download Vosk...** Vosk is a tiny, very light offline dictation and
transcription engine for older or low-memory computers with no graphics card.
It is not bundled. **Tools > Speech > Download Vosk** (or the Optional
Components list) installs it when you ask, checksum-verified and turned off in
Safe Mode, from QUILL's own verified download, falling back to the public
package index. whisper.cpp stays the default engine; Vosk is the lightweight
fallback when you need it.

#### Hugging Face Token

**Hugging Face Token...** on **Tools > Speech** is optional. QUILL's speech
models are open source (MIT) and need **no Hugging Face account** to download.
If you fetch a lot of models and run into Hugging Face's rate limits, a free
access token raises them.

The first time you open it, QUILL explains the steps: sign in or sign up at
huggingface.co, open **Settings > Access Tokens**, and create a token with the
**Read** role. It offers to open the token page in your browser, and then you
paste the token in. The box hides what you type, and the token is stored in
Windows Credential Manager, never in a settings file. Leave the box blank to
remove a saved token.

#### Cloud transcription providers

The offline engines keep everything on your machine. If you also want a cloud
provider, for example **OpenAI Whisper** for its accuracy, install the
**OpenAI Whisper Transcription** Quillin (a bundled extension) and set up an
OpenAI API key in AI Hub. It then shows up as a provider on the **Dictation
(Online)** tab of Speech Settings. That tab is kept apart from the offline
engines, so local engines (install once) and cloud ones (API key, paid per use)
are never mixed in one list. If no cloud provider is installed, the tab tells
you how to add one.

Cloud providers are **opt-in and never silent**:

- Audio is uploaded only when you choose to transcribe a file with that
  provider. Never offline, and never in Safe Mode.
- The watch folder's offline transcription always uses the on-device engines,
  so a cloud provider can never upload your audio automatically.
- An extension that adds a provider contains no code and asks for no network
  permission. QUILL does the upload itself, through its own checked network
  path, so the extension never sees your audio or your key.

Developers can read more in the Quillin guide, "Transcription providers".

#### The Transcription page in Settings

- **Transcription provider preference** is **Local first** (the default) or
  **Cloud first**, for when you have both kinds of provider.
- **Show cloud transcription providers** lists cloud providers beside the
  ones on your computer. On to begin with.
- **Auto-open Status Page on model download** opens the Status Page whenever
  a speech model starts downloading. Off to begin with.
- **Status page refresh announcements** is how often the Status Page speaks
  its updates: **Quiet** (the default) says nothing on its own, **Normal**
  speaks about every thirty seconds, and **Verbose** about every ten.
- **QUILL Whisperer safe mode lock** stops speech-model downloads and retries
  while leaving the status pages working.
- **Voice commands (push-to-talk)** and **Voice conversation mode** turn on
  the voice commands described in Chapter 8.
- **Voice recognition engine** chooses what listens for voice commands:
  **Follow main engine**, **whisper.cpp (accurate)** or **Vosk (fast,
  light)**, which suits always-listening best.
- Four settings pace conversation mode, all in milliseconds, and 0 switches
  each part off: **Conversation: pause before a command ends (ms)** (2000 to
  begin with; 0 uses the engine's own pause), **Conversation: cancel window
  before acting (ms)** (900), **Conversation: keep listening after a command
  (ms)** (3000) and **Conversation: 'still working' tick interval (ms)**
  (2000).
- **Conversation: your name (optional)** lets QUILL use your name in its
  prompts, as in "Listening, Sam." Leave it blank for plain prompts.
- **Conversation: speak prompts aloud** speaks the welcome and follow-up
  prompts with your Read Aloud voice. It is off to begin with, so QUILL does
  not talk over your screen reader; the sounds and the status bar still tell
  you what is happening.

### Download Optional Components (Help menu)

To keep the installer small, QUILL fetches several large or optional pieces
only when you want them. **Help > Download Optional Components...** is the one
place to see, get, test and remove them all.

Everything here is optional. The base app, and the SAPI 5 voices built into
Windows, work without any of it, so download only what you need. In **portable
mode**, components install into your portable data folder, so your whole setup
travels with you on the drive.

#### What is in the list

The list puts the most important first:

- **Pandoc**: document conversion for Word, ODT, EPUB and RTF.
- **PDF and Office text extraction** (MarkItDown, pdfplumber and pypdf): lets
  Import read the text out of Word, PowerPoint, Excel and PDF documents
  without Pandoc or LibreOffice. Scanned or image-only PDFs still need
  **File > Import > OCR** either way.
- The **braille translation pack**: liblouis tables and BRF profiles for the
  Translation submenu and for BRF and embossing export.
- **Dictation (offline speech)**: a guided setup covering Whisper.cpp, Faster
  Whisper and Vosk, described below.
- **Kokoro** and **Piper** neural voices, and **eSpeak NG** and **DECtalk**
  voices.
- **Audio: export, playback & chapters**: FFmpeg for exporting compressed
  audio, the mpv playback engine, and MP3 audiobook chapter markers, all in one
  place. Each piece is fetched only when its feature is first used.
- The **MathCAT** math-speech engine.
- **Git** and the **GitHub CLI**: portable fallback copies for **Tools > Git
  and GitHub > Local Git** and the Codespaces and Copilot commands on **Tools >
  GitHub**. The section "Downloading git and the GitHub CLI", where this guide
  covers Git and GitHub, has more.
- The **Node.js** runtime, for Node Quillins and the Developer Console's
  TypeScript interface. It comes last, as the extra people use least.
- Any non-English **spell-check dictionaries**.

Each row shows whether it is **Installed** or **Available to download**, and
its size. Selecting a row shows a plain description of what it gives you and
what it costs.

#### Download, Test, Remove and Set as Default

- **Download** fetches a component you do not have yet, checksum-verified,
  with its own progress.
- **Test** proves an installed component works, so you can trust it before
  you rely on it. A voice speaks a short sample so you actually hear it. The
  offline speech engine transcribes a spoken phrase and tells you what it
  heard. Tools report their version. If a component just needs one more piece,
  Test takes you straight to it: the guided engine-and-model picker for offline
  speech, or Manage Voices for a voice engine with no voice yet. An unfinished
  setup is not treated as an error, and QUILL only offers to send a bug report
  when a test really fails.
- **Remove** deletes QUILL's downloaded copy of a component and turns its
  features back off. Removing a voice engine you were using, for example,
  switches Read Aloud back to the system voice. It only ever removes copies
  QUILL downloaded, never a system tool or a shared install.
- **Set as Default:** for a voice engine (Kokoro, Piper and the other Read
  Aloud engines), the **Set as Default** button here makes that engine, and a
  voice you pick from it, your Read Aloud default without opening another
  speech dialog. The button is only available for a component that can be a
  Read Aloud default, and only once it is installed. The same **Set as
  Default** is also in Manage Speech Models and Manage Voices (with a
  right-click option on the list), for the offline dictation model and for
  voices. Downloading a model or voice engine makes it the default
  automatically; use these when you want to switch back to one you already
  have. Voice previews stop cleanly when you move to another before the first
  one finishes.

#### Setting up offline dictation

The **Dictation (offline speech)** row opens a guided setup instead of a plain
download. It takes you one step at a time, and a banner at the top always says
which step you are on and the one thing to do next:

1. Pick and install an engine: **Whisper.cpp** (light and fast), **Faster
   Whisper** (most accurate), **Parakeet 3** (the most reliable for dictation,
   described earlier in this chapter), or **Vosk** (tiny, best for old or
   low-memory machines).
2. Download a model. The best fit for your computer is already selected.
3. Choose **Test dictation** to make sure it works, then set it as your
   default.

QUILL remembers the engine you chose, so the setup reopens where you left off
instead of going back to the built-in engine.

#### Pandoc on demand

**Pandoc downloads itself when you need it.** You do not have to visit this
dialog first. The moment you **Import** or **Export** a Word, ODT, EPUB or RTF
document (or run **Convert File**) without Pandoc, QUILL offers to download the
official, pinned build right there: about 45 MB, verified, with a progress bar.
The conversion is ready as soon as it finishes. Plain text and Markdown never
need Pandoc, which is why it is not bundled.

#### On a Mac

**On macOS, several of these come from Homebrew rather than a QUILL download.**

- The braille translation pack download contains a Windows `lou_translate`
  program, so on macOS QUILL points you to `brew install liblouis` instead.
  QUILL finds a Homebrew liblouis by itself, so no download is needed.
- Pandoc and Tesseract work the same way. Install them with Homebrew (`brew
  install pandoc`, `brew install tesseract`) and QUILL finds them.
- LibreOffice, used to import older Office formats and Apple Pages, is found
  automatically at its standard `/Applications/LibreOffice.app` location on
  macOS (it is never on PATH there). Install it from libreoffice.org or with
  `brew install --cask libreoffice` if you need those imports.

### Performance and Memory

QUILL is built to run all of its AI and speech features on a modest computer
with no graphics card and not much memory. It does that by being careful with
memory, never by switching features off. Two settings under **Settings >
Performance and Memory** control it:

- **Unload idle models after (minutes)** frees the memory used by an AI,
  read-aloud or dictation model you have stopped using. The next time you need
  it, QUILL loads it again by itself. Set it to **0** to keep models loaded
  until you close QUILL.
- **Low-resource mode (one model at a time)** keeps only **one** model loaded
  at a time and prefers
  the smallest model that fits. It never turns off AI or speech. It loads them
  one at a time, so you wait a moment for a reload in exchange for using much
  less memory. On a machine with very little memory it turns on
  **automatically** and tells you once, out loud, so it never takes you by
  surprise.

You do not have to touch either of these. QUILL picks sensible defaults for
your machine, but they are there if you want to tune how much memory it uses.

### What you learned, and where to go next

You can now dictate with Live Dictation (`Ctrl+F11`), Locked Dictation
(`Ctrl+F9`) or Dictate (Offline), and teach QUILL your own words in
`dictation.md`. You can transcribe a recording on your own computer or with
**AI > Transcribe Audio File...**, turn it into minutes or notes with
Transcript Actions, and set a watch folder to do all of that for you. You also
know where speech models, optional components and the memory settings live.

There is no guided tutorial for dictation yet; the
**[Dictation commands](dictation-commands.html)** page and the Voice
Interaction guide are the best companions to this chapter.

Next, Chapter 10, AI, when you want it, shows what the assistant can do with
your writing, including the AI behind Transcript Actions.

## Chapter 10: AI, when you want it

This chapter is about the AI help built into QUILL, and the first thing to know
is that you never have to use it. QUILL is a complete editor without it, and
nothing you write is sent anywhere until you ask. If you would like a paragraph
summarised, tidied or explained, QUILL's own free AI is ready with no account
and no key. If you already pay for ChatGPT, or have your own key, you can use
those instead, and further on you will find the library where you can save your
own prompts, skills and agents.

### QUILL's own free AI

You do not need an account, a key, or a decision about which company sees your
writing. QUILL runs its own AI service, it is free, and it is the first thing in
the **AI** menu (the `&AI` menu, so `Alt` then `A` opens it).

#### What the AI menu offers

| Key | Command | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Alt+G` | Free AI Assistant... | Summarise, rewrite, proofread, shorten or explain the passage you are in |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Z` | Ask About This Document... | Ask a question about what you are writing |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F2` | Free AI Usage... | What you have used and what is left |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F4` | Connect or Sign Out... | Connect this computer, or disconnect it |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K` | Privacy Agreement... | Read what is sent, and accept or withdraw |
| `Alt+F2` | Use My Own AI Key... | Every limit lifted, billed to your OpenAI or Google Gemini account |
| `Alt+F5` | Use My ChatGPT Subscription... | Every AI command on the ChatGPT plan you already pay for |
| `Ctrl+F5` | Ask About an Image... | A picture described, on your ChatGPT subscription |
| `Ctrl+F3` | Tidy Dictated Text... | Dictation's misheard words and punctuation corrected, nothing else changed |
| `Ctrl+F10` | Dictionary > Word Explorer... | Everything about the word you are on, as used in this sentence |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+'` | Dictionary > Define in Context | What the word means here, and what you might be confusing it with |
| `Ctrl+Shift+;` | Dictionary > Synonyms That Fit | Replacements that keep the sentence's meaning, already in the right form |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+]` | Dictionary > Find the Word For... | The reverse dictionary: describe the meaning, get the word |

The first five are the same five commands QUILL Lite has, so anything you learn
in one editor you have learned in both. Three of the five keys are the same as
well. Usage and Connect differ: in QUILL, `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F7` to `F12` open the
other QuillVille apps, so QUILL uses `F2` and `F4` for those two, while QUILL
Lite, which has no apps to open, uses `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9` and `F10`.

#### What it works on

The free AI works on the selection. With nothing selected it takes the
paragraph you are in, or else the section. It never sends the whole file.

Nothing is applied without a keystroke from you. Every answer arrives in a
window with **Replace** and **Insert** buttons, and both go through the ordinary
undo list. If you typed over the text while the answer was on its way, Replace
is not offered, and QUILL tells you so instead of writing the answer somewhere
it does not belong.

You never wait for it, either. Requests run in the background, so you can keep
typing, save, switch documents or close the window while an answer is coming.

> **QUILLBee's tip:** Changed your mind about an AI edit? Press `Ctrl+Z`. It
> comes back out exactly like anything else you typed.

#### The Free AI Assistant pad (Ctrl+Alt+G)

The pad has a list called **What do you want done?** with seventeen choices.
Press a letter in the list to jump.

- The four basics: Summarize, Rewrite, Proofread and Explain.
- Ten writing tools: **Shorten**, **Simplify**, **Make more formal**, **Make
  friendlier**, **Turn into a list**, **Find action items**, **Suggest
  headings**, **Continue writing**, **Write an email reply** and **Translate**.
  When you choose Translate, a **Translate into** list appears with twenty
  languages.
- Three that need you to type: Ask a question about the document, Ask a
  general question, and Have a conversation.

Every one of them is a single request of the same size, so the writing tools
cost no more of your allowance than Summarize.

#### Having a conversation

Choose **Have a conversation** in the pad, or press **Follow Up** in any answer
window, and the **AI Conversation** window opens. Here you can talk back and
forth, and each reply remembers what was said before.

1. Focus is in **Your message**. Type, then press `Enter`.
2. Each reply is read aloud as it arrives and added to the **Conversation**
   above. Press `Shift+Tab` to reach it.
3. Beside Send are **Copy Last Reply**, **Insert Last Reply Below** and **New
   Conversation**.

If you started with a question about the document, each follow-up keeps
sending the same passages, so you can keep asking about them.

On the free AI each message counts as one request, and conversations have a
monthly share of 40 of your 100 requests. The conversation so far goes with
each message only as far as the ordinary size limit allows, so no message costs
more than any other, and a long conversation slowly forgets its beginning. The
window tells you the first time that happens. With your own OpenAI or Gemini
key there is no such limit: the whole conversation goes, billed to your
account.

There is a monthly, a daily and an hourly allowance, and a smaller one for a
computer's first 48 hours. Free AI limits, later in this chapter, has every
number and every rule.

#### Nothing is sent until you ask

The free AI makes no request when QUILL starts, while you type, when you save,
when you are idle or when focus moves. If you leave it switched on and never
use it, QUILL makes no network call for it at all.

The first time you reach for it, QUILL shows you exactly what is sent and what
is kept, and nothing leaves your computer until you accept. You can come to that
same agreement three ways: **AI > Privacy Agreement...** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K`),
Preferences, and Customize Features. All three show the same answer, so they
never disagree.

If you withdraw, QUILL signs this computer out of the free AI as well, so no
sign-in is left behind for a service you have said no to. QUILL remembers which
version of the agreement you accepted (the setting
`ai_privacy_accepted_version`), so if what is sent ever changes in an important
way, you are asked again.

### Basic and Advanced menus

The AI menu starts out **Basic**. It shows the five free AI commands above, the
**Use Artificial Intelligence** switch, and **Show advanced AI features**. Basic
is for everybody who just wants a paragraph tidied up.

The full menu has much more: provider setup, Ask Quill, the agents, Proofread,
Transform, Translate, Read Aloud, Transcribe, More, the AI Library and the AI
Hub. It is worth having once you have chosen which company should see your
writing and have a key to paste in.

Nothing is taken away in Basic. Every advanced command keeps its keyboard
shortcut and stays in the Command Palette; Basic only changes what the menu
offers. Check **Show advanced AI features** near the bottom of the AI menu and
everything comes back at once. QUILL remembers your choice.

If you already had AI set up when you updated (you had run the wizard, or saved
a provider key), QUILL leaves you in Advanced, so no menu you were using
disappears.

### Setting up AI with the wizard

The first item in the AI menu is **Set Up AI...**, labelled "start here" until
you have used it. It is a short wizard that gets you to working AI in a minute,
in plain words.

1. **Welcome.** A short note on what QUILL's AI does, and that it is optional,
   shown to you before anything changes, and private by default.
2. **How would you like AI to run?** Pick one:
   - **On your device with Ollama.** Private and free. It runs on your computer
     with no account or key, and QUILL connects to Ollama installed there.
   - **Use an AI account.** The most capable models. Connect Claude, OpenAI,
     Gemini, OpenRouter or Ollama Cloud with a key you paste once, which QUILL
     stores safely on this computer.
   - **Not right now.** AI stays off, and you can set it up any time later.
3. **Connect.** For an account, pick a provider, paste your key, and press
   **Test connection** before you go on. For on-device AI, QUILL points itself
   at Ollama.
4. **You're all set.** A short summary of what you can now do, and a **Keep it
   simple** checkbox that turns on **Basic mode**.

QUILL also offers the wizard when you reach for AI before it is set up, for
example when you ask for minutes from a transcript, so you never hit a dead
end. Run **Set Up AI** again whenever you want to change provider or mode.

Basic mode is the default on a new install, and it hides the whole advanced
menu, not just the agents. The wizard's **Keep it simple** checkbox turns it
on, and **Show advanced AI features** turns it off.

### Using AI for free

You never have to pay to use AI in QUILL. Besides QUILL's own free AI, the
Connect step of the wizard recommends two free paths and picks good settings
for you.

- **Most private, free.** Pick **Ollama (on your device)**. A model runs on your
  own computer: no account, no key, it works offline, and nothing you write
  leaves your machine. The quality is more modest than the big cloud models.
  If Ollama is not installed yet, do not install it by hand. **AI > Set Up Local
  AI (Ollama)...** does the whole job: it reports your computer's memory,
  graphics card and free disk space, downloads and starts the official
  installer, downloads a model that suits your computer, and connects QUILL to
  it. Each step tells you what to do next, and it never moves on without you.
- **Best quality, free.** Pick **OpenRouter**. Choose **Get API key** to open
  OpenRouter's key page in your browser, create a free key and paste it back.
  QUILL picks a strong free writing model for you (at the moment a free Llama
  3.3 70B model). The model's description says **Free**, so you always know a
  choice costs nothing.

Every provider that needs a key has a **Get API key** button beside the key box
that opens the right sign-up page.

A few honest notes:

- Free cloud models can be **slower** and are **rate-limited**. Because the
  key is **your own**, that limit is yours alone; nobody else shares it, and it
  costs nobody anything.
- Free hosted models may keep or train on what you send, under their own terms.
  If your writing is confidential, use the private **on-device** option.
- **What works on free models:** everyday help works well, such as Rewrite,
  Summarize, Expand, Continue, Fix Grammar, Table of Contents, translating and
  proofreading. **Ask Quill** works too; on a small model it keeps its steps
  simple so it answers instead of stalling. The longest multi-step agent tasks
  are where a stronger paid model still does better. QUILL tells you when a
  task would benefit from one, but never stops you trying on a free model.
- **QUILL tidies on-device answers for you.** Small on-device models have a few
  habits. When you use Rewrite, Summarize, Expand, Continue or Shorten on the
  on-device model, QUILL gives the model worked examples first, then checks the
  answer for hedging ("it seems", "arguably"), editorialising ("clearly",
  "obviously") and filler openings ("In today's world", "It is important to
  note"), and tries once more to remove them. Fix Grammar and Improve Reading
  Order are left alone, so your own wording is never changed. This happens only
  on the on-device model; cloud answers are left as they come.

You can change your provider or model any time from **Set Up AI** or the **AI
Hub**.

### AI Assistant

Beyond the free AI, QUILL has a full AI assistant. You can run it on your own
computer (llama.cpp with a local GGUF model) or connect a provider: Ollama
(local), Ollama Cloud, OpenAI, Claude, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, or a custom
OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Every provider is optional, and you choose it
yourself. Keys are kept in the Windows Credential Manager, with a
DPAPI-encrypted file as a fallback, and are never written to disk as plain
text. Where your keys are kept, later in this chapter, has the details.

#### Setting up an AI provider

Open **AI > AI Hub...** to set up your providers. The AI Hub is the one place
for every provider's key, model, **Test Chat** and key removal. If you are
looking for the old **AI Model and Connection** or **Forget API Key** menu
items, they are part of the AI Hub now.

- **OpenRouter.** Paste your key into the OpenRouter API Key field. One
  OpenRouter key reaches many models, including Claude, GPT-4o and Gemini.
- **OpenAI.** Paste your OpenAI API key.
- **Ollama.** No key needed. Install Ollama on your computer (`ollama serve`)
  and QUILL finds it by itself at `http://localhost:11434`. If you run Ollama
  on a different port or computer, change the Ollama Base URL setting.

You can also set a **Default model for prompt runs**
(`ai_prompt_default_model`). Leave it blank and Ask AI and the Prompt Library
use the same model, or name a more capable model here for prompt library work.

#### Ask Quill (Alt+Q) and Ask AI

**AI > Ask Quill...** (`Alt+Q`) opens the assistant as a conversation.
You can ask questions, draft text, suggest edits, and run QUILL commands, and
nothing changes until you approve it. The window shows the provider and model in
use, and you can switch either one there.

When you only want a quick answer, with nothing to insert and no follow-up, use
**AI > Ask AI...** from the Command Palette. It is a simple question and answer
window.

1. **Provider** and **Model** already hold the last ones you used. If they are
   set up, focus goes straight to the Prompt field so you can start typing. If
   not, focus starts on Provider so you can set it up.
2. Type your question and press `Ctrl+Enter`, or the **Send** button. QUILL
   says "Sending..." and the button is unavailable until the answer arrives.
3. The answer opens in a read-only window. Read it with the arrow keys, and use
   **Copy to Clipboard** to copy all of it. Closing the answer brings you back
   to Ask AI, ready for a follow-up.

**Clear** empties the prompt field and puts you back in it.

#### Check Grammar with AI

**Edit > Grammar > Check Grammar with AI** sends the selected text, or the
whole document if nothing is selected, to your AI model and asks it to review
the grammar. The answer lists each correction as the original phrase, the
corrected phrase and the reason. Nothing is changed for you; you make the
corrections yourself.

Out of the box, the model is told to list only the corrections needed and not
to rewrite the passage. To give it different instructions, open the Prompt
Library, find the built-in "Check Grammar" prompt and edit its text. The
command uses your version from then on.

### Free AI limits, and when they start again

QUILL's free AI is free because everybody shares it, so it has limits. Here is
every one of them in one place. **Free AI Usage** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F2`) shows
where you stand.

#### Your allowance at a glance

These are the service's current settings. QUILL reads them from the service
