- Press **Escape**, or **Enter on Close**, to go back to where you were.
- **Tab to Open User Guide** and press it to jump to the part of this guide
  that covers the control.

Here is how the Help keys fit together:

| Key | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| `F1` | Help on the control that has focus |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F1` | Open the full User Guide |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F1` | Open What Can I Do Here? for the document you are in |
| `Ctrl+F1` | Open the Key Cheatsheet |
| `Shift+F1` | Open About Quill |

A few things worth knowing:

- In the main editor, F1 tells you the editor shortcuts and some writing tips.
- In dialogs such as Preferences, Find/Replace and Spell Check, F1 names both
  the dialog and the setting you are on.
- In the Personalise QUILL wizard, F1 on any control explains what that
  setting does and what you can change later.
- When you use a menu and come back to the editor, QUILL remembers which
  control had focus, so F1 still talks about the right one.

#### Personalising QUILL

The **Personalise QUILL** wizard runs on its own the first time QUILL starts.
You can run it again at any time from **Help > Personalise QUILL...**.

It has six short pages, or five if you leave AI writing help off on the
Extras page:

1. **Welcome** introduces what the wizard covers.
2. **Intent** is the page that matters most. It asks one question: *What kind
   of writing do you do?* and shows a list of seven starting points. Arrow up
   and down the list. As you move, a large read-only text area below it
   changes to tell you, in plain English, exactly what you will get if you
   choose that one. No feature codes, no jargon, and no list of what you will
   miss out on. Just what you get.
3. **Extras** offers a few optional extras, such as AI writing help, Braille
   Mode and typing automation. You only see the ones your starting point does
   not already include. Each is a single checkbox, and ticking one adds a
   sentence to the preview, so you always know what you are agreeing to.
4. **AI Provider** appears only if you turned AI on in Extras. It asks for
   your provider and your API key. The providers are Anthropic (Claude),
   OpenAI (GPT), Google Gemini, OpenRouter (many models), and Ollama, which
   runs models on your own computer or connects to an Ollama-compatible cloud
   host. Your key is kept safely in the Windows Credential Manager, not in a
   settings file. You can skip this page and add a key later.
5. **Keyboard and Sound** is where you choose a keyboard pack and whether
   QUILL plays sound cues. QUILL detects your screen reader and picks
   accessible defaults for you.
6. **Summary** lets you check every choice before anything happens. It is
   plain text: your profile name, which features are on, which Quillins are
   turned on, your keyboard pack and your sound setting. Use Back to change
   any page. Nothing in QUILL changes until you press Finish.

Every page starts with a heading that takes focus, so you land on the page
title first. The preview is a read-only document, so VoiceOver on the Mac
does not call it an editable text field.

**Important:** nothing is saved until you press Finish. If you close or cancel
the wizard, none of your settings change.

##### Profiles explained

QUILL comes with eleven built-in feature profiles: the ten described under
Choosing a profile, plus the QUILL Lite profile. Each one starts you at a
different amount of features and a different level of accessibility support.
The wizard offers seven plain-English starting points that lead to them; its
Writer starting point is the Casual Writer profile. You can
switch profile at any time from **Tools > Customize and Support > Profiles and
Features...** or by pressing `Alt+Shift+P`.

Choosing a profile, earlier in this guide, says who each one is for.

### Tutorials

**Help > Tutorials...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F1`) opens 23 guided tutorials: 136 steps,
about 120 minutes in all. They cover the parts of QUILL worth learning first,
in the order you would naturally learn them. They are not a second copy of
this guide. A guide can tell you what something does. It cannot tell you what
to do next, because it cannot see what you have already done. The Tutorials
window can.

#### How the lessons work

- **They show the keys you have.** A step names the command it is about, and
  the key is filled in when the step is shown. If you have rebound a key, the
  tutorial says your key.
- **Try it runs the step.** Any step that names a command can be carried out
  from the lesson. A tutorial can open a window for you and then talk you
  through what you are looking at.
- **Follow me notices when you have done it.** Tick **Follow me** and the
  lesson keeps an eye on QUILL, once a second. It watches what changed, never
  which key you pressed, so however you do the step, it says what it saw
  ("Done: the document changed") and reads you the next one. It never takes
  over the keyboard, and nothing is marked. Every step still has **Next**, so
  if the check never notices, it costs you one keypress.

The Tutorials window is an ordinary window, not a wizard. Leave it open, go to
your document, do the step there, and hear the lesson move on in the
background.

#### Finding a lesson

The lessons are in six tracks, in teaching order. Each row says how many steps
it has, about how long it takes, and whether you have finished it. The filter
box narrows the list: every word you type has to appear somewhere in a
tutorial. Type **here** to see only the tutorials about the window you came
from.

#### Your place is kept

Close a lesson half way through and it opens at the same step next time.
Finishing a lesson is remembered separately from where you are in it. **Forget
my progress** clears all of that and changes nothing else. Nothing about your
progress leaves this computer.

#### Reading instead of doing

**Read it all** shows a whole tutorial as one page of text. **The whole book
as a document** opens all 23 as one page. It is made from the same lessons the
window teaches, so the two always agree. It also comes as `tutorials.md`
beside this guide. The document gives the keys QUILL comes with; only the
window knows the ones you have rebound.

Quill Radio, QUILL Cast and Quill Weather each have their own lessons, opened
with the same `Ctrl+Alt+F1` in every app. QUILL's own set covers your first
hour, writing, reading, how much QUILL says, the assistant, and the things you
meet in your second week. The menus and the command palette cover the rest.

#### QUILL, Step by Step

Prefer to learn by listening? [QUILL, Step by Step](quill-step-by-step.md) is
a separate, slower manual written to be read aloud. It has seventeen short
chapters, one skill each, with practice moments and recaps, and none of this
guide's reference tables. It comes beside this guide as Markdown, HTML and
EPUB. The EPUB opens straight into ElevenReader, Voice Dream or any reading
app, so it can talk you through QUILL while your hands stay on the keyboard.

### Get Help from Support, step by step

Use this whenever QUILL does something you did not expect, when you are
stuck, when you have a question, or when you want to suggest something. It is
the same form QUILL Lite and Quill Radio use, and it reaches a person at
**Community Access**, not a public issue tracker.

1. Choose **Help > Get Help from Support...**, or press `Ctrl+Alt+F2` from
   anywhere in QUILL. On the Help menu its letter is **L**, because **G**
   already opens the user guide. If you gave it a different key in the past,
   that key still works.
2. The form opens on **What kind of message**. Choose one of: something is
   broken, a question, an accessibility problem, or an idea or request. This
   only helps the message reach the right person.
3. Tab to **Subject** and type one short line, as you would for an email.
4. Tab to **What happened** and describe it in your own words. This is the
   part a person reads first.
5. **What you expected** and **Steps to reproduce** are optional. If you can
   give steps, they help more than anything else.
6. **Your email address** is optional too. The message goes from your own
   mail account, so support can already reply to you there. Only fill this in
   if you want the reply to go somewhere else.
7. **Screen reader** is filled in from whatever is running. Change it if it is
   wrong.
8. Below the fields, QUILL tells you what else is included: its version, your
   Windows version and, when this computer is connected to QUILL's free AI,
   your **QUILL AI support ID**. That is the number support asks for first.
9. Press **Send** (or Enter). Your own mail program opens with the whole
   message written and addressed to **support@community-access.org**.
   **Nothing is sent until you press Send in your mail program.** Read it
   over, attach a diagnostics bundle if you like, or close it if you change
   your mind. Pressing Escape in the form cancels without writing anything.

#### If something gets in the way

- If a required field is empty, QUILL tells you which one and leaves you in
  the form.
- If the message is too long for a mail link, your mail program opens with the
  start of it. QUILL puts the complete text on your clipboard and tells you to
  paste it in with Control V.
- If this computer has no mail program set up (you only use webmail, say),
  QUILL shows you the address and puts the whole message on your clipboard,
  so nothing you typed is lost.
- Writing to **support@community-access.org** yourself always works just as
  well.

Want to share more detail? **Help > Save Diagnostics...** writes a bundle with
private details removed, which you review and can attach to the email.

#### No more GitHub reports

QUILL no longer files GitHub issues for you, and no copy of QUILL carries a
built-in GitHub "reporting token". Your own GitHub sign-in, for QUILL's GitHub
features, is separate and has not changed. Check for Updates used to offer to
"restore the token" by reinstalling the same version; that offer has gone
too, and Check for Updates now only ever offers a newer version.

### Checking for Updates

QUILL can check for updates and install them while you carry on working.

#### Manual update check

To check for updates now:

1. Press `Alt+H` to open the **Help** menu.
2. Press `U` for **Check for Updates**.
3. If a newer version is out, QUILL tells you and asks whether to download it.
4. If you say yes, QUILL downloads it in the background and tells you when it
   is ready.
5. The next time you close and reopen QUILL, the update is applied for you.

#### Automatic update checks

QUILL can check for updates each time it starts:

1. Press `Alt+E` to open the **Edit** menu.
2. Press `Shift+S` for **Settings**.
3. In the **Updates** section, turn on **Check for updates on startup**.

With automatic checks on, QUILL lets you know quietly when a new version is
available, and you download it when it suits you.

#### Update size and speed

QUILL uses small incremental updates ("micro-updates") instead of a full
reinstall. They often download in seconds, and your settings, documents and
preferences are kept.

#### Updating a portable copy

If you run the **portable** copy of QUILL, Check for Updates notices and
offers the portable `.zip` for the new version instead of the installer. It
downloads to your updates folder, and QUILL offers an **Extract now** button
that unzips it into a ready-to-run folder next to your current one.

Putting a portable update in place is always a job you do yourself. QUILL
never replaces its own files while it is running, because they may be locked
while it is open. After extracting, copy your `data` folder into the new
version's folder and start QUILL from there.

Installed copies keep getting the installer, which does put itself in place
when you run it.

#### Staying on a release channel

By default, QUILL follows the Stable channel and only offers you finished
versions. To try new features early, see [Release Channels](#release-channels)
below.

### Release Channels

QUILL comes in three flavours, and you choose which one this copy follows. They're called release channels.

- **Stable** is the version we recommend. It has been checked with JAWS and NVDA, and it's what most people use. Every copy starts here.
- **Beta** gets new features a few weeks early. It's mostly finished, but some things may not work right yet.
- **Dev** is the work in progress, sometimes several builds a week. Things will break. Only choose it if a developer asked you to, or you enjoy testing.

#### Choosing a channel

1. Open the **Help** menu, then choose **Release Channel...** (press **Alt+H**, then **I**). You can also get there from Settings: on the **Administration** page, the **Release channel** row has a **Change release channel...** button.
2. Arrow through Stable, Beta and Dev. As you move, the box below tells you what each one means and what choosing it would do. Nothing changes yet.
3. Press **Switch** to move. Press **Close**, or Escape, to leave everything as it was.

If you choose Beta or Dev, QUILL shows a short warning first: what could go wrong, how your settings are protected, and how to come back. Read it, tick the **I understand** box, then choose **Move to Beta** (or **Move to Dev**). **Stay on Stable** changes nothing, and so does Escape.

#### What happens when you move to Beta or Dev

- QUILL saves a copy of your settings, keys and preferences first. If it can't, it stays where it is and tells you why. Your documents aren't copied, and updates don't change them.
- QUILL then checks for updates on the new channel straight away, and offers you the newest Beta or Dev version if there is one. Nothing is installed unless you say so.
- From then on, Check for Updates offers you versions from your channel. On Stable, you're never offered a test version.

If you installed a Beta version yourself, QUILL notices the first time it checks for updates. It puts itself on the Beta channel and tells you so, and you can change it in the Release Channel window whenever you like.

#### Updates on Beta and Dev

When QUILL's startup check finds a new version, it downloads it for you, as it always has, so it is ready when you are. It never installs anything without
asking: when the download is done, it says so and shows you what's new, and you
choose when to install.

On Beta and Dev, it waits instead of downloading on a metered connection, during Quiet Hours, and while Quill Radio is recording. The notifications list and Update History tell you why it waited.

#### If an update doesn't start

After an update, QUILL checks that the new version really opens. If it doesn't
open within two minutes, the update undoes itself and puts back the version you
had. The next time QUILL starts, it tells you so. Nothing of yours is changed,
and Update History has the details.

To make this possible, QUILL keeps a copy of the installer for the version you
have: on Beta and Dev for as long as you have that version, and on Stable for a
week or three starts after each update. That copy takes about 200 MB of disk
space, which Stable gives back once the week or the three starts are up. After
an update, the previous installer is kept until the new version has started
three times, or for a week, and then it is deleted.

#### Coming back to Stable

Open **Release Channel** again and choose **Stable**.

- If the version you have is already a Stable one, you're back straight away,
  and nothing is installed.
- If you have a newer Beta or Dev version, QUILL checks whether Stable can read
  everything you have saved. If it can, choose **Go back to** (the Stable
  version) **now**, and QUILL downloads Stable and offers to install it. Your
  settings and keys come with you.
- If Stable can't read something yet, QUILL says so and gives you two safe
  choices. **Wait for Stable** keeps the version you have, stops test versions,
  and moves you to Stable by itself as soon as Stable catches up. It tells you
  when that happens. **Use the copy from** (the day you joined) puts back the
  copy of your settings and keys saved when you joined, then installs Stable.
  Anything you changed since then won't be in it, but a copy of how things are
  right now is saved first, so nothing is thrown away.
- If there's no saved copy, waiting is the only choice, and the window says so.

#### Moving your other apps together

If QUILL Lite, Quill Radio or QUILL Cast is on this computer too, the Release Channel window lists it under **Also move my other QuillVille apps on this computer**. Tick any you'd like to move in the same step. Every box starts unticked.

Those apps run on one shared engine. When one of them moves to Beta or Dev, it gets its own copy of that engine, so the apps you leave on Stable are never touched. That copy takes about 335 MB of disk space, and it goes away by itself when the last of them comes back to Stable. QUILL itself doesn't use the shared engine, so moving QUILL on its own needs no extra space.

#### Update History

The **Update History** button in the Release Channel window shows what the updater has done for QUILL: channel changes, the copies of your settings it saved, and so on. It's a record to read; nothing in it changes anything.

#### Your privacy

Switching channels sends nothing about you. When QUILL checks for updates, the only thing it sends is a request for the list of versions.

### Beta Feedback and Bug Reporting

QUILL is ready for serious beta use, and it has a real support starting point
built in.

#### What you can use today

- Recovery state.
- Notifications.
- Extraction review.
- Exporting a bad-extraction package, for problems with extraction.
- **Save Diagnostics...**, a general command that writes a bundle on this
  computer.
- **Get Help from Support...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F2`), which writes a message to
  support@community-access.org in your own mail program, with details about
  your setup already filled in. It used to be called **Report a Bug...**.
- A diagnostics runbook and a documented support process.

QUILL helps you gather diagnostics on your own computer, check what you are
about to share, and start a clear support message without leaving QUILL.

#### What is still to come

QUILL does not yet have a secure way to upload straight from the app without
signing in anywhere. For now, the **Help > Get Help from Support...** form is
the one route: it emails support through your own mail program and never
files anything on GitHub. A fuller route that needs no GitHub sign-in is
planned:

1. a Community Access feedback form on a secure (HTTPS) web page,
2. an optional upload of a diagnostics bundle you have reviewed,
3. a plain-language bug template with a summary of your setup and the steps
   to reproduce the problem,
4. alongside the in-app **Help > Get Help from Support...** form.

### Control Reference

The Control Reference lists every control in QUILL that can take focus,
grouped by section. For each one it says what the control does, which keys
apply to it, and which part of this guide covers it in depth.

The full list is in the [Control Reference](CONTROL_REFERENCE.md).

If you build QUILL yourself, you can regenerate it after adding new help
topics:

```powershell
python -m quill.tools.build_docs
```

### What you learned, and where to go next

You now know your way around the Help menu, including Activity (`Shift+F9`)
and Repeat Last Result (`F9`). F1 explains any control, What Can I Do Here?
helps on the spot, and the Personalise QUILL wizard can be run again whenever
your needs change. You can send a message to a real person with Get Help from
Support (`Ctrl+Alt+F2`), and you know how to check for updates.

To practise, open **Help > Tutorials...** (`Ctrl+Alt+F1`) and try "Getting
unstuck" and "Do anything by name" from the Your first hour track. On the
website,
[Your first hour with QUILL](https://www.quillforall.org/tutorials/01-your-first-hour.html)
covers the same ground at a gentler pace.

That is the last chapter. The appendices follow, including the Glossary of
QUILL Terms and Getting help, for whenever you need them.

## A last word

The best way to get to know QUILL is to use it on something real: a note you
care about, a PDF you scanned and need to check, an EPUB chapter you want to
find your way around, a Markdown file that needs tidying, or a web page you
want to make easier to use.

I would like QUILL to feel like a good guide sitting beside you while you
work, never one standing in your way. If it does its job, you will spend less
time wondering what it can do and more time on what you want to write next.

### Acknowledgments

QUILL stands on the shoulders of the screen-reader-first editors that came
before it. The keyboard-first way of comparing documents, and selecting with
`F8` from an anchor, were inspired by EdSharp and Boxer. I am grateful to
those projects and the people who made them, for showing what an accessible,
keyboard-driven editor can be.

## Appendix A: The QUILL Developer Console

This appendix is for people who like to script and automate. Nobody needs it
to write, and if you never open the console you are missing nothing you use
every day. If you are a developer, a power user, an accessibility tester or
someone building a Quillin, read on. The QUILL Developer Console (QDC for
short) lets you look inside the running editor and drive it from code.

### What the QDC is

The Developer Console is a scripting window built into QUILL. You can inspect
and automate the editor while it runs, without rebuilding anything or adding
temporary menu items.

It is switched off by default for the Essential, Casual Writer and Reader and
Student profiles.
You will find it under the Developer, Power Text and Full QUILL profiles.

There are two consoles:

- **Python console.** Runs inside QUILL, with full access to the scripting API
  through the name `q`. Its prompt is `>>>`, and `...` while you are in the
  middle of a block.
- **TypeScript console.** Runs through a Node subprocess. Its API is
  asynchronous and is called `quill`. Its prompt is `ts>`, and `ts*>` while an
  async operation is still running.

Both share the same transcript window, and both speak through QUILL's usual
announcements.

### Opening the console

Choose **Tools > Advanced > Developer Console > Open Python Console** or
**Tools > Advanced > Developer Console > Open TypeScript Console**.

From the Command Palette, the commands are `quill.console.openPython` and
`quill.console.openTypeScript`.

The console opens as its own dialog. Press `Esc` to send focus back to the
editor. The dialog stays open, and keeps everything you defined, until you
close it yourself.

### Console layout

Press `F6` to move between the five areas of the console:

1. **Transcript.** Read-only. Shows prompts, output, errors and return values.
2. **Input.** One line by default. `Shift+Enter` adds a new line, so you can
   type a block of several lines.
3. **Language selector.** Switches between Python and TypeScript.
4. **Status line.** The current language, prompt state, active document and
   worker status.
5. **Buttons.** Run, Clear, Copy transcript, Save transcript, Insert snippet,
   Help and Close.

### Keyboard reference

These keys work inside the console window.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Enter | Execute current command |
| Shift+Enter | Insert newline (multi-line input) |
| Ctrl+Enter | Force execute multi-line block |
| Up / Down | Previous / next history (when cursor is at line boundary) |
| Ctrl+L | Clear transcript |
| Ctrl+Shift+C | Copy transcript |
| Ctrl+S | Save transcript |
| Ctrl+F | Find in transcript |
| F6 | Move between transcript, input, status, and buttons |
| Esc | Return focus to editor |
| F1 | Console help |
| Ctrl+Space | Trigger completion |

### Python console

#### Available names

These names are ready for you as soon as the console opens:

| Name | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `q` | Primary QUILL scripting API, start here |
| `app` | Application-level read-mostly object |
| `commands` | Command registry facade |
| `doc` | Active document snapshot |
| `editor` | Active editor snapshot |
| `sel` | Current selection snapshot |
| `caret` | Current caret snapshot |
| `profile` | Active feature profile snapshot |
| `settings` | Safe settings facade |
| `diagnostics` | Diagnostics facade |
| `a11y` | Announcement / testing facade |
| `log` | Console-safe logger |
| `wx` | wx module (Developer profile only) |

`doc`, `sel` and `caret` are read-only snapshots, taken at the moment they
were captured. They refresh when the active document changes. Otherwise, call
`q.refresh_context()` to pull in the current state.

The `q` API also has these facades: `q.selection`, `q.doc`, `q.editor`,
`q.settings`, `q.profile`, `q.bookmarks`, `q.quillins`, `q.macros` (with
`q.begin_macro` and `q.end_macro`), `q.spell`, `q.diagnostics`, `q.a11y`,
`q.commands`, `q.focus` and `q.support`, plus `q.describe_command`.

#### Basic operations

Insert text at the cursor:

```python
>>> q.insert_text("Hello from QUILL.")
```

Replace the current selection:

```python
>>> q.replace_selection("Replacement text")
```

Jump to a line:

```python
>>> q.goto_line(42)
```

Run a built-in command by its ID:

```python
>>> q.run_command("quill.document.wordCount")
```

Send a screen-reader announcement:

```python
>>> q.a11y.announce("Test announcement.")
```

#### Inspecting state

Read the name of the active document:

```python
>>> doc.name
'notes.txt'
```

Read the current selection:

```python
>>> sel.text
'selected words here'
```

Read where the caret is (line and column both start at 1):

```python
>>> caret.line, caret.column
(12, 5)
```

Search for commands by keyword:

```python
>>> commands.search("spell")
['quill.spell.check', 'quill.spell.addWord', 'quill.spell.nextError']
```

Get a diagnostic summary, which is handy when you are asking for support:

```python
>>> q.support.diagnostic_summary()
```

#### Accessibility diagnostics

Hear again what QUILL last announced:

```python
>>> q.a11y.last_announcements()
['Title Case applied', '5 words selected']
```

Describe where focus is right now:

```python
>>> q.focus.describe()
'Editor: notes.txt, line 12, col 5, no selection'
```

#### Multi-line blocks

Press `Shift+Enter` to add new lines, then `Enter` or `Ctrl+Enter` to run the
block:

```python
>>> def count_words(text):
...     return len(text.split())
...
>>> count_words(doc.text)
487
```

#### Macro recording

You can record a run of commands as a macro and use it again later:

```python
>>> q.begin_macro("Clean OCR text")
>>> q.run_command("quill.text.normalizeUnicode")
>>> q.run_command("quill.text.dehyphenateLines")
>>> q.run_command("quill.text.reflowParagraphs")
>>> q.end_macro()
Macro saved: "Clean OCR text"
```

### TypeScript console

The TypeScript console needs Node.js on your PATH. If QUILL cannot find it, it
tells you so and offers to help you install it.

#### TypeScript prompt behavior

```text
ts> await quill.insertText("Hello.");
ts*>
Result: undefined
```

`ts>` means the console is ready. `ts*>` means an async operation is still in
flight. Results and errors land in the transcript by themselves.

#### Available globals

| Global | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `quill` | Async QUILL scripting proxy |
| `console` | Captured: `.log()`, `.warn()`, `.error()` appear in transcript |
| `setTimeout` / `clearTimeout` | Standard timer |
| `AbortController` | For cancellable operations |

#### Basic TypeScript operations

Insert text:

```ts
ts> await quill.insertText("Hello from TypeScript.");
```

Replace the selection:

```ts
ts> await quill.replaceSelection("Replacement text");
```

Jump to a line:

```ts
ts> await quill.gotoLine(42);
```

Run a built-in command:

```ts
ts> await quill.runCommand("quill.markdown.normalizeHeadings");
```

#### Inspecting state from TypeScript

```ts
ts> const doc = await quill.activeDocument();
ts> console.log(doc.name);
notes.txt
```

```ts
ts> const stats = await quill.documentStats();
ts> console.log(`${stats.words} words, ${stats.lines} lines`);
487 words, 38 lines
```

#### Multi-line TypeScript

Press `Shift+Enter` to build a block over several lines, then `Ctrl+Enter` to
run it:

```ts
ts> const text = await quill.getText();
ts> const words = text.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
ts> await quill.announce(`${words.length} words`);
```

#### TypeScript type definitions

QUILL comes with a file called `quill-console.d.ts`. If you have Node.js and a
code editor that understands TypeScript, copy the file into your project and
you get completion:

```ts
// quill is typed as:
interface QuillConsoleApi {
  insertText(text: string): Promise<void>;
  replaceSelection(text: string): Promise<void>;
  gotoLine(line: number): Promise<void>;
  runCommand(commandId: string, args?: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;
  activeDocument(): Promise<QuillDocumentSnapshot>;
  documentStats(): Promise<QuillDocumentStats>;
  announce(text: string): Promise<void>;
}
```

### Screen-reader notes

- New output in the transcript is announced, and focus stays where it is.
- Errors are announced starting with the word "Error".
- Return values are announced starting with the word "Result".
- Long output is summed up in the announcement. Read the transcript with your
  screen reader for the full text.
- `Ctrl+Shift+C` copies the transcript at any time.
- The console speaks through Prism, the same announcement path every other
  part of QUILL uses.
- Every control is a standard Windows control. Nothing is custom-drawn.

### Console safety settings

Open them with **Tools > Advanced > Developer Console > Console Safety
Settings**, or run the command `quill.console.openSafetySettings`.

| Setting | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python console enabled | Profile-dependent | Off for Essential / Casual Writer |
| TypeScript console enabled | Profile-dependent | Off except Developer profile |
| Require developer profile | On | Prevents accidental access in the Casual Writer profile |
| Max execution time (Python) | 30 s | Hard kill after timeout |
| Max execution time (TypeScript) | 30 s | Worker restart after timeout |
| Allow `wx` module access | Developer profile only | Not available in any other profile |
| Remote console | Locked off | Not available in QUILL 1.x |

### Transcript commands

You can run these from the Command Palette while the console is open.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `quill.console.copyTranscript` | Copy entire transcript to clipboard |
| `quill.console.saveTranscript` | Save transcript to a file |
| `quill.console.clear` | Clear the transcript |
| `quill.console.saveInputAsSnippet` | Save the current input as a named snippet |
| `quill.console.insertSnippet` | Insert a saved snippet into input |
| `quill.console.runSelection` | Run selected text in the transcript as a command |
| `quill.console.runCurrentDocument` | Run the active QUILL document as a script |
| `quill.console.showContext` | Print current snapshot values to transcript |
| `quill.console.resetNamespace` | Reset the Python namespace (clears all variables) |
| `quill.console.restartTypeScriptWorker` | Kill and restart the Node worker |

### For Quillin authors

The console is a good place to try out a Quillin while you build it. Load
your Quillin, open the Python console, and look at its manifest and the
commands it adds:

```python
>>> from quill.core.quillins.loader import get_loader
>>> loader = get_loader()
>>> ext = loader.get_extension("com.example.myextension")
>>> ext.manifest
ExtensionManifest(id='com.example.myextension', runtime='python', ...)
>>> ext.manifest.contributes.commands
(ExtensionCommand(id='ext.myext.run', title='My Command', ...),)
```

Run one of its commands straight through the command registry:

```python
>>> q.run_command("ext.myext.run")
```

Then check what it announced:

```python
>>> q.a11y.last_announcements()
['My command completed: 3 items processed']
```

For a Node.js Quillin, the TypeScript console is the natural place to test:

```ts
ts> await quill.runCommand("ext.myext.nodeHandler");
ts> // Check the last announcement
ts> const ann = await quill.lastAnnouncement();
ts> console.log(ann);
```

### What the console can and cannot do yet

The console is built and working under the Developer, Power Text and Full
QUILL profiles, at **Tools > Advanced > Developer Console**. Here is what you
get today:

- The Python console and its console window.
- The TypeScript console, running through a Node subprocess.
- The `q` scripting API: the text, navigation and command methods, plus the
  facades `q.selection`, `q.doc`, `q.editor`, `q.settings`, `q.profile`,
  `q.bookmarks`, `q.quillins`, `q.macros` (with `q.begin_macro` and
  `q.end_macro`), `q.spell`, `q.diagnostics`, `q.a11y`, `q.commands`,
  `q.focus` and `q.support`, plus `q.describe_command`.

Some examples in this appendix were written for a fuller API than the console
has today. If a call shown here does not work, the list above is the one to
trust. The full scripting contract, with its own map of what is implemented,
is in `docs/quillins.md`.

### Where to go next

The thinking behind the console, and the plans for it, are in Appendix E,
Developer Console design document. If you build Quillins, `docs/quillins.md`
is your reference.

## Appendix B: Writing skills for QUILL

This appendix shows you how to write, check and share your own skills. A skill
lives in a `.sqp` file (Skill Quill Pack). It is a multi-step AI workflow,
written in plain Markdown. If you can write a prompt, you can write a skill.

### What a skill is

A QUILL prompt is one instruction. A skill is a short conversation: a series of
instructions, where each step can see what the step before it produced.

A skill is the right tool when:

- You want to analyse your text first, then act on what the analysis found.
- You want to gather information in one step and write with it in the next.
- You want to check something (is this a question or a statement?) and go a
  different way depending on the answer.
- You want a better result on the same task, by giving the model context it
  built for itself in an earlier step.

### Your first skill

Create a file called `my-first-skill.sqp` and open it in QUILL. Type this in:

```markdown
---
schema: quill.skill/1
name: Explain Then Simplify
description: Explains the selected text in plain terms, then simplifies it further.
author: Your Name
version: 1.0.0
---

# Step 1: Explain

Explain the following text as if the reader has no prior knowledge. Use simple
vocabulary and short sentences. Aim for 50-80 words.

Text to explain:
{selection}

# Step 2: Simplify further

The explanation below is good, but we need it even simpler. Rewrite it so a
twelve-year-old would understand it immediately. Keep the core meaning.

Explanation to simplify:
{step1.output}

```output
format: text
label: Plain-language explanation
accept_into: clipboard
```
```

The part between the two `---` lines is the front matter: the skill's name and
details. Each line that starts with `# Step` begins a new step. `{selection}`
is your selected text, and `{step1.output}` is whatever step 1 produced.

Save the file, then check it with the validator:

```powershell
python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator my-first-skill.sqp
```

If all is well, you will see:

```
my-first-skill.sqp: OK
```

### Adding parameters

Parameters let the person running the skill choose options first. Before step 1
begins, QUILL shows a small dialog that asks for those choices.

Here is the same skill with a choice of reading level added:

```markdown
---
schema: quill.skill/1
name: Explain Then Simplify
description: Explains and simplifies selected text at a chosen reading level.
author: Your Name
version: 1.0.0
parameters:
  - name: level
    label: Target reading level
    type: choice
    choices: [Grade 4, Grade 6, Grade 8]
    default: Grade 6
---

# Step 1: Explain

Explain the following text so it is accessible at {parameters.level} reading level.
Use simple vocabulary and short sentences. Aim for 50-80 words.

Text to explain:
{selection}

# Step 2: Simplify further

Rewrite the explanation below to be even clearer. Target: {parameters.level}.
Keep the core meaning intact.

{step1.output}

```output
format: text
label: Plain-language explanation
accept_into: clipboard
```
```

Now `{parameters.level}` can be used in both steps. Its value is whatever the
user picked in the dialog.

There are five kinds of parameter:

| Type | UI control | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | Single-line text field | A keyword or name |
| `multiline` | Multi-line text area | A block of context |
| `choice` | Drop-down list | Reading level, tone, language |
| `bool` | Checkbox | Include citations: yes/no |
| `number` | Numeric field | Word count target |

### Using the input block

A long piece of text can bury the instruction it belongs to. The `input` block
adds the data after the instruction, so the step stays easy to read:

```markdown
# Step 1: Extract key claims

Read the following document and list the five most important claims it makes.
Number each claim. One sentence per claim.

```input
{document}
```
```

Without the `input` block you would write:

```markdown
# Step 1: Extract key claims

Read the following document and list the five most important claims it makes.
Number each claim. One sentence per claim.

Document:
{document}
```

Both do the same thing. The `input` block is just tidier when the data is long.

### Branching on an answer

A `condition` block sends the skill down one path or another, depending on what
a step produced.

```markdown
# Step 1: Detect intent

Read the following text. Is it asking a question, or making a statement?
Answer with exactly one word: "question" or "statement".

```input
{selection}
```

```condition
if: "{step1.output}" contains "question"
then: step2
else: step3
```

# Step 2: Answer the question

Answer this question clearly and concisely:
{selection}

```output
format: text
label: Answer
accept_into: clipboard
```

# Step 3: Expand the statement

Expand the following statement into a full paragraph with supporting detail:
{selection}

```output
format: text
label: Expanded statement
accept_into: clipboard
```
```

Here is what happens. After step 1 runs, QUILL checks the condition. If the
output contains "question", it jumps to step 2. Otherwise it jumps to step 3.
Whichever step runs last is the one that produces the result.

You can use these operators in a condition:

| Operator | Matches when |
| --- | --- |
| `contains` | Subject contains value (case-insensitive) |
| `equals` | Subject exactly matches value (case-insensitive) |
| `starts_with` | Subject starts with value |
| `ends_with` | Subject ends with value |
| `length_gt` | Subject length > number |
| `length_lt` | Subject length < number |
| `is_empty` | Subject is blank |

### Controlling the output

The `output` block on the last step decides what happens to the result.

```markdown
```output
format: text
label: Rewritten paragraph
accept_into: selection
```
```

It has three settings:

- `format`: `text` (the default), `list` (the AI should return a bulleted or
  numbered list), or `json` (the AI should return valid JSON).
- `accept_into`: what happens when the user presses Accept in the result
  dialog. `selection` replaces the current selection in the editor.
  `clipboard` copies the result to the clipboard. `none` just shows it,
  read-only (this is the default).
- `label`: the heading of the result dialog, so the user knows what they are
  reviewing.

### A complete example, Accessible Rewrite

Here is the "Accessible Rewrite" skill that comes with QUILL, in full.

```markdown
---
schema: quill.skill/1
name: Accessible Rewrite
description: Rewrites selected text for plain-language accessibility.
author: QUILL Project
version: 1.0.0
parameters:
  - name: reading_level
    label: Target reading level
    type: choice
    choices: [Grade 6, Grade 8, Grade 10, No target]
    default: Grade 8
---

# Step 1: Analyse accessibility issues

Review the following text for plain-language accessibility issues. List the
problems as a numbered list. Focus on: sentence length (over 25 words), passive
voice, unexplained jargon or acronyms, abstract nouns where concrete ones would
serve better, and complex nested clauses. Be concise — one clear problem per
line. If the text has no issues, say "No issues found."

```input
{selection}
```

# Step 2: Rewrite for accessibility

Rewrite the text below to fix the issues identified in Step 1. Requirements:
- Target reading level: {parameters.reading_level}
- Preserve all factual content
- Do not add new information

Original text:
{selection}

Issues to fix:
{step1.output}

```output
format: text
label: Rewritten text
accept_into: selection
```
```

Step 1 reads the text and makes a numbered list of problems. Step 2 gets that
list through `{step1.output}`, along with the original text, so the model knows
exactly what to fix. When the user presses Accept, the rewrite replaces the
selection.

### Checking your skill

Always run the validator before you share a skill:

```powershell
python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator my-skill.sqp
```

For a stricter check:

```powershell
python -m quill.tools.sqp_validator my-skill.sqp --strict
```

With `--strict`, it also warns you if `description` or `author` is missing.

These are the errors people meet most, and how to fix them:

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema must be 'quill.skill/1'` | Missing or wrong schema | Add `schema: quill.skill/1` to front matter |
| `front matter must include 'name'` | No `name:` field | Add `name: My Skill` |
| `must have at least one step` | No `# Heading` lines | Add at least one `# Step N:` heading |
| `{step3.output} references a step that hasn't run yet` | Forward reference | Steps can only reference outputs from earlier steps |
| `unknown parameter 'tone'` | Used `{parameters.tone}` but didn't declare it | Add `tone` to the `parameters` list in front matter |
| `output format 'xml' is invalid` | Bad `format:` value | Use `text`, `list`, or `json` |

### Sharing skills

A `.sqp` file is plain text, so you can share it the same way you share any
document. There are three ways it reaches other people:

- Through the Skill Library. Whoever receives your `.sqp` file imports it with
  **AI > Skill Library > Import .sqp**.
- Through a Quillin. If you look after a Quillin, put your `.sqp` files in the
  Quillin's folder. QUILL finds them on its own when the Skill Library loads.
- As a file on its own. A `.sqp` file holds everything it needs. Anyone can also
  open it in QUILL's editor to read it, understand it and change any step.

### Tips for writing good skills

- Be specific in each step. "List the five most important claims" works better
  than "What are the claims?" The model follows precise wording.
- Say exactly what you want back. Instead of "Summarise the following", write
  "Write a one-sentence summary of the following text. Return only the summary
  sentence, no preamble." Then `{step1.output}` holds just what you expect.
- Try it on short text first. Type two or three sentences into the editor,
  select them, and run the skill. Short text runs faster, and mistakes are
  easier to track down.
- Put long data in an `input` block. If the selection might be a whole
  document, put `{document}` in an `input` block instead of in the middle of
  the prompt. The step reads more cleanly.
- Give a branch its own detection step. If you are branching on whether the
  text is a question, a statement, a list or something else, let step 1 do only
  that sorting, and ask for a one-word answer. The tighter the answer, the more
  reliably the condition works.
- Choose `accept_into` on purpose. If the skill rewrites the selection, use
  `accept_into: selection`. If it makes something extra (a meeting summary, an
  outline), use `accept_into: clipboard`, so the user can paste it where they
  like. Use `none` for skills that only inform you (a grammar analysis, a
  readability score), where you read the result but do not insert it.

### Reference card

#### Front matter fields

| Field | Required | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema: quill.skill/1` | yes | none |
| `name: ...` | yes | none |
| `description: ...` | recommended | `""` |
| `author: ...` | recommended | `""` |
| `version: ...` | no | `1.0.0` |
| `parameters: [...]` | no | `[]` |

#### Variables

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `{selection}` | Selected editor text (full document if nothing selected) |
| `{document}` | Full document text |
| `{title}` | Document title |
| `{clipboard}` | Clipboard text at skill-start time |
| `{stepN.output}` | Output from step N (must be a lower-numbered step) |
| `{parameters.name}` | Value of a declared parameter |

#### Fenced block types

| Block | Where | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `` `input` `` | Any step | Appends data to the prompt |
| `` `condition` `` | Any step | Branch to `then`/`else` step after this step runs |
| `` `output` `` | Last step | Controls format, label, accept_into |
| `` `use-prompt` `` | Any step | Delegates to a named Prompt Library prompt |

#### Values at a glance

- Condition operators: `contains`, `equals`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`,
  `length_gt`, `length_lt`, `is_empty`.
- Output formats: `text`, `list`, `json`.
- Output accept_into values: `selection`, `clipboard`, `none`.

### Where to go next

Open the Skill Library from the **AI** menu and run one of the skills that come
with QUILL, then open its `.sqp` file and see how it was put together. Chapter
10, AI, when you want it, covers the rest of the assistant.

## Appendix D: Notes from earlier versions

This appendix keeps a record of how some parts of QUILL used to work. You
do not need any of it to use QUILL today. The chapters describe QUILL as
it is now, and where a note here disagrees with a chapter, the chapter is
right.

### Fixed in 0.7.0 Beta 2

The Beta 2 release brought a sweep of accessibility, macOS and crash fixes.
Where a fix changes nothing you can see, the note says so; where it does, the
note gives the detail. The full list is in the
[release notes](../release%20notes/release0.8.0-beta1.md).

- **Closing the last document no longer crashes.** Nothing to change. The
  crash showed up as "QUILL encountered an unexpected error and needs to
  close" when you pressed `Ctrl+W` on a document with unsaved changes, chose
  "Don't Save", and the editor was asked about the caret after it had already
  closed. QUILL now checks first, and you will not see that error any more.
- **Help > Check for Updates opens cleanly.** It used to fail with "QUILL
  encountered an unexpected error." Open **Help > Check for Updates** and the
  update channel selector appears as before.
- **The Setup Wizard opens on a clean window, not on top of an "Untitled"
  tab.** If you have already run the wizard, you see the normal "Untitled" tab
  when QUILL starts. On a first run you see the wizard on its own, and an
  untitled document is created for you when the wizard finishes.
- **`Cmd+Q` now quits QUILL on macOS.** The new default is `Ctrl+Q` (which is
  `Cmd+Q` on macOS). Quote Lines moved from `Ctrl+Q` to `Ctrl+Shift+Q` to make
  room, and Unquote Lines moved off `Ctrl+Shift+Q` (today it is on
  `Alt+Shift+.`). A saved `keymap.json` that still has
  the old keys is corrected the first time QUILL starts, and the correction is
  saved so the next start is clean.
- **`Option+Left` and `Option+Right` are no longer taken by Back and Forward
  Location on macOS.** On macOS, Back and Forward Location are now `Cmd+[` and
  `Cmd+]`, the usual Mac back and forward keys used by Safari, Finder and most
  other Mac apps. On Windows they stay on `Alt+Left` and `Alt+Right`. If your
  saved `keymap.json` on a Mac still has the Windows keys, it is changed to
  the new Mac keys the first time QUILL starts, and the change is saved so the
  next start is clean.
- **The Setup Wizard's page heading is the first thing that takes focus, and
  VoiceOver no longer calls the preview "edit text".** On every wizard page a
  screen reader now lands on the heading, not on the read-only preview. The
  preview is shown as a read-only document, so VoiceOver reads it as a
  document or plain text, not as an editable field. Sighted users see the same
  styled preview as before.
- **The wizard's Back and Next buttons are simply "Back" and "Next".**
  VoiceOver on macOS used to read the old labels ("< Back" and "Next >") as
  "less than Back" and "Next greater than". The buttons now read "Back" and
  "Next", which is what every screen reader says and what is printed on the
  button.
- **Read Aloud and Insert Snippet no longer fire when you type a plain `R` or
  `S`.** The key shown beside those items in the Tools and Insert menus was
  being treated as a real shortcut, so the plain letters R and S were caught
  everywhere. The key is now shown as ordinary text after the item name, and
  the letters belong to your writing again.
- **The Help menu is now the macOS system Help menu.** The usual `Cmd+?` Help
  shortcut now works on the Mac. Windows and Linux are unchanged.
- **AI Hub opens cleanly from the wizard, and the editor no longer trips over
  the caret before a document is loaded.** The AI Hub's tab labels and the
  wizard's AI Hub button had the same fault, and the editor failed silently on
  every keystroke before you had even opened a document.
- **JAWS, NVDA, Narrator and VoiceOver now say the QUILL version.** The window
  title now includes the full version (for example, "QUILL for All 0.7.0 Beta
  2"), so any screen reader that reads the window title (JAWS `Insert+T`, NVDA
  `+T`, Narrator `Caps+H`, VoiceOver) says the version along with the document
  name. JAWS's `Ctrl+JAWSKey+V` still says only "Version" until a launcher
  that carries the version ships; the window title is the change you can hear
  today.
- **VoiceOver now reads the editor as a normal text area on macOS.** The
  editor now tells macOS it is a standard text view (`NSTextView`), so
  VoiceOver treats it as an ordinary editable text area with all its usual
  reading commands. Windows is unchanged.
- **The Report a Bug dialog now speaks field names on macOS, opens in its own
  window so you can Alt+Tab to the editor, and no longer opens a browser by
  itself after you submit.** Every field is tied to its label, so VoiceOver
  reads "Summary, edit text", "What happened, edit text" and so on as you tab
  in. The dialog opens in its own window that does not block the editor. The
  report is always on your clipboard after you submit. Opening the browser
  afterwards is now something you turn on in Settings: "After you submit a bug
  report, automatically open the support form in your default browser".
- **`Ctrl+F4` on a document with unsaved changes no longer crashes when you
  choose "Don't Save".** The close prompt was trying to put focus back in the
  editor after the editor had already closed. Save and Cancel work as before,
  and Save still returns focus to the editor.
- **The print-page detector now treats a right-margin continuation as
  certain, and keeps the trailing letter.** In a braille document with
  print-page numbers in the right margin of line 1, the next braille page can
  carry the same number with a continuation letter (for example `7` on braille
  page 1 and `7a` on braille page 2). The print page has not changed; the
  letter is the braille continuation marker. The detector used to rate this
  as `medium` confidence and drop the letter, so the detailed status read
  `Print 7` instead of `Print 7a`. It now matches the previous page's
  right-margin number, rates the boundary `high` confidence, and keeps the
  letter. In practice: open a braille document with right-margin print-page
  numbers, move the caret across a continuation, and the status bar (and
  "Read Detailed Braille Status") reads the full `7a`, not just `7`.

### The original Copy Tray guide

This is the first guide to the Copy Tray, from when it had nine slots. The
Copy Tray now has twelve slots and opens with `Ctrl+Alt+V`. Chapter 4,
Writing and editing, describes it as it is today.

#### Overview

Copy Tray gives you nine independently addressable clipboard slots. Each slot
holds a piece of text that you copy there explicitly. Slots survive application
restarts -- their contents are written to disk automatically so nothing is lost
when you close and reopen QUILL.

Unlike the system clipboard, which is shared with every other application and
holds only the most recently copied item, Copy Tray slots are exclusive to
QUILL and hold their contents until you explicitly replace or clear them. This
makes Copy Tray well suited for accumulating related fragments across a long
editing session: quotes from multiple sources, code snippets, address blocks,
standard disclaimers, or any text you paste repeatedly.

#### Keyboard Access

##### Paste from a slot

Hold `Ctrl+Shift` and press a number key. That is all.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+1` | Paste from slot 1 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+2` | Paste from slot 2 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+3` | Paste from slot 3 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+4` | Paste from slot 4 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+5` | Paste from slot 5 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+6` | Paste from slot 6 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+7` | Paste from slot 7 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+8` | Paste from slot 8 at cursor |
| `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+9` | Paste from slot 9 at cursor |

If a selection is active when you paste, the pasted text replaces it.
If the slot is empty, QUILL announces "Slot N is empty".

##### Copy to a slot

Hold the QUILL key (`Ctrl+Shift+Grave`), release, then press `Shift+digit`.
The QUILL-key bare digits 1-6 are heading shortcuts; adding Shift is a distinct
binding with no conflict.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+1` | Copy selection to slot 1 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+2` | Copy selection to slot 2 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+3` | Copy selection to slot 3 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+4` | Copy selection to slot 4 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+5` | Copy selection to slot 5 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+6` | Copy selection to slot 6 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+7` | Copy selection to slot 7 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+8` | Copy selection to slot 8 |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Grave, Shift+9` | Copy selection to slot 9 |

You must have text selected. QUILL announces the slot number and a text
preview: "Copied to slot 2".

##### Management

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+Alt+V` | Open Copy Tray dialog |

All bindings are reassignable in `Tools > Customize & Support > Keymap Editor` or the Command
Palette.

#### Using the Edit Menu

All commands are available in `Edit > Copy Tray`. The submenu contains:

- `Copy to Slot 1` through `Copy to Slot 9` -- copy the current selection
- `Paste from Slot 1` through `Paste from Slot 9` -- paste at the cursor
- `Open Copy Tray...` -- open the management dialog
- `Clear All Tray Slots` -- clear all slots after confirmation

#### Using the System Tray Icon

Right-click the QUILL icon in the system notification area (bottom-right
taskbar area). The context menu includes a **Copy Tray** submenu that lists
every occupied slot with its label (if any) and a text preview. Clicking a slot
pastes its content into the currently active QUILL document. This lets you
paste from the tray without bringing the main window to the front.

#### Using the Dialog

Open the dialog with `Ctrl+Alt+V`, `Edit > Copy Tray > Open Copy
Tray`, or the Command Palette (`edit.open_copy_tray`). The dialog shows all
nine slots in a list. Each row displays:

- The slot number
- An optional label
- A preview of the stored text (empty slots show `(empty)`)

Navigate the list with the arrow keys. The following buttons appear below the
list:

- **Paste** (Enter or double-click) -- paste the selected slot's text at the
  cursor position and close the dialog. Disabled when the selected slot is
  empty.
- **Copy Selection Here** -- copy the current editor selection into the selected
  slot and refresh the list. Disabled when no text is selected in the editor.
- **Set Label...** -- open a text-entry prompt to name the selected slot. Labels
  appear in all slot listings and in screen-reader announcements.
- **Clear Slot** -- empty the selected slot. Disabled when already empty.
- **Close** (Escape) -- close the dialog without pasting.

#### Labelling Slots

Slot labels are optional but recommended for any slot you use regularly. A
label makes the slot identifiable in the dialog and in every spoken
announcement. Labelling slot 1 "signature" means you will hear "Pasted from
slot 1 (signature)" instead of "Pasted from slot 1".

To set a label:

1. Open the Copy Tray dialog.
2. Select the slot you want to label.
3. Press `Set Label...`.
4. Type the label and press Enter.

Labels are persisted alongside slot text and survive restarts.

#### Accessibility Notes

- Every Copy Tray operation announces its result through QUILL's screen-reader
  interface. Copy, paste, clear, and label operations all produce spoken
  feedback.
- The slot list in the dialog receives initial focus when the dialog opens.
- Slot labels, when set, are included in every announcement.
- Empty slots are clearly identified as `(empty)` in all contexts.
- The `Clear All Tray Slots` confirmation dialog defaults to No to prevent
  accidental data loss.
- The `Ctrl+Shift+N` paste scheme is designed for screen reader users: one
  familiar chord activates slot N instantly, no menu navigation required.

#### Tips

- **Research accumulator.** Assign each tray slot to a document section. Copy
  a relevant excerpt to each slot as you read through a source, then paste
  them in order when drafting.
- **Code boilerplate.** Keep import blocks, standard headers, and closing
  patterns in labelled slots for one-chord insertion.
- **Cross-document paste.** Copy a phrase to a tray slot, switch documents,
  paste from the tray -- the system clipboard is untouched.
- **Persistent library.** Slots survive restarts. Build a set of standard
  fragments you reach for daily.
- **System tray access.** Paste into any QUILL document directly from the
  notification-area icon without bringing the window to the front.
